12 Years a Slave is Steve McQueen's most Hollywood friendly and least symbolic movie to date, but it's by all means another masterpiece that is as heart wrenching as Hunger and as emotionally aching as Shame. Although 12 Years a Slave has the most eventful plot between his movies, McQueen still manages to pull out every single special touch of his; the long uncut steady shots, the very long dialogues with close ups on his actors faces, and mixing voiceovers, which all show his unique style and talent and cements him as one of the best filmmakers alive right now.

McQueen shares all the successes of his career with Michael Fassbender. Whether as the heroic riot who starves himself to death (literally and figuratively) in Hunger or as Brandon the self abusive sex addict in Shame, he carried the movies' weight on his shoulders as much as McQueen did. There is no difference about that this time around, in fact Fassbender gives one of the most complex and multi layered roles of his career and does that without any help from the dialogue or the camera angles, that he makes it feel like an easy task to be that invested into a character and to show such obsession without ever explaining it. The biggest difference that 12 Years a Slave offers from McQueen's body of work is that it's only Fassbender who carries its weight with him this time around. There is a whole star studded cast, with the likes of Brad Pitt, Benedict Cumberbatch, Paul Giamatti and Paul Dano all appearing in just a scene or two, who all deliver memorable performances, and they're all lead by a very genuine, powerful and precise performance from Chiwetel Ejiofor. There are several scenes in the movie where the camera only takes a long shot of his face, and that's enough for us to be emotionally there where Ejiofor's Solomon is and needs us to be, with only the look on his eyes explaining it all. And just when you think this movie has enough great performances and that it couldn't get any better than that, then comes Lupita Nyong'o, a first time actress who wipes every other actor with her in a scene away and demands your attention from the minute she appears on screen, she gives, easily, the best supporting actress performance of the year and proves to be a force to be reckoned with and an actress to watch for in the future.

The writing might seem abstract at times, but as the movie gets nearer to the end, the plot gets less eventful, which gives the space for the obvious character development and the long, skillfully written dialogues to take place. The cinematography by Sean Bobbit (Shame, Hunger, The Place Beyond the Pines) is beautiful, sensational, smart and creative as usual, especially in that one very long uncut scene where Patsey gets whipped, I can't even start imagining how many times it took them to perfect it that way and for the camera to catch all the needed emotions and not miss anything at the same time. Hans Zimmer's masterful score is a major player that made everything that's going around in that movie feel more emotional, have more meaning and sometimes gave you the idea of what's going to happen in the next scene.

Ha habido un crecimiento de películas que tratan de la esclavitud, lo cual es un avance hacia un mejor entendimiento y aceptación de este oscuro período en nuestra historia, y es importante que el tema no se mantenga enterrado. Películas como Django Unchained y The Butler muestran una realidad distinta respecto al tema, pero ninguna otra película como 12 Years a Slave logra capturar en una manera tan brutal los horrores de la esclavitud.

Steve McQueen tiene la habilidad de mostrar la brutalidad de estos capítulos en la historia, tal como hizo en Hunger, de una manera que es atroz pero a la vez que es casi sutil. Logra explorar estos dos extremos y lograr la mezcla perfecta. 

La historia de Solomon Northrup, que está basada en una historia real, es poderosa y dolorosa. Solomon fue engañado al ser secuestrado para ser vendido como un esclavo, y fue forzado a dejar su libertad y a su familia atrás. El contraste entre él y los demás esclavos es sorprendente, ya que la mayoría ya habían perdido cualquier esperanza, al estar en esta situación por muchos años, y es impresionante ver lo rápido que Solomon va perdiendo su espíritu, y muestra lo fácil que es desmoralizar un hombre. 

12 Years a Slave es una película hermosa en cuanto a fotografía y imágenes, que contrasta con el horror de la violencia y heridas. Las actuaciones son igualmente trágicas, como la de Lupita Nyong'o (Patsy) que a pesar de ser su primera película logra capturar el dolor de la manera más real posible, y Michael Fassbender es el hombre más cruel, su carisma y falta de consciencia sólo lo hacen peor, y por supuesto Chiwetel Ejiofor como Solomon, que dio la actuación de su vida, y es difícil imaginar otro actor que hubiera logrado un trabajo tan impecable.

12 Years a Slave en mi opinión es 
la película más completa y mejor lograda sobre esclavitud, y debería ser obligatoria para todos de ver.

"12 Years a Slave" dirigida por Steve McQueen ("Shame", 2011) se podrá catalogar -incluso cuando se trata de la segunda película con posibilidad de nominación al Oscar que he visto- como la mejor de todas, basándome en la excelente dirección de McQueen y el protagonismo de Chiwetel Ejiofor, sin dejar de lado los actores secundarios Michael Fassbender y la increíble revelación Lupita Nyong'o. 
Estoy seguro de que Chiwetel Ejiofor merece la nominación a Mejor Actor, así como de la misma forma Michael Fassbender y Lupita Nyong'o la nominación a Mejor Actor y actriz de reparto. Pero me atrevo a decir, que merecen ganar. ¡GANAR! Como todavía no se dan a conocer als nominaciones a los premios de La Academia, me basaré con Los Globos de Oro (sabiendo que estos no son confiables y le podrían dar el premio a Jennifer Lawrence o Bradley Cooper, que, incluso aún que no he visto "American Hustle" del estafalario David O. Russell, puedo apostar a que NO fueron tan buenos como el elenco de "12 Years a Slave"). Ahora, mi preocupación más grande es MEJOR DIRECTOR, ¿lo merece? ¡Claro que sí! Vamos a darle un gran premio a McQueen que ha crecido inmensamente en su última película.
Aunque la historia no nos envuelva en absoluta acción, la película es perfectamente capaz de transmitir sentimientos y una indudable excelente dirección, un gran elenco y sin duda, con la historia MERAMENTE REAL que demuestran, nos transporta -tal vez no a algo muy agradable-, al 1800's y pico, donde la crueldad del ser humano no tiene límites y el negro debe ser sumiso a sus leyes. Aquí, todo tiene su simbolismo. Tal vez la crueldad y la rudeza de la proyección es lo que más acapara la perfección del filme.
Brad Pitt hace un cameo, no llega a los diez minutos en las dos partes que aparece, pero él es la esperanza para Platt, lo cual resulta aún más esperanzador, ya que él es un hombre blanco. 
Es una película bien hecha, para muchos resultará un relato más acerca de negros esclavos, para otros representa HISTORIA. Nadie puede vivir bajo la ley del hombre, el hombre NO tiene palabra contra su misma raza. Cada vez que veo una película como esta, cuando ya no se trata de racismo, sino de odio, de algo que realmente sucedió, es cuando me convenso más de que muho de lo que se juzga en la actualidad, no es más que ignorancia.

12 YEARS A SLAVE is one of the most uncomfortable viewing experiences I've had in recent memory. It wasn't because I felt guilty for something my ancestors may (or may not) have had responsibility for, but because occasionally I felt that the movie wallowed in its own misery. It also felt exploitative and emotionally manipulative at times. That said, if one does not come away from this absolutely detesting slavery as an institution, there is something truly wrong with you. Fortunately, this story has a happy(ish) ending. Otherwise, the oppressive atmosphere might have choked all the life out of the story. On a technical level, the movie is astounding. Steve McQueen is an auteur to watch, now having three critically praised films under his belt. I also loved the score by Hans Zimmer, which was stark when it needed to be, but also filled with tenderness and longing. There are also several Negro spirituals peppered throughout which were also uplifting. Overall, this is a must-see film, not just because it's won a lot of awards, but because it treats a touchy subject with the honesty it deserves. However, I wouldn't watch it more than once unless you're a glutton for punishment.

Brutal, harrowing, unflinching, and ultimately hopeful are just a few of the (many) ways to describe Steve McQueen's 12 Years A Slave. The Academy's pick for the film of 2013 is a powerhouse of acting talent, incredible storytelling, and passionate filmmaking, rife with stunning vistas and scenes of stomach-churning cruelty.

In the year 1841, Solomon Northup (Chiwetel Ejiofor) is a free black man living in Saratoga, New York. Husband to a loving wife, and father to two children, Northup works as a carpenter, in addition to his work as a skilled fiddle-player. He is a beloved figure in his community, and has attracted the ire of no one.

That changes, however, when he meets Hamilton and Brown (Taran Killam and Scoot McNairy), two circus promoters who offer Northup a job playing the fiddle for two weeks, in exchange for fair pay. Unable to refuse such a lucrative offer, Northup agrees, departing for Washington with the two men. There, he has dinner with the pair, before becoming sick and passing out. Northup awakens in chains, about to be shipped to New Orleans. In one of the film's most-brutal scenes, Northup is viciously beaten for protesting his captivity, before being renamed 'Platt', the identity of a runaway slave.

Before long, Northup is in the hands of a remorselessly cold slave trader (a tour-de-force scene for Paul Giamatti), who sells the rechristened Platt to a benevolent plantation owner, William Prince Ford (Benedict Cumberbatch). From there, Northup's journey truly begins.

Wow, where to start with 12 Years A Slave? It is quite easily the best film I've seen of 2013, and that's against technical groundbreaker Gravity, moody thriller Prisoners, and sensory joy Rush. On all levels, 12 Years A Slave wows, from it's incredible acting, to it's brutally-real direction, to it's palpably-realistic writing. There is little, if anything, to complain about.

Chiwetel Ejiofor (best known for his work on the stage, where he is among the greatest of his generation) delivers a towering performance as Solomon Northup. The struggle to retain his dignity, while managing to survive in the face of unimaginable cruelty is played out on his face and in his voice. Fear laces his every vocalisation, with undercurrents of a strength, and will to push forward, no matter the cost. It is difficult for many a great actor to truly express absolute, unfettered desperation, but Ejiofor pulls it off brilliantly. I'm sure Matthew McConaughey was more-than-deserving of his award, but Ejiofor too would have been an excellent recipient.

And if that's not enough praise, consider this: He is overshadowed by a co-star! Ejiofor goes to hell and back as his character, but it's The Devil that truly ignites the screen. Michael Fassbender (Shame, Hunger) delivers a searing, oft-terrifying and always-mesmerising performance as Edwin Epps, the blackhearted plantation owner that takes in Northup following his departure from the Ford Plantation. "He is a hard man. Prides himself on being a 'nigger-breaker'" says the kindly Ford of Epps, but not even that can represent the monstrosity we are about to meet.

Fassbender provides the most-cruel, callous, truly horrifying vision of unrepentant evil I've seen in film since I don't know when. I love Fassbender as an actor - I think he's one of the most daring, purely-talented actors working today - and when he's on his game, he is on. This is perhaps the finest example. As Edwin Epps, Fassbender is a melting pot of bigotry, hatred, and ignorance in it's most basic form, reverting to an animalistic nature he displays at moments of great frustration. I mentioned that Ejiofor lets his guard down to play a truly desperate man, and the same goes for Fassbender here, only his is a portrayal of depthless hatred and pure villainy. He too lost out on an Oscar last night, but I wouldn't be surprised if he was a close runner-up.

And of course, the supporting cast is a perfect frame for the clash at the centre of the film. Lupita Nyong'o deservedly took home an Oscar for her role as the hopeless, truly-defeated Patsey, apple of Epps' eye. In the most eye-opening scene of the film, Nyong'o wrenches the hearts and minds of cinemagoers everywhere, sealing her as the pick for Best Supporting Actress. Sarah Paulson too, delivers a knockout, as Mary Epps, domineering wife of Edwin. Her jealousy of Patsey, and hatred of Edwin's lust adds a startling amount of depth to the couple, as well as showcasing Paulson as the reason behind Epps' cruelty.

Others come in and out in glorified cameos, from Paul Dano (a rising star and notable member of Prisoners' cast), Benedict Cumberbatch (best known as TV's Sherlock), and Paul Giamatti all deliver the goods as their respective characters.

And what better to portray a time of such depravity than some of the most beautiful cinematography of the year? Sean Bobbitt wisely employed a widescreen format to convey the grandiosity of Solomon's journey, and accurately represented the vibrant colours of the south (a stark contrast to the horrors committed therein). Oftentimes, McQueen (a very laid-back director, who allows us time to soak in the often-contradictory prettiness of his vistas) spends an inordinate amount of time lavishing us with gorgeous shots of the landscape, before delving into the savagery of the material. It's this toying with our emotions that continues the emotional rollercoasterdom of the film.

This is certainly a raw, passionate, indescribably powerful film (if not as immediately hard-hitting as McQueen's previous effort (with Fassbender), Shame. Nevertheless, under his watchful eye, the film comes together stunningly well. The score by Hans Zimmer (notably restrained here, in comparison to his virtuoso work on 2013's Rush) is well-placed, punctuating Northup's struggle suitably well. The production design is sparkling, providing the film's scenes with an eerie, painted feel. The cast is uniformly marvelous, and the cinematography couldn't be better.

So what have we learned? Aside from a rarely-seen look into the darkest recesses of man's capacity for cruelty, we have witnessed the incredible story of one man's ability to survive and to hope, another's to coerce and torture,  the kindness even a stranger can impart upon another. There are many miraculous things going on in 12 Years A Slave. About hope, kindness, courage and cruelty, and for all those, and so much more, it is without a doubt the best film of 2013.

Final Grade: A+

12 Years a Slave is one of the most unflinching movies I have seen in my entire life. It holds a mirror up to the institution of slavery and forces you to watch the horrors that happened during that period of American history. I think sometimes films try to portray what slavery was actually like, but they add in too much sentimentality and they basically "Hollywoodize" it. Almost like they're excusing what happened. Here there is none of that. This film takes a hard look at slavery and at times it is quite difficult to watch. The main reason this film works so well is through the performances, more specifically Chiwetel Ejiofor as Solomon Northup. This is one of those performances that simply exists. While I was watching this movie I didn't see an actor playing Solomon Northup, I simply saw Solomon Northup. As the film went on I found myself just wanting things to be okay. I wanted him to get through this even though the odds are stacked against him. Ejiofar gives such an amazing and understated performance that I would be absolutely shocked if he doesn't get a Best Actor Nomination, if not win. For every protagonist there is an antagonist and in this film it is Michael Fassbender's Edwin Epps. He is utterly terrifying in this role. The way he portrays this completely evil man makes you ashamed with humanity. To me his performance was very reminiscent of Ralph Fiennes in Schindler's List. Just wholly deplorable. The other members of the supporting cast were great as well. I can't go into talking about all of them because the cast list is as long as my arm. However I do want to mention Sarah Paulson specifically. I went into this movie knowing Ejiofar and Fassbender were going to be good, but Paulson's performance came out of nowhere and really impressed me. She was just as terrifying as Fassbender, but not in the same way. He was very abusive physically and verbally, but she just had this eerie calmness to her that made her lines even more shocking. Everything out of her mouth seemed like it was laced with venom and wow she was good. Another aspect that made this film feel so incredibly real was the directing. I was a fan of Steve McQueen's previous film, Shame, and this one is even better in my opinion. The cinematography in this movie is immaculate. Every shot feels necessary, and perfect for what the film is trying to accomplish. There are a couple of shots in this film that it is almost impossible to watch without looking away. It truly feels that real and intense. The only aesthetic that bothered me was the score. Hans Zimmer scored it, and it is at times too bombastic and distracting. Zimmer just can't seem to help himself. Perhaps the weakest part, though still excellent, was the writing and the plot. There were times when I felt like we were moving from one situation to another. All the singular events didn't feel like a cohesive narrative at times, but not enough to hinder the overall experience. Though not a perfect film, it is one of the most important of the last decade. It is imperative for people to watch this movie because American slavery is often swept under the rug. Watching this film forces you to confront the past head on and recognizing its significance is the only way to truly grow as a society. Everyone go see 12 Years A Slave now because I promise this film will go down as one of the most culturally important films ever.

A harrowing and occasionally brutal experience, 12 YEARS A SLAVE captures the horrors of slavery in an utterly unflinching fashion.  As directed by Steve McQueen, the film features two of the stand-out performances of 2013, as well as a surprisingly low-key and measured tone that makes the brutality all the more effective and pronounced. As Solomon Northup, our protagonist, Chiwetel Ejiofor gives a tremendous and moving performance.  Obviously the particulars of the (true) story make him an incredibly sympathetic figure to begin with, but Ejiofor doesn't take that for granted; he earns the audience's sympathy through his delicate work, and the pay-off at the end of the movie is as satisfying and affecting a conclusion as I've seen all year.The more explosive performance of the movie belongs to Michael Fassbender, playing the slave owner for whom Northup ends up enslaved.  Fassbender is utterly magnetic, and he manages to wrap the character's deeply evil deeds inside a complex, all-too-human psyche, which grounds the evil in a realistic - rather than over-the-top or silly - way.  The remainder of the roles in the cast are filled-out by an impressive roster of actors.  Brad Pitt, Pauls Giamatti and Dano, Benedict Cumberbatch, and particularly Lupita Nyong'o (in a heartbreaking performance) all show up to one degree or another.  Granted, some of these are glorified cameos, but they all feel of-a-piece, and they don't distract from the issue at hand. Speaking of that issue, the film's treatment of the issue of slavery is highly commendable.  We all know that it remains the darkest section of American history, but it's another thing to see the casual, almost perfunctory ways in which the slaves where belittled, abused, and murdered.  It's tough to watch at times, but it's necessary to witness it.  As with SCHINLDER'S LIST before it, 12 YEARS A SLAVE should (one day) be used as a teaching tool for younger generations, and in that respect, it's an incredibly important film. All of that having been said... I don't think the film is unassailable, or perfect, or "The Best Film of the Year!"  McQueen's direction is workmanlike, which is fine, but on a cinematic/technical level, there's nothing truly exceptional here.  It's very good work, no question, but I think the reactions in the film criticism intelligentsia are more a reflection of the movie's importance than its cinematic prowess.  That, I suppose, is valid... to one extent or another. That's not to downplay the movie's merits in the slightest.  It comes with my highest recommendation because it's vitally important that people - on occasion - be confronted with some of the less-honorable parts of our country's past, and even if its subject matter alone can't entice you to see it, go for Ejiofor and Fassbender; they're as good as any performances you'll see this year.

Chiwetel Ejiofor stars as Soloman Northup, a free black musician living with his equally free wife and kids in New York. While traveling with a supposed band he is kidnapped in Washington D.C. and forced into slavery, where he encounters a number of different charactered slaves and slaveowners all while trying to find a way to regain his freedom and get back to his family.

Despite being only the third feature film directorial effort by director Steve McQueen, the film is expertly crafted. McQueen utilizes lingering shots and angling to amplify the intensity and brutality of the true story.

With a stacked and talented supporting cast including Paul Giamatti, Benedict Cumberbatch, Michael Fassbender, and Brad Pitt it would have been easy for the (relative) unknown Ejiofor to get lost in the shuffle and upstaged, however he more than held his own and stole the film up to the point when Michael Fassbender was introduced. Since the movie came out rumors have been running rampant about Fassbender getting physically ill due to his portrayal being so brutal, and whether that is true or not, it is believable. If he will accept it Fassbender deserves a best supporting actor nomination for his role, while Ejiofor deserves a best leading actor nomination. Both brought an unbelievable amount of emotion to their portrayals (Ejiofor bringing pain and anguish, Fassbender bringing brutality). 

Overall, the film was immensely brutal and troubling that it was all based on actual events, and it was truly a film to behold. However, despite having nothing bad to say, I can't give it a perfect rating, or necessarily recommend it, because it's such an intense film (even making me cringe multiple times) and definitely not for the faint of hear. I also can't see myself watching it many (if any) more times, if you think it is something that won't disturb you, absolutely go see it.

As Brad Pitt's character Bass states after hearing Solomon Northup (Chiwetel Ejiofor) recount the story of how he was wrongly kidnapped and sold into slavery, this is an amazing story, but in no good way. There has been much made of director Steve McQueen's third feature that adapts the autobiography of Solomon Northup and takes an unflinching look at how slavery and ownership dominated the south and was inflicted upon the unfortunate souls born into that time period. Northup's tale is one of emotional and physical devastation and the success of the film hinges on being able to convey both of those impressions with equal weight. If there is an ideal director to take on this stark subject matter it would be the fresh pair of eyes and mind that is McQueen who, after his previous two films (Hunger and Shame) has focused on the downsides of humanity enough to understand where he needed to go to reach the emotional depths that the subject of slavery needs to take on. It is a subject that deserves this unflinching look illustrating how slaves were treated, how they were perceived, and how some plantation owners saw them and treated them as employees while others saw them as little more than property they could with what they please. 12 Years A Slave doesn't dive into the politics of what started slavery, why these white owners saw these people as they did, or how our main characters might put a stop to the tragedy, but instead we are forced to accept the facts that define our history and that is the true story of Solomon. Neither Solomon nor any of the slaves he comes to meet along the way knew why there were some slavers like William Ford (Benedict Cumberbatch) and others like Edwin Epps (Michael Fassbender), why it all began or how it was going to come to an end, but they simply had to accept the idea that this was their life and that they were meant to deal with it and that harsh reality is what McQueen forces his audience to accept as well with the only glimmer of hope being implied by the title. This is a film both so involving and at the same time so draining that you feel exhausted after having experienced it. It is a damn tough film to watch, but a necessary lesson in perspective that ultimately makes you appreciate what you've seen if not for the unflinching history lesson, but for the craft in which it is conveyed.

"Quite possibly the greatest movie ever made about American slavery"
Movie Review: 12 Years a Slave
Date Viewed: November 11 2013
Directed By Steve McQueen (Shame)
Screenplay By John Ridley, based on the autobiography by Solomon Northup.
Starring: Chiwetel Ejiofor, Michael Fassbender, Benedict Cumberbatch, Paul Dano, Paul Giamatti, Sarah Paulson, Lupita Nyong'o, Garret Dillahunt, Brad Pitt, Alfre Woodard, Adepero Oduye, Scoot McNairy, Taran Killam, Chris Chalk, Jay Huguley and Michael Kenneth Williams.

"12 Years a Slave" is the best movie of the year. It is easily the greatest movie movie ever made about American slavery. It is not a usual sentimental history lesson like "Lincoln" or "Lee Daniels' The Butler" or a bloody revenge tale like "Django Unchained", "12 Years a Slave" is a stunning historical tragedy that shows you what truly happened in slavery in 19th Century America.

"12 Years a Slave" takes place in 1841 and it is based on the true story of Solomon Northup (Chiwetel Ejiofor), a free black man living in Saratoga Springs, New York. He lives with his wife and two children and he works as a skilled carpenter and he is also a violin player. After two men (Scoot McNairy and Taran Killam) lure Solomon for a night out in Washington, D.C., Solomon wakes up and he finds himself chained to the floor. Solomon realizes he has been drugged and is sold into slavery.

Solomon is know named "Platt" and is transported by to New Orleans, where he is purchased by plantation owner William Ford (Benedict Cumberbatch). Northup soon learns to adopt into his new life and he stays on good terms with Ford even though one of Ford's workers John Tibeats (Paul Dano) resents and hates him. Northup is soon bought by another plantation owner, a more racist and abusive planter named Edwin Epps (Michael Fassbender). Northup's latest job is to pick cotton out from the fields, where he is expected to pick out 200 pounds of cotton each day. Northup soon befriends a young female slave named Patsey (Lupita Nyong'o), she picks out the most cotton than any of her workers. Patsey also gets abused and raped by Epps, but Epps' wife Mary (Sarah Paulson) is even more cruel to Patsey, she also abuses Patsey and she wants her thrown out of the plantation.

A Canadian carpenter named Bass (Brad Pitt) is soon hired by Epps but Bass soon expresses his opposition to slavery. Northup tells Bass about his life and kidnapping and Bass soon orcastrates his escape. 

Director Steve McQueen (Hunger and Shame) has delivered an emontional and powerful movie. He delivers a film filled with anger, rage, fear, horror, hatred, tragedy and sadness. "12 Years a Slave" maybe painful and heartbreaking to watch but many people felt the same way about Steven Spielberg's "Schindler's List" (another tragic historical lesson) when it came out 20 years ago. Solomon Northup's autobiography was adapted for the screen by John Ridley (Red Tails) but I can't help but give most of the credit to McQueen, He is in full command of the story and this movie is not just great, it is a masterpiece. 

Chiwetel Ejiofor a well known character actor in movies like "Inside Man", "American Gangster", "Children Of Men", "Talk To Me", "2012" and "Salt" gives one of the most powerful performances of the year. I don't know what he was thinking about when he took the most challenging performance of his career, but I think he was ready for this part. He is absolutely compelling. Michael Fassbender creates one of the sadistic and vicious historical characters I've ever seen. He is more powerful I think than Ralph Fiennes' nazi lieutenant from "Schindler's List". My one holdout going into "12 Years a Slave" wasn't its director, Steve McQueen, a filmmaker who in every regard deserves the title "visionary". It was screenwriter John Ridley, whose past credits include "Undercover Brother" and "Red Tails" (remember it? You and no one else.) Another big 2013 film whose script was also a reservation for me was "Gravity's" by Alfonso Cuaron and his son Jonas. But in that case Cuaron is such a herald he was able to twist, tweak and fine-tune even the most melodramatic aspects of that space adventure into something literally out of this world. And though Ridley's script is chill and all (groovy even) judging from his previous work my guess is McQueen is a good filter. Adapting from Solomon Northup's 1853 memoir of the same name -- the wicked tale of a free black man (played with a flawless mix of rage and eternal disbelief by Chiwetel Ejiofor) drugged, kidnapped and sold into slavery -- "12 Years a Slave" is a tale that inherently idles between beauty and pain, sweat and tears.

McQueen's two preceding features -- his near-masterpiece "Hunger" and his flat-out one "Shame" -- found redemption ironically in their protagonists' own self-infliction, the way out of twin tunnel-vision nightmares in the bleak acceptance that nothing was, and ever could be, the same. So maybe it makes sense to hold out on "12 Years a Slave" -- it's McQueen's first feature where the demons swelter from the outside world, getting under its center character's skin to the diminutive point of second-nature survival. It cuts so figuratively and literally to the bone without ever becoming blind to the bloodshed. Like "Gravity's" Dr. Stone, we don't need a bubble of personal history to shadow Northup in order to feel for him. And we ultimately don't get any later history at all -- his date, place and cause of death remain unknown. Twelve years of torture doesn't have to be the means to an end. Because "12 Years" -- the greatest film ever made about American slavery in the capital-s South -- is powerful and haunting enough to blister open the discussion of possible new beginnings. (97/100)

It's not easy to watch by any means, but 12 Years a Slave is an emotional tour de force that is arguably the greatest slavery film ever made and essential viewing for just about everyone. In a minimalistic style typical of director Steve McQueen's work, he pulls no punches and depicts slavery with brutal realism and a complete lack of sentimentality.

	12 Years a Slave is structured as a sprawling epic following Solomon Northup (Chiwetel Ejiofor), a free black man living in New York who is kidnapped and sold into slavery. As Solomon is sent from plantation to plantation, he is introduced to the horrors of slavery just as the audience is, giving the story a first-person perspective that only serves to make it more intense.

	Like Steve McQueen's previous two films Shame and Hunger, 12 Years a Slave features flawless performances from every single member of its star-studded cast. Although Chiwetel Ejiofor isn't exactly a household name, it really should be, because Ejiofor gives one of the most raw and powerful performances of the year as Solomon Northup. Ejiofor, who was previously known primarily for his roles in the criminally underrated science-fiction drama Children of Men and American Gangster, demonstrates the kind of acting ability that rivals that of the best actors working today. Speaking of the best actors working today, frequent McQueen collaborator Michael Fassbender plays a remorseless slave owner and he is at the top of his game. Fassbender's grotesquely cruel character is transfixing in his evil, yet he has depth and a wider range of emotion that makes him even more frighteningly real (and he is real, as the film is based on a true story). Fassbender is in my top five favorite actors because of his performances in films like 12 Years a Slave. His acting is so intense that he literally passed out on camera while filming one of the more disturbing scenes, and that take is used in the film. Paul Dano's character is equally if not more appalling than Fassbender's. Unlike Fassbender's psychotic character, Dano's doesn't demonstrate emotional depth beyond his violent hatred for slaves; his only desire is to break Solomon's will to live. I could go on about how great all the other actors are, but I'd be wasting your time; there is not a single performance that is anything short of mesmerizing.

	Of course, this wouldn't be a Steve McQueen film without hauntingly gorgeous cinematography full of beautifully framed shots that linger for extended periods of time. 12 Years a Slave is the kind of film that has camerawork that is genuinely memorable, as strange as that may sound. There are stationary shots that last for minutes at a time, and one particularly powerful image halfway into the movie will undoubtedly leave an imprint on every viewer's mind for a number of reasons, not the least of which is because the shot lasts for nearly five minutes.

	12 Years a Slave isn't necessarily the type of film that you're going to love and cherish and buy on Blu-ray to show all your friends. It's more likely that you'll watch it once, think it was astounding and incredibly well made, and then vow never to watch again. It's a very uncomfortable film, but a very necessary one. Although it's easy to claim that it's just about slavery and racism, its themes of cruelty and faith are wholly universal and more than anything else it shows the horrific acts that humans are capable of committing against one another. Don't expect to feel uplifted afterwards, but 12 Years a Slave is a work of intense dedication from everyone involved that shines through as an unforgettable artistic triumph.

With 12 Years a Slave comes a dour and distressing story about Solomon Northup, a freedman and a talented violinist, who was kidnapped one night and sold into slavery.  This true story vividly captures his struggles and grueling journey through a very dark time.  Now, black slavery has recently become a relevant topic even though it mostly no longer exists, but several films have released nonetheless, forcing us to relive the horrors that beset a once troubled race.  As a matter of forewarning, this film is raw and relentless in its presentation for it's bound to disturb and place you in a level of discomfort that's rarely visited.  You will be forced, as a viewer, to witness atrocious scenes of torture and whippings specifically as misty blood sprays into the air and the sight of deep and thick cuts makes you cringe to no end.  By the end of the film, half of the theater was in tears, blowing their noses and withdrawing their tissues.  It was certainly difficult to bear the missed opportunities and even larger troubles in a stricter environment.  

         Ultimately, the most crucial services to the power of this picture relates to its performances.  Chiwetel Ejiofor, Michael Fassbender, and Lupita Nyong'O all putting in terrific effort and fully exhausting us with deep emotion.  In addition, the rest of the supporting cast features the likes of Brad Pitt, Paul Dano, Paul Giamatti, Alfre Woodard, Benedict Cumberbatch, and more- very impressive indeed.    At the rolling of its credits, we are officially drained of any sense of happiness.  Though the film isn't economic and takes its time with some ironic shots of beauty and others of a grim terrain, it's mercilessly saddening once its content fully sinks in and you understand the "bigger picture."  The film's pacing relaxes in certain moments as particularly lengthy shots are utilized in order to realistically depict a situation, excluding any cinematic distractions.  As I've mentioned before, this method produces the kind of footage that's raw and gritty; a scene will persist as it's gradually encompassed by a hopeless tone and hurtful details.  

         What packs the punch to the fullest extent of emotion is the incredible score by Hans Zimmer.  It does sound a bit like Inception's soundtrack, but it's undoubtedly effective in its complement to a disheartening segment.  "I survive!  I will not fall into despair...I will kick myself harder until freedom is opportune."  Powerful words are spoken, and although a film with such subject matter could've easily hit the point of excessive sentimentality and corny dialogue, the conversations actually carry some very strong points.  This experience is arguably an incredibly important one, which is likely why it's garnering this amount of praise and hype.  

          The treatment of the white supremacist race towards a seemingly dissimilar kind can apply to any generation of our history and though the relationship isn't nearly as cruel, the feeling of utter discrimination is what faces both immigrants and homosexuals in contemporary times.  Frankly, it's fascinating how modern peoples remain disgusted by these practices, but if you were to somehow teleport them to the age of slavery, would they feel exactly the same way?  Racism has not ceased to exist, and most of the informed and aware would surely agree.  Hopefully, this film will stir awareness within the more ignorant and prejudiced; I won't point any fingers, but you know. Most likely the film to beat in 2013, 12 Years a Slave is a courageous, stunning and graphically brutal depiction of a dark time in our nation's past that should never be forgotten.  It is not easy to watch but I don't believe it should be either.  It is the true story of free man Solomon Northup (Chiwetel Ejiofor - Dirty Pretty Things) who -- in the mid 1800s -- is duped by some seemingly nice guys to accompany them to Washington DC where they have asked him to play his violin for polite society as they secretly wish to apprehend him and sell him back into slavery.  Which they do ... to horrifying results over a 12-year span for Solomon.  Leaving behind a wife and two young children on the outskirts of NYC, Solomon is sold to a somewhat benevolent plantation owner (Benedict Cumberbatch - 'Sherlock') in Louisiana who takes a liking to the slave's musical ability; but the resentment Solomon encounters at the hands of the master's racist and uber-ignorant slave-driver, Tibeats (Paul Dano - There Will Be Blood), requires Solomon to be transferred to another plantation to spare his life.  His new master and missus are nowhere as kind as his previous one and it is here he befriends a young slave named Patsey (a FANTASTIC Lupita Nyong'o making her debut) who has won the unwanted eye of their master, Edwin Epps (Michael Fassbender - Shame), making Epps' wife (Sarah Paulson -- 'American Horror Story') quite the jealous, intolerant one.  Solomon and Patsey merely "survive" the rest of the film ... as my jaw dropped a few times and tears streamed down my cheeks rather freely (much freer than either Patsey or Solomon).  The acting is outstanding and I'd nominate Ejiofor, Fassbender, Nyong'o and Paulson in their respective categories.  The film is rather grapic but saying that I still think the film wasn't as off-putting as it could have been in some of these scenes.  My face was turned to the side a time or two to avert seeing what was onscreen and my body pushed firmly into the back of my theater seat as I tried to remove myself from what I was seeing; but ... poor me I realized in disgust.  12 Years a Slave should be seen ... it is a new Schindler's List-of-a-movie.  Oscar will see it and reward it.

REVIEW OF "12 YEARS A SLAVE"

I saw this at Century Boulder last night, in the jam-packed Theater 9.  But the audience and I were dead silent from the opening scene to the closing credits.  Why?  Because the story was that powerful, that gripping, that tense, that profound.  The director, Steve McQueen III (no relation that THAT SMcQ, this one's a Brit) uncovered a long out-of-print 1853 memoir (with the movie's title) and turned it into this year's Oscar front-runner.  The original memoir was written by the central figure in it, Soloman Northrup, a free black man with a lovely wife and two seemingly-perfect kids from Saratoga Springs, NY.  Soloman was a talented fiddle player and made a good living playing it.  Two self-described fellow musicians, both whites, lured him down to New Orleans on the pretext of a job playing gigs with their traveling band, but they actually worked for a slave-trader who, with their help by spiking his drinks, sold Soloman to a Louisiana plantation owner (Benedict Cumberbach), a decent man who treated his slaves with humanity. 

For a while, it seemed Northrop might be the rare person to make the best of the horrors of slavery, even "partnering" with his owner to devise a plan for getting logs from the plantation to the Mississippi River via a narrow canal. The owner even gave Solomon a fiddle as thanks and arranged for him to play it at a masquerade ball at a neighboring plantation and to keep the money paid him for the gig.  Then the owner fell on financial hard times and sold some of his slaves, including Soloman, to another neighbor (Michael Fassbender), a seriously disturbed monster slave-owner.  That's when the true horrors of slavery fell on Soloman Northrop and stayed there for another decade, until by a miracle, his former white friend from Saratoga Springs found out where he was and traveled to Louisiana to rescue him.  The closing scene, where Soloman reunites with his family in Saratoga Springs, brought me to tears.

"12 Years A Slave" is every bit the equal of "Lincoln" and as important to the terrible story of slavery in America as "Lincoln" was to the ending of it.  It will garner multiple-Oscar nominations, including Best Picture, Best Director, Best Adapted Screenplay (John Ridley), Best Actor (Chiwetel Ejioforr), Best Supporting Actor (Fassbender), and Best Supporting Actress (Lupita Nyong'o).  Fassbender, in particular, gave a powerful portrayal of the unrelentingly-cruel plantation owner, given to waking the dead-tired slaves up in the middle of the night to dance in the plantation mansion to entertain him and his equally-cruel wife (Sarah Paulson).  The mark against Fassbender amongst the Academy voters is that his character represents the worst caricature of an anti-bellum Southern plantation owner Hollywood has ever depicted on film, but Fassbender played that character assigned to him to perfection, so I think he deserves the Oscar.  Brad Pitt put up a chunk of money to help produce the film and played the choice cameo-role of the itinerant anti-slavery Canadian responsible for letting Soloman's white friend in Saratoga Springs know where he was.  Some reviewers think he was mis-cast (Brad playing Brad), but I thought he was just fine.  No, Angie wasn't in the cast, but she could've been!

12 Years A Slave is a remarkably harrowing and uncomfortable watch based on the true story of Solomon Northup, a free black man living in pre-Civil War New York, abducted from his wife and family and sold into the diabolical slave trade where he spent each day doing all he could to survive.
Director Steve McQueen (no, not that one) isn't afraid to show all the horrific ordeals of forced slavery, mothers separated from their children, 'inferior' workers flogged, whipped and occasionally hung.
Every single performance in this film is fantastic, Chiwetel Ejiofor appears in virtually every scene, mostly as a passive character who witnesses and experiences all the atrocities, but his performance is nevertheless excellent, especially in the closing stages. Lupita Nyony'o thoroughly deserved her Supporting Actress Oscar as Patsey, whom Solomon befriends on a cotton plantation owned by the seething, dictatorial, cynically evil Epps (Michael Fassbender).
Not all the white people are the bad guy though, and some of them even help Solomon to win back his freedom, but these characters are few and far between and even those who do have redeeming qualities simply don't lessen the impact of Solomon's ordeal.
It's no surprise at all that this film was named Best Picture of 2013. An accolade most truly deserved.

Never has a film, novel, play, or any other art form stared so deeply into the helpless abyss that is slavery until now, until 12 Years a Slave. Never has art embodied slavery so exactly, so broadly, and most importantly, so truthfully. Steve McQueen has crafted a masterpiece from beginning to end, it is a film that will not, and cannot, be forgotten. It insists from the opening shot onward that we gaze at our original sin, and look warily and shamefully into our victims faces. We see their humanity and their scars and the innocence under those scars. No, it is not an easy viewing, however, it is essential, it is an instant classic, and it is a piece of American Art which stands tall alongside our giants. 

You may think that this praise is a little too much, a little too boastful and blind to the faults of the film, however, I can say confidently that this is as perfect as a film gets. This is remorseless art which seeks to express human truth and universal truth in gentle strokes of beauty and pain. The imagery is poetic, the depth of the story is novelistic, and the nakedness of the emotions are so much so that it must be cinema at it's finest. For example, the scene where we see Solomon Northrupp (Chiwitel Ejiofor) first captive, is in a dingy, dark room. A single block of light is exposed above him, the light is there, yet hovers above him, it is as hopelessly gone as his past life, his love, and his freedom. He's chained and he pulls and he struggles to break free, but it is all hopeless.  He's in the middle of Washington D.C., yet there is no justice and no hope. A man comes in, tells Solomon what his new life is, what his past is now, and when Solomon denies this fallacious history, he is beaten so savagely, so ruthlessly into submission that his back is nothing but flesh and blood, and his clothes but blood-soaked bandages. The emotions and actions and motives are laid so boldly and nakedly in this scene that we feel the whip and pain of Solomon, but we also feel just as powerfully, the self-righteousness, vanity, and the just plain evil nature of his captors. 

Solomon is then sold to Ford (Benedict Cumberbatch) by a white man (Paul Giamatti) with no sentimentality in his heart, as he sells a women to the same man, the man asks to have her children as well, but the seller, without guilt or emotion, tells him no, that the family must be separated. This scene in particular really got to me, we deprived them of so much, of everything, of life, love, hope, happiness, freedom, and now we are going to deprive of them of their most basic necessity, their children's love. Yes, that got to me, it brought tears to my eyes as many scenes in this film did. 

Solomon is now forced to deal with a vile, despicable man named Tibeats played by Paul Dano, a man who would just as soon kill a black man as listen to him speak. Solomon hears enough of him, and takes the whip to him, beats him as he has been beaten. He is then put in a noose just low enough to put his toes on the ground, just enough to stay alive. He hangs there for hours until he is saved by Ford, yet now he must be moved to a different plantation. One run by Epps (Michael Fassbender,) a man consumed by temptation and fear of God. He preaches a barbaric gospel to the slaves, one which justifies all his foul intentions. And who is the unfortunate soul who gets caught in his temptuous gaze, but Patsy (Lupita N'yongo.) He casts all his most sinister desires onto her without guilt, as if God had made her specifically for this purpose, and to him that is her purpose, "She was born and bred to the field," he says with lust in his eyes. He rapes her, whips her, hovers over her, and his wife hits her, casts jealous eyes her way, and Patsy simply asks Solomon to spare her life and "to carry her to the lonely place of dying." She is a child whose innocence was never felt, and a soul where love has never been. Solomon says no to her request, he doesn't understand it, and that's the difference between her and him, he has felt love and life, she doesn't know the meanings of the words, she's only felt fear, pain, and misery; she's been reduced, as all slaves have been, to a fledgling and animalistic state which in no way resembles the transcendence of human life.  

However, hope comes in the form of Bass (Brad Pitt,) a Canadian abolitionist who speaks to Epps greatly about the inadequacy of his treatment of black people. Epps shrugs him off, thinking him to be a fool wrapped in meaningless words. Bass lends a sympathetic ear to Solomon, and helps him to escape, but only Solomon can leave, Patsy and all the others must stay in these horrid, hopeless, and horrific conditions, Solomon is forced to save only himself, as an animal would, reducing him even more, leaving him with guilt beyond mention, as he says to his family upon his return, "I'm sorry," apologizing for his absence, and I'm sure, for the cruel things he was forced to do while a slave. Guilt consumes him, then his daughter eases it with her love, saying, "You have nothing to be sorry for." And the music plays and goosebumps rise and tears fill your heart for the freedom, the love, and the humanity he may now feel. 

You will not see a better film this year, and maybe not for awhile. I saw an early screening of 12 Years a Slave back in March, 2013; I have yet to see the final edits but I trust that director Steve McQueen has kept the integrity of the film intact. The film tells the story of Solomon Northup. a free black man (born free in 1808, in Saratoga, New York) who's unwittingly sold into slavery in 1841. The film chronicles Solomon's experiences over the 12 years he's held captive in Louisiana - going from a life of freedom as a husband and father to a life as chattel for more than one slave owner. Chiwetel Ejiofor gives a stellar performance as Northup, as do Paul Giamatti and Benedict Cumberbatch who portray the slaver who sells Northup and the first white owner to buy Northup, respectively. However, it is Michael Fassbender, who portray's Northup's 2nd master, who takes this film to a place that no previous film on slavery has ever gone before. 

In reading reliable accounts of American slavery, I've always been struck by the lack of reality that so many films convey. They seem to gloss over the harshness of slavery, making the filmgoer feel as if the life of a slave wasn't so terribly bad, once you got past the long hours of toiling in the hot fields. McQueen's film, in my opinion, does an exceptionally credible job of helping the filmgoer to understand the harsh realities of slavery in a way that I've never seen portrayed on the screen - not in Django Unchained and not in Lee Daniels' The Butler (which provides a look at the lives of black people post slavery, in the Jim Crow south), both being films that I loved and respected. But Michael Fassbender's portrayal of Edwin Epps, a brutish and violent slave master, is something else altogether. Somehow, this performance takes it all to an entirely new level, helping us better understand the extent to which a slave's life was completely not his or her own in any way.

Sarah Paulson, as Epps' evil and jealous wife, rounds out the other half of the slave owner's control over their chattel and Lupita Nyong'o, as Patsey, Epps' prize slave/cotton picker, gives a magnificent performance as well. Brad Pitt and Alfre Woodard have relatively small but important roles, each of them contributing an important aspect of the storyline.

Note, while it's Michael Fassbender that left me breathless after watching this film, that's not to say, in any way, that Chiwetel Ejiofor's performance was in any way lacking - because it is not. Both Ejiofor and Fassbender should win an Oscar for their contributions to this film (Best Actor and Best Supporting Actor, respectively), without a doubt. Again, I'm writing this review based upon an early screening but I can't imagine how they could possibly edit this film in any way that would change the energy, emotion and vibrance of the story it tells. 

Many reviews are calling this film "necessary" - and I agree completely. I've also read one review that disagrees with this, saying that the film is preaching to the converted choir of the 21st century; that we, as a country, no longer need to have this story told because we've already moved past it all. To that reviewer, I say hogwash - I so wish that we were living in a post-racial America but we are not. Slavery, in general, and the harsh realities of slavery, in particular, continue to be a topic of conversation that most Americans, both black and white, don't really want to have in a meaningful fashion. But that conversation is long overdue and very necessary if we are to ever move forward as a nation, since so many of the issues plaguing Black communities today are tied to the still lingering effects of slavery. 

So that, in my opinion, makes this film very necessary in every way imaginable. In watching this film, Steve McQueen made me laugh and made me cry - and despite the tragedy of having lost 12 years of his life to slavery, Ejiofor's portrayal of Solomon Northup is incredibly inspiring. Go see this film and take every young person you know to see it as well!

12 Years a Slave is a masterpiece of its time, a true work of art and an unforgiving reminder from director/artist Steve McQueen.  I have never seen a film that so brutally and truthfully has shown the evils of slavery, and how their lives were seen as property other than humans.  This film involves a free black man that is sold into slavery and held kidnapped for twelve years as the title suggests, and how he must learn to accept his fate if he ever wants a chance at his old life again.  Some people may know the history of slavery better than I, but what I do know is that I have seen many films on the subject and none of them have been as honest and unforgiving as this.  Let me just say right now that this cast is phenomenal, and they all deserve recognition for their brilliance, especially the performances from Chiwetel Ejiofor and Michael Fassbender.  They really come to the point where they have become their characters in full form, and I wouldn't be surprised if Ejiofor is nominated and wins an Oscar for his performance.  The script is beyond brilliant and took me on a journey of tragedy and hope.  I will even say a few tears were shed watching this film, and itâ(TM)s such a monumental and pivotal film that I'm not afraid to admit it.  Everything from the directing, acting, camerawork and the score from Hans Zimmer were pure art and seeing it was both an honor to behold.  If you enjoy films or art, and are prepared to witness an unforgivable testament to a dark time in our history, I urge you to see this and appreciate the greatness unfold.

  The story follows Solomon Northup (Chiwetel Ejiofor), a free black man living in New York with his wife and two kids.  One night he is tricked into getting drunk and sold into slavery, which begins his long twelve year journey for his survival with a violent planter (Michael Fassbender).

  The plot of this film cannot be described in a few words, just like how twelve years of pain and suffering cannot be summed up in 134 minutes.  But in that time John Ridley's script takes form as one of best representations of slavery and brutality in American cinema.  Ejiofor's character of Solomon is very sympathetic and relatable, as you can tell he is a truly decent man and a good father, who is what, makes his journey that much tougher to watch.  You see moments where stands up against his captures which are the moments where we can see his anger and resentment towards these people come to play.  He is a real and beautifully written character that is the heart and soul of the film.  Fassbender's character is also surpringly very well written, as he is a very complex and disturbing man that only sees his slaves and his property to do what he wants.  Itâ(TM)s scary to watch him on screen because they set him up to be such a threat, and we can never tell what he is think and going to do next.  Inside all this darkness and evil, there is still a glimmer of hope in the film that keeps Solomon moving forward with life, and that is where the emotion from the film comes from.  Once the climax hit, I wasn't able to keep in the tears, and as the films credits rolled I had never heard such a silent theater from people who are stunned with the film they just witnessed.  Knowing that some people didn't receive the justice they deserved is also a harsh truth that the film shows us, and as much as we would've liked to see some people get what was coming to them, you cannot change a fact of life and I commend the director and writer for not making it a Hollywood ending.  It isn't Django Unchained where the protagonist gains his vengeance on the bad guys, although this film will make you want to go home and watch this to see some slave owners get whatâ(TM)s coming to them.  This story is a marvel to behold, and I couldn't compliment it more if I tried.  

  The cast is one of the main reasons this film is a masterpiece, because with such a large cast of big stars you would imagine at least one performance that was less than perfect, and I couldn't find one.  Chiwetel Ejiofor should be commended for his heartfelt and chilling performance, as he has given what I believe to be one of the best performances of the year.  I have seen this man in other films but never has his true talents been revealed until this film, and I believe this is the start of a good future for him.  Just the look of despair or hope on his face is believable to the point where he isn't acting anymore.  Please, somebody, hand this man his Oscar.  Michael Fassbender has become one of the actors I respect the most, as with every performance he gives there is a vibe that no other performer gives me.  He has a way to turn a character into his own completely, and when he and McQueen team up there are endless possibilities.  Lupita Nyong'o is not very well known, but her performance truly impressed me and she gives us a scared and heartbreaking performance.  Benedict Cumberbatch is brilliant as always, and for the brief time Brad Pitt is in the film his character gives us a bit of hope in the film which I adored.  Paul Dano gives a sniveling and cruel performance, and as always he is one of the strangest and best younger actors working today.  Overall, this entire ensemble cast threw me into a world of unforgiving truth, and they all should be commended.

  12 Years a Slave is a film that I could talk about for hours and speak of its heart, its evil, and its reminder that the history was anything but ideal.  We see in the film that while some people owned slaves, they had a conscience and tried their hardest to be decent people.  The sad fact is that many people owned slaves and that for many people that were a normal way of life and there was no changing it.  The film brilliantly demonstrates that whether or not a slave owner is a good or bad person, he is still a slave owner and will treat you like a slave.  Brad Pitt has a great speech about how in the eyes of God we are all the same, in which Fassbender compares the life of a white and black man the same as a white man and a baboon.  This really had me curious and made me think about how they saw owned slaves as nothing more than property on a piece of paper.  You cannot hide these facts and pretend that some of the worst thing imaginable happened to these people, because it did.  I won't say itâ(TM)s a happy movie because itâ(TM)s anything but that, but I would say itâ(TM)s a hopeful movie because it really does believe in hope even in the darkest situations.  This is a theme that makes films like The Shawshank Redemption some of the greatest movies of all time.  I don't know if I am one to say if this is one of the greatest films ever made, but I do believe that if you named off some of the most important films to watch in your lifetime this would more than definitely be on that list.  This film is a front runner for Best Picture at the 2013 Academy Awards, and so far this is the film I will be cheering for on that day.  Treasures like this phenomenal film rarely come around in cinema that so masterfully and hauntingly gives us not a movie, but an experience.  Please do yourself a favor and see this film right away, itâ(TM)s that great.

12 Years a Slave - British / American historical film based on true events, directed by English director Steve McQueen from the screenplay written by John Ridley. Film is based on an autobiography by Solomon Northup (played by Chiwetel Ejiofor) written more than a century ago. This is the third collaboration between Steve McQueen and Michael Fassbender. Filming took place in New Orleans, Louisiana - 12 Years a Slave was made over the budget of $20 million and earning domestic amount $37,164,225 (Dec/22/2013). 12 Years a Slave premier took place at Telluride Film Festival - New York Film Festival - Toronto International Film Festival.

Set in 1841 a New Yorker carpenter a free-man Ejiofor, lives with his wife, daughter and a son. One day he is deceived by two white-fellas, to earn extra shots in Deep-South - the two booze him up and sell into slavery. Ejiofor is purchased by benevolent slave-owner Cumberbatch, however, slight fight between Ejiofor and racist Dauno - in order to save him from lynching, Cumberbatch is forced to send him to ruthless slaver Michael Fassbender. 

Here is a complete, and most-cherished movie on subject of 'slavery' from English director Steve McQueen; a subject that remains a stain on American history, along with ethnic-cleansing of Native-Americans. Steve spoke out during luncheons and buffets in honor of movie screenings, everywhere 'do not forget your past, just like the Jews keep remembering holocaust'. One might agree with Steve, since there has been no work on shameful misdeeds perpetrated against humans in the history of human-endurance. 

Chiwetel and Fassbender give astoundingly superior performances; filled with anguish and calamity of era of the events. Careful and perfect attention has been levied to costume-designs (going so deeper to resemble soil-color on clothes, accordingly) - biblical accent for many of the characters, while also balancing the upper-class verbalism, for Michael Fassbender and Cumberbatch vice-versa.

I wouldn't say it's a stretch to say that this movie will be studied in schools in the years to come. Many movies have dealt directly with slavery before, but none quite this dolorous. It's almost unbelievable - the film is about the incredible true story of Solomon Northrup. Chiwetel Ejiofor plays Northrup, a "free negro" from New York who was kidnapped and sold into southern slavery and kept in bondage for twelve years before the Civil War.

The most resonating theme is the idea of survival and how different reactions to threats to survival. Each character acts differently. Some revolt immediately, some cry for despair, and some look to their inner strengths.   This theme is echoed in every character, even the slavers. It's not by accident that slavers William Ford (Benedict Cumberbatch) and Edwin Epps (Michael Fassbender) differ drastically in their morals.

Beyond just being such an important historical film to watch, it's quite beautiful too. Steve McQueen serves as an excellent director with some unforgettable camerawork and gorgeous shots of the natural landscape of the American South. And he directs his cast, who deliver their best all-time work. Ejiofor conveys such a strong, introverted, and deep pain of a man in suffering. Fassbender plays the all-to-real misguided, nonredeemable villain. And standout newcomer Lupita Nyong'o will break your heart as Patsey, the 'favorite' of Epps.

"12 YEARS A SLAVE" is on much more of a grand scale than McQueen's previous films "SHAME" and "HUNGER." But his signature up-close personal touch is not lost on this masterwork. It's a superb and life-changing film that one cannot soon forget.

Praised and favored for all possible awards, 12 Years a Slave is an extraordinary, brutal and depressingly emotional movie. Depicting in almost documentary way the darkest part of the slavery period in the US, it is an extremely challenging and uneasy movie to watch. It does not impress with an amazing escape story, but with graphic portrayals of cruel characters, ruthless habits and the tragic lives of Afro-Americans during the slavery period. 
Almost entirely based on the true story of Solomon Northrup, 12 Years a Slave goes back to 1841 when the free-born Solomon, living in Saratoga with his wife and kids, is kidnapped by slave traders and illegally sold in slavery in New Orleans. With a new name and no hope to regain freedom, Solomon's life becomes a daily struggle to survive. In terms of a story development and getting free again, 12 Years a Slave is far from being an adventurous movie. On the contrary, it is a delivery soaked with brutality, violence and hopelessness. 
Director Steve McQueen has focused himself on depicting the life of Afro-Americans as slaves in the deep American South as well as beliefs, understandings and way of thinking of their enslavers. Every single character in 12 Years a Slave is an embodiment of particular stereotypes and groups of people. Chiwetel Ejiofor is simply terrific as Solomon Northrup, disturbingly honest, vulnerable and yet willing to survive. Together with Michael Fassbender they are one of the reasons why this movie is so engaging. Speaking of Fassbender and his third collaboration with Steve McQueen (after Hunger and Shame), his brutal and ruthless characterization of the Edwin Epps is mesmerizing. An embodiment of a whole social sub-group his delivers a performance that would irritate every stomach. To some extent Fassbender outshines Ejiofor thanks to Steve McQueen's skilful depiction of the way of thinking and reasoning of slave owners during these years. What is even more shocking is the frightening, stone-cold performance of Sarah Paulson as Mistress Epps. In the very few scenes she is involved in; it is her female coldness, lack of compassion and humanity that truly will shock you.  

As a whole, it is the way Steve McQueen portrays a world that seems so distant and illogical to us, that creates the feeling of being utterly uncomfortable while watching his delivery. Apart from the graphic scenes (the whipping of Patsey was completely unbearable for me) it is also the logic and reasoning; the points of view of slave owners shown in the movie that shock. From our post-modern point of view that society and period would seem completely unacceptable, but Steve McQueen manages to show a world in which modern thinking is non-existent, in which slavery, brutality and the worthlessness of human lives are a common sense.

12 Years a Slave has definitely been slightly overhyped, but given the fact that it was shot in only one month it deserves all the standing ovations it could get. A movie which would test your senses and emotions, it constitutes Steve McQueen as one of the directors-to-follow and getting some Oscar Awards are just a matter of time. With 9 nominations it could be considered a favorite in the Best Motion Picture, Best Editing and Best Adapted Screenplay. Definitely a must see !!!

After the rocky Shame, it wouldn't be wrong of anyone to have hesitation going into McQueen's next film, especially to see how he'd handle such emotionally dense subject matter when his last film was so melodramatic. Yet Steve McQueen has created brilliance in this, his newest work. The story of Solomon Northrup is astoundingly undertold, and almost unbelievable. It brings the horrors of slavery to the forefront, unflinching without being exploitative. Skin is shown being ripped from the backs of slaves under the lash. Rape isn't implied but shown, and the slave owners are brutal without being cartoons, compassionate without being saints. The film relies very much on its main performer, and Chiwetel Ejiofor delivers so raw, so fierce and so magnificent that no man but the most bitterly prejudiced can't relate to such intense suffering. Somber cinematography and an incredible supporting cast, including a heart wrenching turn as Patsy by Lupita Nyongo and a horrifying Michael Fassbender as the wicked Edwin Epps, help anchor the film in such an extraordinary emotion that the film becomes the definitive take on this tragic time in history, without ever once feeling exploitative or self-important (this isn't the time or place to wonder why there are far more holocaust films than slavery films, but at some point that should be wondered about). McQueen has done a remarkable thing with this film, an inimitable type of magic that occurs when everything comes together perfectly, and a film can plunge into the depths of the human soul and plant something that stays there forever

While it isn't quite the earth-shattering masterpiece it has been hailed as, 12 Years a Slave is still a praiseworthy piece. Steve McQueen's historical drama has the guts to look at the brutality of slavery and maintain the gaze, without ever succumbing to sentimentality, sermonizing or sensationalism. A lot of the film's success is to do with that it is seen through the eyes of the slaves themselves; Solomon Northup (whose story is the basis of the film) may be a too easy lead character in all his nobility, but his job is also to work as an observer, through whose eyes the audience look at one of the darkest periods of American history. And dark it is indeed; while Quentin Tarantino exploited slavery and grotesque violence in Django Unchained to deliver another indulgent yawn (and then gratuitously said he wanted to inspire "conversation"), McQueen's film  takes every facet of the topic seriously. There are numerous both physically and psychologically violent scenes that make the film sometimes revolting to watch. But the violence, like everything else in the film, is never played out for entertainment. The film is particularly accomplished in that none of the characters feel like caricatures; the slave owners are more than just piggish villains, and Northup, while somewhat underdeveloped as the lead character, is not a larger-than-life hero who finds perfect redemption at the end. While some other characters appear on the screen for only a minute (but played by renowned actors like Paul Giamatti and Brad Pitt), they help to form an overall picture of how slavery functioned as an institution. If the film attempted to make all of them three-dimensional figures, it would only drown in its own ambition. McQueen's direction is unflinching, and some of the most unforgettable scenes include Solomon joining to a slave choir and accepting his fate, and the slave girl Patsey's brutal whipping scene, for the sole fact that it is so traumatic. Chiwetel Ejiofor delivers a perfectly understated performance, Michael Fassbender is unforgettably ferocious, and the newcomer Lupita Nyong'o will break the hearts of everyone despite very little screen time. The rest of the supporting cast (Benedict Cumberbatch, Sarah Paulson, Paul Dano) is first-rate as well. The only problem is that due to Solomon's lack of character development, the film too often feels like a chilling and distant history lesson than an emotionally wrenching drama. The lead characters in McQueen's two previous films (Hunger and Shame) have also been mysterious ciphers, so that is something he'll have to learn to fix in the future. But 12 Years a Slave is nevertheless an important film and a potent reminder about a period in history that has too often been belittled and distorted. While it is easy to accuse it of trying to provoke liberal guilt, it deserves to be seen.

One of the most profound films you'll see this year, 12 Years a Slave sheds light on a personal account of slavery, a topic Hollywood has interpreted for years. This film, however, seems different from films of the past. Steve McQueen holds zero punches when it comes to conveying the brutality of slavery. Chiwetel Ejiofor's performance as Solomon Northup is excellent. Northup was a learned man with a fortunate upbringing; one can only imagine the culture shock that occurred upon his disposal into the slave trade. Ejiofor, even through his non-speaking scenes, captures the frustration and the confusion that Northup must have been going through at the time; this is extremely evident in one of the many consuming scenes with Paul Dano's character. Michael Fassbender's performance as slave owner Edwin Epps is worthy of an Oscar. He plays a Simon Legree-esque figure and again, nothing was sugar coated, especially during an extremelely hard to watch scene that occurs 3/4 into the film. 
The cinematography and direction does something beautiful within the grit and brutality of the subject matter. The backdrop of the film, the antebellum South, is emphasized with shots of cotton fields and the dense wilderness. One of my favorite scenes involves one of the characters, Patsey, crafting cornhusk dolls; amidst all the ferocity, these people, who have every reason to abandon all hope are able to find solace even in the darkest of times. The score by Hans Zimmer is perfect and embodies the tenacity of Solomon Northup, especially with the selection called Solomon. When it comes to biopics, 12 Years a Slave sets a new standard.

It gets harder and harder as time moves on to produce a successful film on such a difficult topic that invokes such deep emotional success as the first films which set successful precedent in the brand of drama before. 12 Years a Slave offers up to the viewers a powerful eyes-wide-open look upon the life of a man dealt a new level of injustice which has not before so powerfully ripped it's way onto the Hollywood spotlight.   Slavery continues to be a topic which is disillusioned in the toll it takes upon a human being in the perspective context of contemporary American society. In 12 Years a Slave it is important to remember that this is not simply a slave from a perpetuated system of slavery but instead a man born free and brought into the shroud of slavery despite all the odds which stood against such an event and all the rejection he receives as to the acknowledgement of his very nature from that moment until the near end of the film. By simply trying to remain true to himself as a human being, he is forced to realize the twisted nature of man. Casting is of the highest caliber within this film. Each part played by significant actor in the film is brought an essential flavor which only such an actor could deliver. The production elements are well executed with calm control and commanding knowledge of the atypical path which the film must follow. The production is delivered in a satisfactory manor which is not bad nor exceptional forgoing some tense moment of sustained continuous shot outside the typical Hollywood formula of constant progression of story, which revoke the luxury of the audience to quick emotion and a return to reality. Instead the scenes sustain bringing the story to a painful slow, forcing the audience to wallow in the uncomfortable pain and anguish which the scene delivers with unflinching detail. 
The mood of the film is captured in exquisitely brutal detail through the voices and actions of the center cast. The film does what many others in this genre of drama fail to: bring the primitive truth about the history of our nation to a quality of three dimensional reality through a two dimensional representation.

Based on the fascinating memoir, "12 Years A Slave", this film recants the true story of Solomon Northup, a free-born African American man who lives in New York with his wife and children until he is coerced under false pretenses into joining a couple of circus performers for dinner. These two turn out to be con-artists who drug him, sell him, and aid smuggling him out of the country to Georgia, where he is forced into slavery under the moniker of "Platt". As the title suggests, he spends the next twelve years of his life enduring the brutal horrors of American slavery.
"12 Years A slave" is stupendously well directed by Steve McQueen, and the cinematography is some of the best ever: as a die-hard fan of Stanley Kubrick's iconic long-take-oriented style, I have to exclaim what a joy it is to see the form has not gone extinct -- a scene in which the character Patsey is violently and gruesomely whipped, is a 6 and-a-half minute long-take that sucks the air of the room as it plays -- and McQueen's jumpy camera holds and near-claustrophobic close-ups add authenticity to the visuals as well. It can be said with certainty that this movie is as beautifully filmed as it is beautifully written -- even as it depicts horrible things.
The story here could easily be called "The Diary Of Anne Frank" of American slave stories, it could also be called an important piece of work for today's culture. The only thing that impresses me more than the amazing story itself, is the modern day subtext it presents: a clear problem that many stories like this have with contemporary audiences is their incidental unrelatablity due to America being over 100 years sober of slavery; but "12 Years A Slave" (I feel) bridges that gap quite easily with a story that could be fundamentally compared to the modern day worldwide crisis of human trafficking (a tragedy that takes place even here in the US), and the depiction of illegal slavery and it's relationship with the once-legality of slavery in America could be used as a reference guide to explain the context to young American viewers of illegal human trafficking and it's relationship to the legality of prostitution in foreign countries.
Behind the fantastic writing and directing that's occurred here, there's also a veritable barrage of master acting and thoroughly enthralling music -- speaking of which, composer Hans Zimmer is at the top of his game. There's a scene in the film (in which the lead has been hanged from a tree) where an electric cello plays as the score, and to ominous effect.
The award-winning film, "12 Years A Slave" tells a story more terrifying (and more gruesome) than most horror films and may, as a result, be very difficult for some stomach watching, but for those who wish to: it is without a single doubt, a powerful work of art that is hard to look away from -- even for those that might want to.
