Slavery remains a troubling issue so much in fact that we feel more comfortable viewing dozen Holocaust films than a single film on slavery. It's an certain period in human history no one is proud off and willingly attempt to prevent from ever occurring again. However, simply labeling this film with a single intention is saying very little of its true power. What many hailed as being the greatest film about slavery I dare say is an essential statement on humanity. It's not just a film about slavery, but rather about the common man.

12 Years A Slave is set in antebellum United States, Solomon Northup, a free black man from upstate New York, is abducted and sold into slavery. Its biggest strength is being able to depict slavery how it is without feeling exploitative. This film always walks on a thin line of being one hanging, one whiplashing, one beating from being deemed tasteless. All the more praiseworthy when its difficult depiction is pulled off successfully. On paper it's easy to sympathize for Solomon Northup just as a slave, but that was not the intention. Solomon is not just a free black man; he's a common man, with common features, common dreams, sharing a common will for the desire to live in his harrowing endeavor. Sympathizing with Solomon for who he is and not what he became. Enduring as much as the human spirit could living and entrapped in a cruel world that coexist with his former one. Much like Solomon, we never forget the freedom we have while attempting not to lose the shred of humanity we have left as the world around become engulfed in seemingly never ending tragedies. We feel what Solomon feels and think what Solomon's thinking. Reflecting upon Solomon with ourselves of how something like freedom no matter the world around you can be taken for granted.

Interpreted directly "12 Years A Slave" is a harrowing and even inspiring story. Beyond that interpretation are many metaphorical meanings both simplistic and in depth. The "N" word for example is not simply use as a profane word. Its first usage in the film is profoundly powerful. Perhaps for some it will be the first time ever truly understanding the strength behind this single word. Being able to reduce a loving father, skilled musician, husband, and highly intelligent human into an animal to be bought and sold. Another subtle use of metaphorical symbolism is a fiddle. What it represents is rather simple and difficult to miss. On the surface the fiddle represents freedom; however, music present another form of hidden expression. What you hear can be calmly and joyous while in context that piece of music being played comes across differently. As a form to remind slaves of their oppressive position, provide a small taste of freedom, or further reminds them of the consequences if attempting to run away. Music expresses many emotions and has the same power to conceal truth; it can be use to hide the ugly nature of the person's intention or in this film as a form to defeat racism. 

Steve McQueen direction is relentless and one of sheer brilliance. His decision in not telling the audience the passage of time directly is genius. Only giving audiences subtle visual clues on how long has time has past never eliminating the sameness of Solomon endeavor. Getting across that perhaps there is no end in sight in this dehumanizing time. Utilizing long, steady single shots to emphasize various emotions. When events on screen become their most horrifying and ugly is when his camera becomes the most unflinching. One powerful scene involves an excruciatingly long shot of a punished Solomon. When Solomon is hanging on the tree the other slaves go on with their business, seemingly oblivious to the man literally hanging in their midst, until one slave woman gives him a glass of water and meekly scurries away. Showing the true fear and power the slave owners possessed over them. Agonizing scenes like these can make audiences become increasingly uncomfortable in a situation we desire to be removed, but powerless and unable to realizing the outcome if we do. Capturing the rawest of human emotion feeling, thoughts, and seeing how Solomon views things. Even when it draws to a close were left to ponder the long forgotten thought of what does freedom mean to a free man?

Chiwetel Ejiofor's acting excels with facial expressions you realize when he succumbed to his situation versus how he emotionally fought his sudden twist of fate. A mentally and physically challenging role becoming cold himself and attempting to conceal his own emotions completely understanding and sympathizing him. Spacing out in despair as the camera lingers onto him for solid minutes at times with no spoken words. Ejiofor I'll dare even say provides one of the best performances not just in his career, but in one of the best of the decade. Benedict Cumberbatch portrays a slave owner yet he treats his slaves humanely. He makes you ask yourself if neutral people like him are good or bad for progress. Michael Fassbender is a raving dog one minute, and calmly ordering everyone to dance the next, he knows he can make these slaves do anything, they are toys to him, puppets. It is that controlled rage that makes his performance have an eerily threatening presence even when he's not on screen. Lupita Nyong'o gives one of the most devastating performances. She retains a level of innocence that only heightens the tragedy of her character. The cast is flawless no matter how small or big the role is.

12 Years A Slave is brutally honest and heart wrenching for a that does not chooses to play by traditional rules. It's more than a film about slavery and more so a statement on humanity in its gloomiest state never losing sight of one's self. For some it'll be difficult to watch, but even harder to accept the honest truth that McQueen presented to the world. With all the hype surrounding "12 Years A Slave" it might be easy to forget that it's a humble film. Truly deserving of its praise, but should be seen without the hype for it never presents itself to be bigger than life. Rather it presents itself honestly with good intentions and heartfelt emotions for many who can't share a similar story.

A New York musician is drugged, kidnapped and sold to human traffickers. With that set-up director Steve R. McQueen uses his masterful talents to literally chain us to that very man and drops us hard into the chamber of horrors that seem to horrific to be true until it hits you that this is the American slave trade defined. 

That's 12 Years A Slave, a knockout, powerhouse film that begins its true story in 1841 when Solomon Northup (Brit actor Chiwetel Ejiofor), a violin player born a free man and living in Saratoga with his wife and children is coaxed into traveling to Washington D.C. under false pretenses and is made into human chattel in the Deep South. Solomon published a memoir of his experience in 1853, just eight years before the Civil War. Ancient history its not. McQueen, a conceptual artist turned filmmaker from London, born to West Indian parents, dusts off any tired tropes that slavery is something to be dismissed as happening over a hundred years ago and nothing more. His film is the cinematic equivalent of a punch to the gut, a film that tears to shreds Mammy-loving fantasies that has long been what's passed for deep truths and muckracking in Teflon Hollywood. Working from a script from black screenwriter John Ridley, McQueen takes the story of slavery and leaves behind safe remove of television screens as seen in roots, or any and all Hollywood sugarcoating, and even Tarantino-esque satire to lay bare the painful truths of America's original sin. This is a film that will make you believe movies can make a difference and convey harsh truths that cut deep. You do not just watch 12 Years A Slave, you feel it, you bleed with it and are doused in the wounds that may be impossible to heal. 

As Solomon, Ejiofor is pure volcanic force, delivering an engulfing performance that will live on for years to come. The educated Solomon is advised not to protest his circumstances or else risk a beating or worse, but Ejiofor's deep, expressive eyes do the talking for him, barely repressing the rage and confusion and pain roiling inside him. This is acting raised to the level of art and it's dynamite. 

McQueen, coming off two terrific features with 2008's Hunger and 2011's Shame unfolds this tale in long, fluid takes that spit in the face of typical Hollywood bluster, and it pays off in dividends. McQueen puts us with Solomon at every turn as he is renamed Platt Hamilton by a slave trader (a charmingly slimy Paul Giamatti) and sold to plantation owner Ford (Benedict Cumberbatch), an avid Bible thumper. But Ford's benign ways are undermined by Tibeats (a scary good Paul Dano), who prods and baits Solomon until Solomon finally beats him. In retaliation, Tibeats strings him up on a tree, but forced to stop until Ford returns. As he waits, Solomon literally hangs there, his toes touching the ground just enough to keep him from dying, and McQueen shoots the would-be lynching in harrowing detail, showing the routine of plantation life carrying on as Solomon struggles to stay alive. It's an excruciating microcosm of the indifferent world around him, a stunning sequence that has us gasping for breath along with him. 

Things worsen for Solomon when he's sold to cotton-plantation owner and self-described 'nigger breaker' Epps (Michael Fassbender). Epps is an unmitigated drunk who wields scripture as justification for his sadism. He makes a mockery of his wife (a terrific Sarah Paulson) by carrying on with abusing and raping Patsey (Lupita Nyong'o), a slave girl who one night begs Solomon to drown her and end her pain. In the film's most stomach-churning segment, Epps forces Solomon to whip Patsey until her fragile flesh and slender back has flesh literally flying off of her, leaving her in shreds. Even in these harsh scenes, melodrama is nowhere to be found. It's all played for real. Kenyan actress Nyong'o, turns in a spectacular performance that is bursting with grit and true grace. And cheers to Fassbender (star of McQueen's Hunger and Shame) who is all kinds of outstanding as a monster who strains to hide his all too human feelings. Fassbender embodies how slavery dehumanizes its practitioners as well as its victims. He's astonishing. 

When Solomon meets Canadian carpenter Samuel Bass (Brad Pitt), he finally finds someone willing to aid in his escape, and succeeds, but it brings little comfort and relief. McQueen, for one, is not interested in presenting slavery as mere nostalgia and history---not in a world still festering with racism and racial resentment, where black men and women are often 'accidentally' shot by cops or people just standing their ground. He makes slaves of us all, and in doing so, shows himself to be a filmmaker worth following anywhere. There's no erasing 12 Years a Slave from your mind, it sticks with, burns in the memory. A new American classic.

A fascinating true story of a free black man smuggled into slavery and through his willpower and love for his family is able to not fully succumb to the horrors of the Antebellum South.  From the initial beginning of when Steve McQueen (director of 2011 Shame)  stated this was his next project, and when the casting list was set, I put this on my top 10 Watch List for this year. With a fantastic director with an amazing cast I couldn't possibly see this going down badly. My inference was correct and 12 Years a Slave is one of the most emotional films to come out this year. 
   The cinematography was beautifully done with long takes that didn't seem to end. There were two distinct scenes where I was waiting for a cut to someone jumping in and stopping the atrocities that were unfolding in front of our eyes, but there was neither a mediator or a cut. 
  The sound in the film was a low key orchestra from Hans Zimmer's compositions.  It mixed well with the somber tones of the film and slowly went silent as a horrific situation began to grow more intense. The sound design emphasized a heavy tone in the beginning with close ups of what normally can be seen as majestic tools of the  period.  In a way representing a deeper inside look of what we would regularly see just as slavery, a dark part of our nation's history, but then giving us an insider's look through the eyes of a normal man put in an abysmal circumstance.
    Every actor plays his/her part extremely well. Chiwetel Ejiofor as Solomon Northup gives actual justice to the real life man who went through this travesty.  I wouldn't be much surprised of this man getting nominated and winning an Oscar for Best Male Lead; he rightfully deserves it in my opinion. Michael Fassbender (previously starred in McQueen's film Shame) as Master Epps was scarily good. He had total command over everything and created such a despicably hateful man that in his own right deserves some form of recognition for his role. Everyone else (there is so many people and recognizable faces that I can't possibly name them all, from Cumberbatch to Nyong'o) were respectful and fulfilling in their roles. 
   This is defiantly a film to be seen if anything just once for the experience. It delves deeper into the past of American darkness and allows us to reflect more thoroughly  on the subject.  The overall purpose was not to be another movie about slavery and to give Oscar noms. to hopeful actors. The purpose was to discuss slavery through an inside and mature way. Our vessel was Solomon and through him we could witness the Plantations for ourselves. We weren't action heroes out for revenge. We weren't men who were abolitionists fighting against the South. We were a man in a troubled situation that he never asked for or never thought he be in.  It was his journey to never lose hope in the ones he loved, and his thoughts that he kept deep inside to not just survive but to live.

12 Years A Slave has been praised by critics for a while now. I have been somewhat skeptical about it because I do enjoy Steve McQueen's directing style and I wasn't sure what direction the film would take. I was worried that the film would be too lighthearted and that is not a bad thing, considering that the movie is about slavery. What you get is a well directed film about the troubling times of slavery, and one that doesn't cut any corners.


  I was not expecting 12 Years to be as graphic as it was. While many moments, like one long scene involving the main character standing tip-toed in the mud, were unsettling, the fact that Steve McQueen didn't hold back with the images makes 12 Years' long lasting impact much more powerful. 12 Years is a movie that you can't watch more than once but Steve McQueen gets the message across loud and clear. He also manages to put through a much more powerful meaning by the end of the film, which is something only a skilled director could do.


  The acting is phenomenal by the whole cast. Chiwetel Ejiofor gives a very powerful performance as Solomon Northup. While Steve McQueen takes a lot of credit for the way how situations were presented on screen, Chiwetel does phenomenal job at capturing every emotion possible with every moment. The best film of the year and quite possibly the best film of any year; 12 Years A Slave is a powerful cinematic statement that elevates the art form to places it rarely goes and attempts to atone for a Century's worth of popular misconceptions about slavery.  This film, based on the personal biography of Solomon Northup is the singularly best piece of cinema that has ever been devoted to showcasing the retched regime.  The film does not satisfy itself with documenting the horrors of the flesh which go hand and hand with slavery.  It goes far beyond that and explores the darkest recesses of the institution; the emotional, dehumanizing and emasculating toll that it takes on those under its constraints and the dynamics of power inherent in the interaction between those who serve and those who set the lash.  It is clear from this film's portrayal that the institution was as much about the tantalizing grip of holding power over someone else as it was about the fiscal rewards of the thing.  Director Steve McQueen delivers his most emotionally satisfying film to date while still maintaining the raw verbosity that have made his previous films such as Hunger and Shame so compelling.  McQueen has never relented in his ability to capture the deep struggles within ourselves; mainly the struggle to suppress the beasts of our human nature.  McQueen shows in this film how a societal paradigm such as slavery can draw forth our basic inhumanities when we are given legal leeway to hold sway over another's existence.  Ultimately though what 12 Years A Slave questions is how does one maintain hope when the crushing weight of the world is demanding that you give in.
Chiwetel Ejiofor delivers a performance for the ages.  The quiet pain and selflessness his character endures is deeply felt and portrayed and tugs at the heart strings in ways that are unimaginable and impossible to describe.  This performance must be seen, it must be watched and it must be felt.  Ejiofor connects with the audience as an outsider submerged into the filthy institution; as a man stripped beyond recognition of what it is not to just to be a free man but a man unto himself.  The emasculating nature of slavery is hard to bear witness to as Solomon early on in the movie cannot face the satisfaction of being with a woman because of the condition of his station in life and the powerlessness he feels as a slave.  Awards will come.  Oscar accolades will be garnished.  But the importance of this portrayal goes well beyond mere congratulatory recognition or the affirmation of a 20 year career finally being acknowledged.  This performance is revelatory.  It would have been so easy to fall into an unconvincing and unworthy performance; but Ejiofor brings a level of grace to this performance not achieved since Ben Kingsley in Gandhi.  
Michael Fassbender, a Steve McQueen mainstay, is honestly terrifying in the movie; albeit a little over the top.  It's a flashy performance and not at all as nuanced as several of Fassbender's previous performances in films like Hunger, Shame, Eden Lake, or Inglorious Bastards.  However, despite this he is still a clear front runner for a nomination for best supporting actor and deservedly so.  Then there is Lupita Nyong'o whose heartbreaking portrayal as the slave who is constantly objectified and tortured by Fassbender's Master Epps, is nothing short of masterful and is sure to mark the beginning of a great acting career.  Also there are juicy performances from Paul Dano, Sarah Paulson and Alfre Woodard, as well as appearances from Beasts of the Southern Wild's Quvenzhane wallis and Dwight Henry.
The whole film is gloriously captured and scored as well which on occasion follows Northup into one of his dazes giving him and the audience time to contemplate the meaning of it all and the importance of what we are watching.  Hans Zimmer delivers his familiar violins to the score, which are apropos and beautiful but which are also reminiscent of too much of his contemporary work like Inception.  But if it isn't broke don't fix it I guess.       
I cannot say enough about the movie though and its place in film history.  In short order it will quickly enter the annals as one of cinema's great testimonials.  It is as much an indictment of slavery as it is of the century and a half that has followed and the white washed retellings that have marred the cinematic art form in films like Gone with the Wind, The Birth of A Nation and The Patriot.  I cannot begin to overstate the importance of a film like 12 Years A Slave which should serve as the defining testimonial of the Antebellum period; least any of us forget while we are watching Hattie McDaniel in Gone With The Wind.

This is an all-around great film - it's the sort of project that might seem like Oscar bait, but in this instance it's a movie that actually deserves all the Oscar nominations it's going to get. It really is a beautiful piece of work in every respect, from the direction to the cinematography to, most especially, the performances. It's probably the best realistic movie about slavery ever made - people will want to compare it to Django Unchained, but that's a bit of an apples and oranges comparison. Django wasn't trying to be realistic, and so should be taken on different terms than this movie should. Neither is better than the other; they're just working to different purposes in different ways. I can say, however, that I did find this movie to be infinitely better than director Steve McQueen's previous film, Shame.

The movie is based on the true story of Solomon Northup, a free African-American man who was kidnapped from his home in New York in 1841 and sold into slavery, ending up in Louisiana. He was a slave for 12 years before finally being set free and returning home, where he wrote a book based on his experiences that became popular among abolitionists. I haven't read the book, so I don't know how much of the movie is taken directly from it and how much is hypothetical or speculative, but the movie never does anything that seems implausible.

Chiwetel Ejiofor is really excellent as Northup. Ejiofor is an actor who's been around for a while, but this is the first time he's really been able to headline a big movie, and he nails it. He'll get an Oscar nomination, and he deserves it. Michael Fassbender has the next biggest role as Edwin Epps, an exceptionally cruel drunkard of a slave owner who owns Northup for many years. This is one of Fassbender's most intense roles yet, one that gives him more to do than his lead role in the recent The Counselor. He'll probably get a supporting actor Oscar nomination. Lupita Nyong'o has a difficult, delicate role to play as Patsey, a female slave on the Epps plantation, but she's very affecting. The rest of the cast has big name stars that often only show up for a scene or two, but their personas help get across what they need to in those brief appearances: Brad Pitt, Benedict Cumberbatch, Paul Giamatti, Paul Dano, and so on.

Like I said, I think this movie was a serious improvement from McQueen's Shame. I found Shame a pretentious and rather empty experience - it was clear that McQueen had a distinctive style with his very long takes, but I found that too many of the long takes in Shame weren't really about much and didn't take advantage of what a long take can do. Here, though the shooting style is on the whole more conventional, McQueen does work in a few of those long takes, and in this case he really manages to make them count. When he shoots a scene a particular way, I got what he was going for, and it worked. The cinematography is excellent; and the musical score by Hans Zimmer is actually rather uncharacteristic of Zimmer, full of strange dissonances. This is one of the strongest movies of the year so far, and should probably join Lincoln on the required-high-school-viewing list.

As we are going into the Fall season, that's where the Oscar buzz begins. Prisoners, Gravity and Captain Phillips have already joined the fray. Now there's 12 Years a Slave, which is based on the life account of Solomon Northup during his twelve years as a slave. Here, we go back to a time before the Civil Rights movements that takes place in the mid-1800s.

This is the fourth film that I know of that deals with African Americans in the past two years. First, there was The Help, which dealt with maids during the Civil Rights movement. Then there was Quentin Tarantino's Django Unchained (my favorite from last year), which brought a more bad-ass take with its stylish action scenes and violence. The Butler was released earlier this year about a butler who worked in the White House. But now, 12 Years a Slave goes into darker areas about the mistreatment of African Americans.

The story begins in 1841. Solomon Northup (Chiwetel Ejiofor) is a free man who lives with his wife (Kelsey Scott) and his two children in New York. While her wife works as a cook, he works as a carpenter and playing the violin. However, everything changes for him when he gets involved with two men (Scoot McNairy and Taran Killam). After one night of drinking, he finds himself in chains and sold into slavery. Whenever he tries to proclaim his freedom, he receives beatings.

He is eventually bought by William Ford (Benedict Cumberbatch), a plantation owner who is also a pastor. While there, he starts to become harassed by John Tibeats (Paul Dano). When tensions became worse, for the sake of his safety, Ford has Solomon sold to another planter, Edwin Epps (Michael Fassbender), who turns out to be quite cruel. He treats the blacks as lower beings and justifies them using the Bible. Meanwhile, Epps also has an attraction to Patsey (Lupita Nyong'o), who is his best slave in picking cotton, which causes some tensions with his wife, Mary (Sarah Paulson).

Unlike previous films that took a more lighthearted touch to how African Americans were treated, 12 Years a Slave doesn't pull punches. There are plenty of beatings seen in the film. Solomon gets beaten while being captive, he later almost dies from a hanging, and a woman is whipped numerous times. Fassbender's Epps is the embodiment of racism in this film. He mistreats his workers and threatens them with many lashes if they didn't pick enough cotton in a day. His wife is a little fairer, but can also come off as quite cold, especially when it comes to Patsey.

But the white characters are not without humanity. While the themes of discrimination are shown through John and Epps, there are also characters who treat their workers with kindness. This was shown through Cumberbatch's Ford and Brad Pitt's Samuel Bass. Ford treated Solomon with kindness and even at one point gives him his violin to play. Bass also goes out of his way to help Solomon even though doing so would get him some scrutiny.

The acting in the film is really good to excellent. The biggest standout is Ejiofor as Solomon. His performance will certainly be given billing for the Best Actor Oscar. He convincingly plays an ordinary man who must learn to survive his twelve years in slavery and shows a lot of conviction in the more serious scenes. Michael Fassbender also gives a really good performance as Epps. He brings a lot of menace to the role as he shows how cruel Epps can be.

The supporting cast is also good. The best of them was Lupita as Patsey, who shows plenty of conviction as she tries to deal with life as a slave and unwanted advances from Epps. Benedict Cumberbatch gives a good performance as he proves that he can play a character without coming off as cold and calculating. Paul Dano does a solid job playing a racist carpenter. Sarah Paulson has a limited role as Epps wife, but she does a decent job at playing a character who looks fairer than her husband while also still having a cold side. Brad Pitt's also gives a solid performance as Bass, though he doesn't show up until the last half hour.

12 Years a Slave is a great movie for this Oscar season, but don't go in expecting something like The Help or The Butler. This isn't light-hearted drama, this is deep drama. It actually shows the dark side of discrimination and human nature. This is nice for a change. With really good performances and a heart-wrenching story, this is a film for those into the more artful films.

Where lesser directors like Howard or Spielberg would resort to teary speechifying in smoky rooms while the music soars, McQueen has the good sense to set his camera away from the action, allowing us to watch clear eyed what unfolds. The story starts in 1841 in New York, where violinist Solomon Northup lives with his family as a free black man. However, after a night of drinking during the course of a touring gig, he awakens chained, kidnapped into slavery and sent to a cotton plantation in the American South. What follows is a painful realistic brutality of one of the most shameful skeletons in America's closet. Based on Northup's own memoirs, McQueen once again steps up to the challenge of dealing with a heavy theme and by making 12 Years a Slave he makes perhaps the first true masterpiece about slavery - the fact that its director and its leading star are both from London is irrelevant yet slightly ironic. Without ever resorting to romanticism or even touching on the political inclinations of its subject, 12 Years a Slave focuses on one man's nightmarish experience in a style that is daring, unflinching and sometimes even uncomfortable to watch due to its torture scenes and dense atmosphere of hopelessness. Its power is enhanced by a harrowing Chiwetel Ejiofor, whose portrayal of Northup's desperation and frightening personal journey through the American slavery is truly praiseworthy.

British director Steve McQueen (not that one) has made three movies, each being harder to watch than the last. He takes subjects that inherently feature as showcases of man's potential cruelty. His last film, Shame, featured Michael Fassbender as a man for whom the act of sex holds no appeal, no matter how he tried to rectify it. 12 Years a Slave, though not as painful, is no less powerful. As with Shame, it features an incredible lead performance, this time by Chiwetel Ejiofor. He plays Solomon Northup, a born-free black man who was kidnapped off the streets of Washington D.C. and sold into slavery.

In addition to the performances, the main stars are the art direction and score. McQueen has a clear eye for striking imagery, but only when he finds time for it amidst the atrocity. Hans Zimmer, the composer who made his name with The Dark Knight and Inception, brings just the right amount of menace to the film's soundtrack, and ends up as one of his more understated works. So while 12 Years is certainly not for everyone, it's something everyone should see.

I have long been waiting for a serious, stripped-down depiction of American slavery.  If you take time to look at previous attempts most have either been melodramatic (anything to do with Uncle Tom's Cabin), fraudulent (Roots), or...something else (Django Unchained, which I liked anyway).  This need has finally been satisfied by 12 Years a Slave, a film that pulls no punches and delivers a perfect stick-to-your ribs experience that one must see once in their lifetime. What makes this brutal, yet earnest movie more effective is that most of the events on screen actually happened:  it is a relatively faithful adaptation of the story of a free northern African-American sold into slavery via treachery and his struggle to survive in bondage. Obvious to my historically minded readers is the Fugitive Slave Act and the growing sectional crisis that forms the context for the time period in which the autobiography was released (1853).  But on a more personal level it is an examination of misery, suffering, and death.

12 Years a Slave is a perfect example of a performance-driven film, aided by subtle direction and an unobtrusive score by Hans Zimmer.  The protagonist, Solomon Northup is played deftly by Chiwetel Ejiofor, who somehow refuses to give in to despair, despite the circumstances he finds himself in until a particular moment late in the movie (you will know it when you see it). These performances also go hand-in-hand in showing the complexities and absurdities of the "peculiar institution." In other words, a slave was completely at the mercy of whatever owner purchased the deed to his life, and could have wildly different circumstances because of it. Under one master underplayed by Benedict Cumberbatch, Northup finds himself on the equivalent of a hard labor camp with an opportunity to utilize his carpentry skills and his intellect, which is recognized and respected by his master.  Under another master (Michael Fassbender) and his sadistic, jealous wife, Solomon is working in a place something short of Auschwitz or Bergen-Belsen.  Said master is an alcoholic, unhinged psychopath, an unapologetic rapist, and incidentally somewhat incompetent in running the day-to-day business of a plantation as he is more concerned with torturing his slaves while justifying it with scripture.  12 Years a Slave also bears one striking similarity with Django Unchained in that both correctly depict American slavery as a trade built on bills-of-sale, debt exchange, ledgers, freedom papers, and shady backroom deals in which human lives were traded in a comparable manner to livestock.

I was also impressed with the subtle feel of the movie.  There is no melodrama or overacting to be had.  The simple humidity-drenched environments are punctuated with the sounds of cicadas and black field spirituals, both singing a somber chorus.  Obviously all these elements make it a shoe-in for this upcoming awards season, but I would ask viewers not to dismiss it outright as Oscar bait and try to evaluate 12 Years on its own merits, which are considerable.

12 Years a Slave has been billed by many to be the definitive depiction of American slavery to ever be seen onscreen, and it's hard to argue because of how powerful and uncompromising a vision it is. Credit for 12 Years a Slave is nearly equally merited across the board, as every department shines and does a phenomenal job. Director Steve McQueen, who's first two films, Hunger and Shame, were great in their own right but not without their faults, has ironed out the wrinkles his third time out to make his most well-rounded effort yet. Outside of the first few minutes, which are awkwardly handled before it settles down into a more linear fashion, McQueen is at the top of his game, creating another artfully constructed film while hitting all the right emotional notes along the way.

The cast deserves just as much credit as well, if not more, as it features several award-worthy performances. Chiwetel Ejiofor is amazing as the central character, and it's a resolute and heartbreaking performance that will likely land him an Oscar. Michael Fassbender as a harsh slave owner and Lupita Nyong'o as one of his slaves who has lost all hope are just as compelling. 12 Years a Slave has gotten criticism for featuring a few too many famous cameos and for Brad Pitt's somewhat deux ex machina appearance. They're valid points and do take you momentarily out of the experience.

12 Years a Slave is as powerful a film I've seen in recent years. It deserves to be seen by as wide an audience as possible and win every award it will get, which I suspect will be many. The film isn't as psychically graphic as it's being made out to be, but does contain the most brutal unbroken take I have seen, and it will shake you to your core. Above all, it will certainly leave an impression about the horrors of racism and slavery and serve as a stark reminder on how far we've come both as a country and species from that horrible time period, and how far we still have yet to go in an age where slavery is more prevalent worldwide than it has ever been.

Based on the historical slave narrative written by Solomon Nothup in the mid-nineteenth century, Steve McQueen's 12 Years a Slave tells the story of the American South in the midst of its most debauched era. Where other films about slavery in the American South have always felt overly clinical and too ostentatiously self-effacing, McQueen's examination of the same subject feels eerily realistic to the point of surrealistic nightmare. The lurid objectivity with which McQueen examines Solomon's initial kidnapping and subsequent enslavement is fascinating in its accuracy, and horrifying in its accusatory representations. British actor Chiwetel Ejiofor is at the top of his game as Solomon, delivering a career defining performance that is supremely effective in its subtleties; wounded, defeated, searching, and hopeful, all at the same time. Never has a film represented the experience of the American slave this truthfully without sacrificing honesty for showmanship; luckily for the viewer, McQueen is modest in his presence as spectator, allowing the performances from his characters to speak for him, delivering a cinematic story that is worthy of the man that inspired it. 

	Starting with the opening sequence of the film, McQueen takes the viewer directly into the mind of his protagonist, wrongfully imprisoned and slowly losing the will to live. McQueen's Solomon is, in this way, heartfelt and tenderly wrought as a cinematic figure, able to stand in for the numerously varied experiences of those around him. Ejiofor as Solomon is forceful in his striving towards life, intelligent in his deceptively hidden depths of humanity, and tender in his state as the downtrodden man. When watching Ejiofor's performance on screen, it's hard to believe that any one man could manipulate his own emotional condition so drastically at will, hinting at the true and horrible nature of slavery as an act of aggressive and violent coercion. When the lashes of the master's whip cracks towards the end of the film, Eijiofor's horror is palpable, merging with the psychological state of the viewer, and granting the film the illusion of reality that all films attempt to capture, but so rarely do.

	Beyond the masterful performance from lead actor Chiwetel Ejiofor, and not to mention the equally stunning turns from supporting actors Benedict Cumberbatch, Michael Fassbender and Lupita Nyong'o, Steve McQueen as director makes his own presence felt definitively as author of this great modern masterpiece. Shot for shot, and sequence for sequence, McQueen's 12 Years a Slave is an intense portrait of the endurance of the human soul, magnificently captured through extended shots of such interminable length that might make the likes of Stanley Kubrick jealous. Instead of moving from location to location with the rapidity of someone afraid of the wretched nature of his subject, McQueen lingers over each scene and landscape, rendering the duration of the twelve years of the title viscerally realized through the cinematic image. Whether it's a shot of ten's of workers in a cotton field, or one single gaze into the face and soul of Solomon, McQueen's camera doesn't miss one moment offered up by his actors and locations. In this way McQueen essentially documents every piece of cinematic artifice as if it was fact, and deceives the viewer into accepting such a fanciful philosophy in the process.

	In what is only his third feature film, Steve McQueen's 12 Years a Slave may very well be not only the greatest film from a singular director, but the greatest film about slavery in the American South ever made. Taking its place beside such important slave narrative films as Roots, McQueen's film about the life of the wrongfully enslaved Solomon Northup is masterfully conceived, acting as a vehicle for historical discussion and interpretation, as opposed to the type of advantageous mythologizing that is more typical from such cinematic adaptations. Led by a stellar cast of leading actors, McQueen's film is powerfully interpreted, leaving nothing unarticulated or left to the imagination of the viewers. Through its brutal honesty, 12 Years a Slave serves as an unflinching reminder of an American past rooted in prejudicial amorality, and reminds us of how far we've come since, and how much father we have yet to go. Steve McQueen and Chiwetel Ejiofor have made the most important film of the year, and now it's up to the viewer to see and champion their picture as the masterwork that it is.

I've said it before and I'm saying it once again: Steve McQueen is a visual artist in every sense of the word. He fully understands the power of the image and brilliantly exploits that in channeling his message. McQueen's films are not made to entertain (those who watched Hunger and Shame will know what I mean); his films are made to shock and engage. He uses gruesomeness to shock, and visual beauty to engage.

12 Years a Slave is shockingly powerful in its adherence to reality and its details. The audience are forced to watch the graphic whipping and torture scenes, and McQueen unapologetically elongates those scenes and strips them of any non-diegetic music so as to deepen their realistic effect. Watching a man hanged to a tree and trying to keep his toes to the ground for a few seconds is an awful thing to watch, and will naturally instigate feelings of pity and sympathy. However, watching the same man with his relentless endeavors to keep standing on his toes for more than 3 or 4 minutes is definitely an agonizing experience for the viewers. The persistence of the silent and still shot invades your comfort zone and forces you to identify with the man.

But being gruesome does not mean the film is not beautiful. Aesthetically speaking, 12 Years a Slave is a cinematographic feat. McQueen's visual trademarks are easily spotted (and admired). Each frame is a triumphant work of art; the placement of the camera, the colors, and the mise-en-scene are all done so carefully that I did not mind having those 'McQueeny' still shots all the time. Each frame is a beautiful painting with an elaborate statement.

Performance-wise, all actors excelled, even though some of them had really small roles. And of course, Ejiofor and Fassbender were phenomenal (surprise, surprise!). The only thing I could not understand is the presence of Brad Pitt in the film. His character is small but important in terms of plot line, but to have him pull this weird southern accent of his and talentlessly preach about slavery is completely annoying! I believe Pitt was used only for publicity; just another big name on the movie's poster.

I don't know why but whenever I write a review on any of McQueen's movies, I end up writing about McQueen himself and his idiosyncratic style (that's how good he is!). Maybe because it is not about what he presents but how he presents it. 12 Years a Slave is a slavery movie but not the usual slavery-is-bad-don't-do-it-again movies. It goes beyond the main theme and takes you by the hand to gruesome/fragile condition of the human soul.

For as long as cinema has existed, there have been movies about human atrocity. It's one of our favorite things to tell stories about. The optimist would say that these films help us to heal wounds, to work through difficult cultural memories by recreating them in a dramatized context. The pessimist would say that these types of films are too often treacly and cloying, and that they inappropriately use real-life horror to yank at your heartstrings, your wallet, and possibly your Oscar vote. But if there's one thing that 12 Years a Slave doesn't do, it's that. Director Steve McQueen favors a distant, removed approach, one that might alienate viewers who expect to be lead by the hand through this story. He doesn't shove his images in your face; he simply places them on screen and leaves them there. This film says "12 Years" right there in the title, and there are scenes where he makes you feel that horrifying length.

There's an extraordinary scene probably a third of the way through the movie where Solomon, played expertly by Chiwetel Ejiofor, is strung up on a tree with a noose around his neck, as a type of punishment. He's left with just enough room beneath his feet to stand so that he won't suffocate. But the ground is muddy and loose. McQueen holds on a wide shot of Solomon hanging for what felt like several minutes. He doesn't give you the safety of a cut. You're forced to watch this awful, awful thing, and what's more, you're forced to feel its duration. McQueen is making a point about all the movies about slavery - and other human atrocities - that have come and gone. This movie doesn't make you feel safe. It doesn't want you to think of Solomon's story as a "learning experience." This actually happened, this is someone's life. This isn't an opportunity for you to feel proud of yourself for watching such a difficult movie. McQueen isn't going to leave any of this to your imagination, because whatever you could come up with wouldn't be half as bad as what actually happened.

The film weaves through a cavalcade of character actors, and most of them come and go without making much of an impression. Quvenzhané Wallis, the young actress who stunned so many people with her performance last year in Beasts of the Southern Wild, shows up very briefly at the beginning of the film. I don't even think she has a line. Michael K. Williams, best known for his role on The Wire, also shows up for one scene. There's a lot of this going on in the movie, but it mostly feels like casting for the sake of casting. The worst example of this is Brad Pitt, who shows up in a pivotal role at the end. I like Pitt, but he's not quite strong enough as an actor to pull off the part. I'd rather have seen a bunch of great unknown actors populate the film, especially considering how great Lupita Nyong'o is as Patsey, a slave whom Solomon meets later in the film. Her performance is mind-bogglingly good, maybe the best in the film, and she was cast straight out of college.*

Michael Fassbender's performance is one that I can really see standing the test of time, much in the same way that Ralph Fiennes in Schindler's List is still a part of the cultural consciousness surrounding Nazism. Fassbender plays Edwin Epps, a brutal plantation owner who Solomon is owned by for most of his enslavement. Fassbender makes an interesting choice to not play Epps as just sadistic and mean. He's a really complex character, who is pressured by his manipulative wife (Sarah Paulson, who crushes it) to use more and more power over the people he owns. Epps is shown to often come home late at night, extremely drunk, and wake up his slaves to dance for his amusement. He's not being cruel to people, in his mind. He's playing with his pets. And he's using his slaves to exert control that he can't with his wife.

He has a sexually abusive relationship with Patsey, who in turn is tormented by Epps' wife out of jealous hatred. In a sick, demented way, he loves her, and his self-loathing for that fact manifests in further torture of her. Lesser actors (under lesser directors) would have just said, "I'll make him one-dimensionally evil, and no one will complain because he's a slave owner." Like Nazis, slave-owning Southerners are seen as inherently evil in a ton of pop culture. McQueen and Fassbender don't excuse Epps' horrific behavior, but they place it in a psychological context that's captivating and intelligent. In fact, "captivating and intelligent" is a good way to describe 12 Years a Slave as a whole.

Of course, the film is anchored by Chiwetel Ejiofor, and it's a testament to the strength of this cast that I've taken this long to get around to him. It's the kind of performance that's so obviously good that there's not a whole lot to say about it. It's all in his eyes. McQueen's camera has a love affair with Ejiofor's eyes, and with good reason. He's able to communicate with a look what some actors couldn't with a three-page speech. That's something you need for such a minimalistic film.

That brings me to one of my few complaints about 12 Years a Slave, which is to do with the screenplay. A lot of scenes feel awfully over-written. I've been praising the movie for not pandering to Oscar voters, but there are a few scenes which lean too heavily on speechifying. Brad Pitt's character in particular is given to lengthy monologues about his beliefs. It's like they lifted passages directly from Solomon's memoir and made him say them on screen. That sort of thing works for direct lines of dialogue, but people probably wouldn't talk in the way that Solomon narrates the book. The screenplay avoids that most of the time, but the moments where it doesn't stand out.

My only other complaint is about the score. I'm not a Hans Zimmer fan, and I think that this might be one of his worst works. He's smart enough to get out of the way and let some scenes play without music, but his score just doesn't fit with the film most of the time. When it's not using some weird, blaring, out-of-place percussion, it's going for the sweeping, weeping strings that slap you until you cry along with them. You know who would have been great instead? Jonny Greenwood, composer of There Will Be Blood and The Master. Again, minimalism is what this film is all about, and he's a composer who bonds tightly with the director's style. Unlike Zimmer, who just does his Zimmer thing all over the place regardless of what the film calls for.

But those are minor quibbles. They don't tarnish 12 Years a Slave's status as one of the most vital films ever made about slavery, or indeed any similarly monstrous institution. It captures tragedy and cruelty with a clinical eye, and by doing so strips away any preconceived notions or emotions. You have to take this movie on its own terms, not yours. You don't get to walk out feeling all happy for yourself because you sat through it. Because what good could possibly come out of something as heinous as slavery? We don't get to stand on top of this movie and feel better about ourselves. That's not fair to the thousands of real people who suffered and died during this time. The fact that 12 Years a Slave understands this makes it smarter than any other movie about slavery that I can think of, not to mention one of the best films of 2013. This is essential American cinema.

The opening shot of Steve McQueen's "12 Years A Slave" is a very long take. What we see is our hero, Solomon Northup (Chiwetel Ejiofor), standing alongside other slaves in a field of sugar canes. What McQueen does here is deliberate (and he'll continue to do it throughout the movie): He's forcing us to watch - to take it all in. We're given plenty of time to study the faces of each slave, whether we want to or not. (Think, for a second, how different our reaction would be if McQueen opted to pan the camera across each slave's face.) 
McQueen's use of long takes is, perhaps, the strongest - and most horrifying - aspect of "12 Years A Slave." The only way not to watch is to close your eyes, or leave the theater (as one African American woman did in the screening I attended). And there will be times you're tempted to look away or close your eyes, and I can't say I'd blame you. Consider the scenes where characters are being whipped. Solomon is the first person we see being whipped. The scene is one shot, one take. There's no edit - there's no break. McQueen doesn't cut to anyone's facial reactions. Instead, we're witnessing - head on - Solomon being whipped. We don't get a breather (and neither does Solomon). The second whipping scene involves Solomon retaliating on a white slave driver (played sadistically well by Paul Dano - who seems to be building off of his "There Will Be Blood" role). In this scene, there are a few cuts - which seems to intensify the rage Solomon is expressing. Our reaction goes from being uncomfortably horrified (when Solomon is being whipped), to feeling a bit of joyous redemption when the slave driver is getting what he deserves. The third major whipping scene (and I do hate referring to these scenes as "the whipping scenes") is one of the hardest to watch. Like the first one, it's a single take - only the camera constantly moves this time. The camera's fluid motion shows us each character's reaction (and, sometimes, point of view). It's one of the most encompassing scenes of the movie, and we are dragged right into the middle of everything. 
Ejiofor's performance (and everyone else's performance - especially Michael Fassbender) is nothing short of remarkable. (He will score an Oscar nomination - and most likely will be the front-runner in what seems to be an incredible upcoming race for Best Actor.) He plays Solomon with a quiet calmness (for the most part). In fact, most of his performance could be summed up by what Solomon says to another slave: "I Survive. I will not fall into despair ... I will keep myself hardy til freedom is opportune." It's interesting to note that this is the third movie we've seen this year that deals with characters struggling to survive (first "Gravity," then "All Is Lost," now "12 Years A Slave"). 
My only complaint with the movie (and this is, indeed, a small complaint) is the rushed climax. Perhaps a movie like this needs to end quickly - after what we witness, it'd be tough to endure a drawn-out ending. Still, I ask you to consider this: At the end, does Solomon look like he's really suffered for 12, long years? His family looks like they've weathered more suffering than he has.

There are two types of movies: Ones where you must exert effort into believing the film, and the few where you must exert effort into releasing your suspension of disbelief. Above all other elements, the one most pivotal to this immersion that is suffering a drought in 2013's Hollywood is the acting. Every actor is completely immersive, absorbed in their role and successfully portraying all exterior and interior struggles that the characters have. The only flaw in this aspect is not anybody's acting, but Benedict Cumberpatch's role as the "good slave owner." Though I understand this is a true story, let it be known that this "good slave owner" character irks the shit out of me and they should've made a point that thought he may have treated Solomon North relatively better he was still practicing a highly immoral act.

But this is not merely the work of God bringing a ton of highly trained method actors together. Such a well-rounded cast can only be conjured by a talented director. Steve McQueen (no, not that one) not only has his footprint of effort and direction firmly ingrained in the performances, he also does on the film's camera work and lighting. Without any excessive fantasy elements or computers, this successively becomes one of the most beautiful movies you've seen in a while. Certainly better than the property damage hungry superhero movies. Attempting to pinpoint details in the visuals would take multiple viewings and many pages to do justice.

The pacing is a tiny bit loopy in some areas. The movie utilizes out-of-order narrative, which is commendable and something that I especially appreciate. However, 65% of the movie is told in linear narrative. The nonlinear aspects appear near the beginning and end of the film and even then it's not highly apparent. It's no Christopher Nolan film where the entire story is told in seventeen different directions. While it's nice that it's no Man of Steel overkill, it's a little underwhelming. Also, sometimes you'll be sitting there, and you'll be so used to the linear narrative that a flashback scene occurs without any significant signals and you'll be thrown off for a little bit. This is only a minor distraction, however.

Otherwise, I don't believe I need to make a further case that this movie is entirely worth viewing. Go watch it. Right now. And while you're at it tell me how to end a review. My grade is an A neutral, with only insignificant problems occurring, this is an extremely powerful film.

A free African-American is sold into slavery. The performances are all strong, and the plot is compelling, and the filmmaking is visceral and demanding, but the film doesn't surpass the sum of its parts. For some reason, the horror piled on horror left me admiring the film but strangely uninvolved. I think that while the central conflict of the film -- Solomon's quest to have the truth discovered and be returned to freedom -- is interesting, there isn't a lot of time spent on working out this conflict; most of the film details the horrors of slavery. Additionally, the language is almost Victorian. Expressive vocabulary and inverted sentence structures may be more historically accurate, but the dialogue felt false. Finally, and this is an undeveloped point, this is the most white-heavy slavery film I've ever seen. Compared to Roots, 12 Years a Slave is far more centered on internal conflicts within the slave owners. Edwin Epps's self-revulsion at his attraction to Patsey, Ford's clear antagonism with the institution of slavery, and Tibeats's need for power and control over the "property" all center on white people's experience with slavery, and the film spends so much time on these conflicts that during the film I actually said sarcastically, "Yeah, slavery was really tough on white people." The danger is that these characters can become flat if they lack internal conflict, but this is not a complaint one would level at Ralph Fiennes's character in Schindler's List whose character arc is both compelling, round (as opposed to flat), and decentered from the film's central issues. Overall, there's no doubt that this is a well-made film, but it's less that all it could be.

12 Years a Slave was beautifully done and much more historically accurate and serious than Django Unchained (seeing as it was based on an actual historical memoir), but honestly I preferred Django.  In Django you see the horrible suffering and the cruelty of the racist slave owners, but the protagonist gets a real chance to fight back.  Sure, Solomon has the revenge of living well in the end and a brief retaliation against the cowardly Tibeats, but it isn't as glorious as Tarantino's revenge fantasy where Django gets to violently slay everyone who contributed to the misery of the slaves.  

Actually, some parts of this movie seemed like they were based on Django, like the way Solomon whipped a slavedriver who was whipping him and the similar archetypes used (the black protagonist who is more educated than the average slave, the cold female mistress, the crazy, racist but somehow fascinating master of the estate, the one white guy who isn't a racist who helps the main protagonist, the protagonist's long-lost wife, etc, etc)

Obviously it makes sense to have a movie about slavery that is a tragedy.  This was basically the Schindler's List for slavery in the south.  One interesting device used in this movie was the way they used long shots of Solomon's face to illustrate how time goes by slowly and the excruciating waiting for the next horrible event to take place.  They also lingered on anything painful or horrible (Eliza's crying, Patsy's whipping, Solomon's whipping, Solomon waiting to be punished, Solomon's hanging, etc) just to show how long and drawn-out the pain feels.  It is definitely uncomfortable to watch but quite effective.  You also start to get really angry at the bystanders but you also realize how risky it is to be a hero and show compassion.  When Solomon was being half-hung, I felt myself mentally screaming at everyone to cut the cord but everyone just walked around going about their regular business.  Even Solomon is a bystander in many situations, and half the time you're angry that he doesn't do anything but you also understand how you just have to do your best to survive no matter how much you wish you could help.  I also found myself wishing Solomon would just punch every racist white person in the face.

I think Solomon was by far a more interesting character than Django and that he was more independent and intelligent than him.  He only gets a little help from Brad Pitt at the end, whereas Django has to hold Christoph Waltz's hand most of the time.  

I think the stand-out performances would be Edwin Epps, John Tibeats and Patsy.  Their psychopathy was astounding to watch as well as the way Patsy almost seemed to be enjoying her whipping because her life was so horrible that she wished she could die.

In short, 12 Years a Slave is a great movie; it's just not very enjoyable to watch.

One of the best films of the year, and, along with Gravity, one of only two films to get a perfect rating from me this year. Not only is it one of the best films of the year, it is damn near the most brutal and honest depiction of slavery since Roots. Unlike some other films like Remember the Titans or 42, which down play the violence and brutality of their eras, 12 Years a Slave never shy away from any of it. Some may find it a bit preachy at times, but I felt like it earned its right after depicting the brutality so well. 

The story follows Solomon Northup, a freeman who is abducted and forced into a life a slavery. At every turn he witnesses the atrocity of the time painted against he backdrop of what looks life a beautiful Louisiana setting. The contrast between the outward beauty of the southern plantations and the horrible underbelly make this film all the more fascinating. 

In many ways this films is the anti Django Unchained. While I love that film, I'll acknowledge that it is in no way an accurate portrayal of the times. Where Django was hopeful and almost gleeful with the violence, 12 Years a Slave is just unsettling to watch. You almost wish that this was a revenge fantasy, but alas this was a real story with a bittersweet ending at best. 

The worst scene being the lashing scene. I've never seen a whipping scene that looked so brutally realistic and it almost made me throw up in the theater. If a film makes you do that, then it is doing something right. 

The two standout performances come from Ejiofor and Fassbender. The former gives on of the most heartbreaking performance in decades, with scenes that will move you to tears. He will most likely either be nominated or win a best actor Oscar. Fassbender trades his anti-villain persona he did so well In First Class, and portrays a evil and monstrous slave owner that will scare you. 

My only grip with the film is the casting for one particular role. Many people know that Brad Pitt has a small role in the film. He is ultimately the one white man who saves Northup from his captivity. Now I know this happened in real life, but the problem is with the casting of the role. Pitt is a fine actor, but he's too damn recognizable. It feels almost like a deus ex machina and it is really distracting when all you are thinking of is "wow, Brad Pitt saved that guy." This is a minor problem, but if the role went to a lesser known actor, I think it would have been more effective. 

Overall, this is not for the faint of heart. There is hardly a moment that goes bye without some moment of horror or sadness. That being said, it is one of the front runners for Best Picture.

Ejiofor, a method actor who has excelled in films like "Redbelt", "Inside Man", and "Children of Men", is absolutely sensational here, in a performance that should definitely earn him not only his first Oscar nomination, but a win as well. Director Steve McQueen ("Hunger", "Shame") holds nothing back, and the result is one of the best films made, one that paints slavery in the most brutal but most fair way possible. It is not an entertaining or fun movie to sit through by any stretch, but it is extremely educational, and an important view of one of the most awful times in our nation's history.

The struggle of Solomon Northup, a free man from New York who is kidnapped and sold into slavery.  We follow his 12 year long journey, dealing with slave owners, other slaves, moral quandaries on all parts, and internal identity struggles of Solomon.  It's a hard to watch movie that will make you miserable at times - but it stares slavery so boldly in the face that it is a must see.  It's also brilliantly shot, exceedingly well acted, and directed fantastically.

One of the best things about the movie is the portrayal of slavery.  We have two main slave owners we see: Ford (Benedict Cumberbatch) and Epps (Michael Fassbender).  Both have different views on their slaves - Epps treats them horribly, as property and as play things.  He is a horribly abusive man to everyone - his slaves, his wife, and even himself with his raging alcoholism.  Ford on the other hand, treats his slaves better, allowing them to earn his respect and giving them a decent life. There is no constant fear of being raped or beaten like there is on the Epps plantation.  However, Ford is still a monster in his own way.....
.....The acting is amazing in this film, with incredible performances from people like Michael Fassbender, Benedict Cumberbatch, Paul Dano, Garret Dillahunt, Sarah Paulson, J.D. Evermore, and a number of supporting characters.  It would be a never ending review if I started to talk about them all.  The only person I had a problem with was Brad Pitt, because I felt he wasn't strong enough for the role that he was.  He was the only person that I didn't fully believe could have been that character.  It was a minor detail, since he isn't in it very long, but was still one of the only complaints I had about the movie.  Back to good acting - there are two real standouts.  The obvious stand out is Chiwetel Ejiofor as Solomon.  Chiwetel Ejiofor is incredible at showing so much emotion with very few words.........  The second standout is newcomer Lupita Nyong'o as Patsey, a fellow slave on the Epps plantation. She has been a slave her whole life and reaches a breaking point while Solomon is on her plantation.  We get to see this girl go through a tiny moment of happiness, surrounded by moments of pain and sorrow, and trying to just survive.....
....McQueen did a fantastic job.  He is a big fan of long, intense steady shots just focusing on one simple image.  They might be closeups of Solomons face or large landscape shots so you can see how everyone else is reacting to a situation.  They really make it so that you have to sit there and confront what is going on in the scene and not just ignore it or push it under the rug......

One of the most important film's about American History ever made.  A beautiful and haunting portrayal of the true story of Solomon Northup, a free man who was sold into slavery.  My only criticism is where the film strays from the story as depicted in Northup's book.  For example, the character of Master Epps (played here by Michael Fassbender) was more one dimensional than the character in the book.  Also, the film should have depicted more aspects of the underground rebellion culture that existed at that time.  One of the reasons that the novel was so historically important was that it was primary evidence of slave resistance.  For example, when Northup beats up the overseer, he becomes a folk hero among his fellow slaves and they openly discuss insurrection among themselves.  Also, Northup attempts to run away by swimming the bayou.  These details are left out of the film.  I remember reading the book, and being inspired by the humanity and strength of spirit of the slaves in spite of the violence and soul-crushing brutality of their world.  But you didn't necessarily get that from the film.   I think it was a near perfect movie, but it would have been even better if the director had been just a little more faithful to the source material.

"12 Years A Slave" is horrifying but not without cause. The film drives on it's sense of hopelessness and despair without letting the audience be blinded by it. Underneath all of the treachery there is thought provoking yet silent commentary delivered by a mix of emotional acting, score and well thought out pacing. This film places it's viewers in a harsh and realistic adaptation of 1850's America and reveals to it the stinging reality of race inequality and prejudice that was sewn into the culture of the time. One of the things that really helps sell the time period is the phenomenal performances   given by the lead and supporting cast. Whether it be the overwhelmingly sad yet subtle acting of Chiwetel Ejiofor, the tyrannical insanity shown by Michael Fassbender or the sometimes unexpected range of Cumberbatch, Giamatti, Dano and many other actors makes everything feel authentic and uninhibited. All of this is set up against the backdrop of a beautiful score that, though simple, can manage to instill you with bursts of unbridled dread or overwhelming feelings of sorrow, it manages this without ever getting in the way of the storytelling. The music plays when it feels right and doesn't when it's not needed. The cinematography is fantastic. Using the lush natural environment as a transition between scenes  is often very impactful due to the settings lack of conflict in a rather violent world set up for us by the filmmaker. There are many scenes which linger for a very long time forcing you to take in and contemplate what just happened, paving the way for larger emotional effect in following events, many of these scenes mainly focus on the turmoil of the protagonist in nearly complete silence even if these moments aren't very vicious or adrenaline inducing, they still exude a feeling of faint  suspense while building an empathetic connection between the audience and the lead character. In conclusion, though this movie may be brutal, unforgiving and heart breaking there is an underlying beauty, sincerity and hopefulness that make this film one of the most thoughtful, eye opening and important films made in recent memory. this is a motion picture you simply must experience.

The protagonist black man played by Chiewetel Ejiofor is a revelation. Surely, the front-runner for this years Oscar Awards for best actor. Michael Fassbender as the cruel slave owner disgusts you so much, you want to kill that bastard. The passion for cruelty which he portrays is awe-inducing. The simultaneous innocence and weakness portrayed by Lupita Nyong'o as Fassbender's sex slave leaves you teary-eyed. Definitely, the break-through performance of the year. A Small role by Benedict Cumberbatch and a cameo by Brad Pitt are perfect. This was the first Steve Mcqueen movie I saw, and I am totally looking forward to complete watching his filmography. Perhaps the most noteworthy thing about 12 Years a Slave is the way that it portrays slavery itself. Instead of taking the easy way out and limiting his exploration of the topic solely to the slaves, Steve McQueen increases the scope and we see how it affects those who profited by it. To watch 12 Years a Slave is to be confronted with the grim reality of slavery in a way that's never been done before. To say this is the best film ever made about slavery feels trivial, as slavery is a subject in film that has been shown with naive romanticism from films like Gone With the Wind or silly exploitation from something like Django Unchained. Both of which serve to make the topic digestible. To watch 12 Years a Slave is to experience a level of despair and misery that can become overwhelming. It's a film of such ugliness, such blunt emotional trauma, that it may haunt you for hours if not days after seeing it.  All in all, if you get a chance to see 12 Years a Slave, don't miss it. Not everyone will be able to stomach it but it's an outstanding film that deserves and needs to be seen.

For a film garnering so much praise as an uncompromising look at the slave culture of the deep south, I have to say I found "12 Years A Slave" somewhat lacking.  All of the buzz surrounding this movie would lead one to believe that you will inevitably leave the theater feeling gut wrenched and heartbroken.  And it does that, but only to a certain extent.  In all honesty there was nothing here to give me a deeper insight into the "real" world of slavery, as so many have claimed.  I have no doubts that everything in this film is completely realistic.  And I am sure everyone involved did their due diligence in maintaining its authenticity.  But in the end none of that aided in offering any harsher portrayal of slavery than anything I had seen before.  
That fact, however, does not diminish the achievements that are made.  First off, the plot is different than other slave stories we know.  We have all seen people taken from Africa into slavery, people traded, sold, and captured, but this is the first in memory that we see a free man in the north kidnapped with the express purpose of slavery.  Solomon Northrup is a successful musician and family man, living in New York.  When his wife and children leave for her annual job, he is approached by two men who offer him work.  Because we know the story (and the title), we know that this is simply a ruse designed to gain his trust and ease his capture.  This scenario might seem far-fetched at first, why go through so much trouble to capture one man, but as we learn through the story, a violin playing slave is quite valuable to the southern elite.  
Thus begins Solomon's journey into slavery.  The director takes no shortcuts in its telling.  And we get an uncensored look at how the slave trade functions.  The most disturbing part though is not the brutality of the slavers on the prospective slaves, but the way in which the slavers seem completely ambivalent about the process.  On the one hand they are incredibly harsh, both physically and verbally, toward their captives, but on the other they comport themselves professionally, as gentlemen in a business transaction.  The majority of the focus of this films reviews seems to be on the harsh reality of the brutality of the slavers; on the punishment, the floggings, and the humiliation.  But in truth, these are nothing new, nothing you haven't seen before in other films, or even seen in more shocking detail.  It's the way the characters interact with each other that creates the drama, not simply what they do to each other.  The realization that they are not simple archetypes but fully fleshed out people, with beliefs and motivations that are understandable.  It's when you see Solomon interact with a slave owner who could be his best friend in another life that you feel the desperation of his situation.  Most slave stories are conflicts between people; the slave vs. the evil slave owner.  Here, he is not fighting the man, but the social constructs.  Even if a man wanted to free him, he would become a pariah, it leaves you hopeless.  
The conclusion of this film may leave you wanting more.  Knowing that it is a true story can only satiate my need for revenge so much.  And the reveal in the epilogue makes the ending more bittersweet.  As good as the acting was, as moving as the cinematography was, and as captivating as the story became, by the end I couldn't help but feel there was something missing.  I always say what separates merely good films from great films is the way you feel when the end credits begin to roll.  Did it give you an emotional reaction?  Were you left thinking about it on the drive home?  Did it resonate with you in the days following?  For me the answer was no.  Perhaps I am so desensitized to violence, perhaps I have seen so much in so many films that I can no longer feel like a normal person, but I was never affected the way a film like this should.  And because of that this never becomes anything more than just good.  I give it a 7/10.

In Washington, DC in 1841, Solomon Northrup(Chiwetel Ejiofor) wakes up in chains.  He remembers dining with Hamilton(Taran Killam) and Brown(Scoot McNairy) the previous night before recalling the full details of how he was shanghaied into slavery with only the memories of his family back in Saratoga Springs keeping him going.  He is not alone in being sent to the slave market in New Orleans where he is purchased to be worked on a plantation.

"12 Years a Slave" excels in certain departments, including the performances of its great cast, especially that of Chiwetel Ejiofor.  And then there are the graphic depictions of floggings, part of the arbitrary cruelties and abuses under the heinous institution of slavery, reinforcing the wrongs done, and continuing director Steve McQueen's running exploration of the horrors committed to the body, as he should be applauded for lingering on particular scenes.  But the movie is too polished to properly convey the day to day privations the characters face, as what is needed is the crudely intense McQueen of "Hunger" rather than the current version who just wants to be Ron Howard.  And while "12 Years A Slave" is based on a true story, Solomon seems maybe more than a little naive in believing the best in people, thus implying the lack of racism in the Antebellum North which I find a little hard to believe.

It reminds me a bit of Polanski's The Pianist from 2002, where the rights of a group deemed "inferior" is taken away just like that *snaps fingers* This is a serious issue that continues to happen in our moment, it's just taken on another form. Like Szpielman, our lead Solomon (played impeccably well by Chiwetel Ejiofor) had it all. He had a great life in the North and is a free man, had a lovely wife and two kids, is well-educated and intelligent and very charming, but all that is quickly turned around when he is kidnapped by some Southern crooks who sell him into slavery. In a flash, everything is taken away from him. He tries pleading his case but is constantly berated and beaten down. "He's a black man, so what?" is the mantra. And thus begins his years as a slave, of eventually losing his identity and becoming completely dehumanized.

This semester I took a class called Earlier American Literature, a lot of it dealt with slavery and other events that lead up to the American Civil War. Many of these texts, the slave narratives, were incredibly disheartening to read which were accompanied by equally hard-hitting lectures (which created context) that never shied away from the truth. To read first-hand testimonies from slaves who have witnessed humanity at its worst is enough to churn my stomach. Even to read or write was perceived as a threat. All this dehumanization that I learned in that class was depicted near-faithfully in this film. Seeing that spark in Solomon slowly die out was tragic and painful to watch. I tear-up just thinking about it.

This film banks on emotion and making sure that every atrocity, every sin, that was committed by this country was made known. Many of us do know our country's history and this film takes delight in making audiences uncomfortable, perhaps as a stark contrast to last year's "lighter" Django Unchained. There are quite a few exceptionally long takes that allow us to get a sense of the characters' plights, and not just limited to Solomon. One of the film's troubling sequences was an attempted lynching on Solomon--it's an oxymoron to rank which act is worse when it comes to slavery. This sequence is quite lengthy and harshly juxtaposes this heinous act with innocence and cultural norms. It's one of many unsettling moments.

I know I said the film "takes delight in making audiences uncomfortable," which makes me think that this film is pure Oscar bait. At this time of the year, almost any kind of film can be considered Oscar bait because, surprise, it's Oscar season! Additionally, at times I felt that the film was too focused on showing the brutality of mid-19th century America that it almost forgot about character development. The film's "villains" are somewhat one-dimensional but they are played with such elegance that I cannot fault their characterization entirely. When your supporting cast includes Benedict Cumberbatch, Sarah Paulson, Paul Giamatti, and badass Michael Fassbender (who is absolutely despicable here), you've got a winner.

The film's other best performance comes from newcomer Lupita Nyong'o, who plays the tragic Patsey. It's a performance that needs to be seen and recognized. Ejiofor was also very damn brilliant that he has given one of the year's best performances; his transition is one of the most tragic characterizations I've seen in film since Adrien Brody's Szpielman in The Pianist.
