The premise of this movie (forgive me for saying) wasn't anything that excited me when I first heard about it, possibly because of the fact that there have been so many films about slavery before. At school when I was 13 we were shown the series Roots, detailing the life of a slave taken from his home, and so I judged this film by its topic and only took a mild interest because of the actors involved. 
However, the moment it started, the film felt different. Unlike many similar films or series' I have seen, this film did more than offer up moral absolutes; slavery is wrong, all slavers were evil etc. Instead, it promoted a connection with the characters that I had not been expecting, and actually made me question the situation of not just the slaves but those who were effected by it. Halfway through the film I was wondering if I would have become an abolitionist if I had been alive at the time. Of course, judging by 21st Century morals we all would say that we would, but the anxieties of the sympathetic white characters did offer up a possible reason for why it took so long for anyone to oppose it.
Reading that back, it looks like I'm trying to justify the actions of white workers and slavers, but I'm not. I won't say too much about the story, as you really do need to see it yourself, but I will say what I think made the film have such an impact on me whilst I was watching it. Of course, you go into the cinema expecting to be shocked, but the emotional impact of this film does not come through the first scenes, in which Solomon is ripped from his life, his home and his family. No, for me the thing that had me close to tears was that by the middle of the film you aren't shocked by the beatings and the cruelty; you simply expect it. In this way, you are almost sharing the journey of Solomon to a degree. The slaves are dehumanised so effectively that it transports you back to the time of the slave trade, in which these were common occurrences. This is of course horrific, but it is then that you appreciate what an effective film this is. It is the ability of 12 years a slave to make the events personal that leads to a true consideration of events, and that is why I urge everyone to go and see it.

From British director, Steve McQueen, based on the memoirs of Solomon Northup.

Starring Chiwetel Ejiofor, Michael Fassbender, Lupita Nyong'o, Benedict Cumberbatch and Brad Pitt, the film tells the remarkable story of an educated, free man deceived, abducted and sold into slavery in pre Civil War America.

Enduring cruelty at the hands of two slave owners, as well as treated with unexpected kindness, Solomon struggles not only to survive but to retain his dignity. In the twelfth nightmarish year of his heart wrenching story, Solomon has a chance meeting with an abolitionist which forever changes his life.

Ejofor is outstanding as the tormented lead, recounting Northup's harrowing journey to a life of liberty. Fassbender puts in his best performance to date as Northup's second master, a monstrous, sadistic tyrant who tolerates nothing from his property except total submission. Newcomer Nyong'o exhibits the strength and frailty of a woman burden by the horrors of a life that has never experienced joy.

12 Years a Slave is an brutal, soberly evocative reminder that shines a light on the most shameful and unspeakable chapter in American history.

12 Years a Slave. It tells the brutal account of Solomon Northup's enslavement. After so vividly scrutinising the agony and the plight of Irish revolutionary Bobby Sands, in his 2008 directorial debut "Hunger" and following that up with an equally agonising portrait of sex addiction in 2011's "Shame", artist turned director Steve McQueen quickly established himself as a very raw and unflinching filmmaker. As did, his fearless leading actor Michael Fassbender. Now, with their third collaboration, it doesn't look like they've had any change of heart and tackle the painful subject of slavery in 1840's America.

Based on the incredible true story of Solomon Northup (Chiwetel Ejiofor), a free black man in pre-Civil War Saratoga. As a talented musician he is lured to Washjngton D.C. with the promise of paid work before awaking to find himself in chains and sold into slavery where he endures a long fight for his freedom.

It could be said that the common theme that runs throughout McQueen's films is polemical; "Hunger" addressed the political atrocities forced upon the Irish while "Shame" addressed the nuerotic, psychological condition satyriasis and how it's just as empty and unfulfilling for men as nymphomania is for women. With "12 Years A Slave", there's no doubt about the polemic that McQueen is addressing. It's one that has resided in the heart and history of America (and the world) since it's inception and one that should never be forgotten. On this evidence it's clear that McQueen is in no mood to allow you to forget. He depicts these atrocities with such brutal condemnation and documents this dark period of American history with the subtlety of a sledgehammer. He refuses to pull any punches, even lingering long on shots of abuse and punishment, forcing you to stay with it and not giving you the chance to divert your gaze. One scene in particular has Solomon on his tiptoes, noose around his neck and struggling to preserve his life by staying upright. Meanwhile, the plantation workers go about their business and children play in the background. It's sobering and excruciating to watch but essential viewing.
Much has been said about the solid work of Ejiofor in the lead and his acclaimed performance is entirely justified. This is an actor that manages to convey emotion with the blink of an eye and extremely subtle facial expressions. He's so subtle that his performance is an absolute masterclass in minimalism. This leaves Fassbender to play the opposite. He tears the screen up with a ferocity and shows why McQueen always manages to get the very best from him. They're starting to develop an almost Scorsese/DeNiro like understanding and I, for one, welcome it wholeheartedly. When "Hunger" and "Shame" were released, there was no other actor that was better or more committed to their roles than Fassbender yet he was shamefully overlooked for awards. It's now time to remedy those mistakes and recognise this man as one of the very best around at present. Fassbender's Edwin Epps is a detestable and highly controlling individual. He's prone to wild fits of rage but under his eyes hide the gaze of a man who's struggling with his own demons while relying on scripture to excuse his abusive behaviour. The object of his unwanted affection and abuse is the fragile Patsey (Lupita Nyong'o) who not only has to endure all physical and sexual abuse from Epps but she must also endure the jealous wrath of his wife (Sarah Paulson). For Patsey, there really is no let-up in the relentless nature of her existence. If Nyong'o is the beating heart of the film then Fassbender is the visceral head and Ejiofor, most certainly, the dignified soul. All three of them deliver performances of such outstanding vigour and commitment. As much as it's these three who shine the most, though, the surrounding cast members deliver some solid work too; Cumberbatch as a more gentlemanly slave owner; Giamatti as a insensitive trader and particularly the aforementioned Paulson as Epps' vindictive spouse. There's also some light delivered from producer Brad Pitt but his late appearance as one of the truly decent white characters seems somewhat misplaced and distracting due to his star wattage. It's also around this point that you realise that the film has no real sense of time, it's hard to decipher where we stand and how long Solomon has been subjected to his detention and labour and even though the film  so thoroughly captures the endurance of the human spirit, ultimately, it fails to add anything further to the ongoing debate about slavery itself.
Despite these were minor quibbles, though, McQueen still delivers a vital and overwhelming cinematic achievement.

With Steven Spielberg's "Lincoln" drawing the film year to a close in 2012, it's fitting that McQueen should end 2013 with what could be considered that film's perfect companion piece. Not easy viewing by any means but this is an important and cathartic elegy about the determination for survival against insuperable odds.

In the past five years, Steve McQueen burst onto the film scene with his chilling portrait of the Irish hunger strikes in Hunger and his intense look at sex addiction in Shame. With only a few films under his belt, McQueen has managed to capture the energy and rhythm of the human condition with the eye of a painter. As 12 Years a Slave is his third film, it is proof positive that he is one of the most revered and phenomenal filmmakers of the last decade as Paul Thomas Anderson was a decade ago. Beyond the intense visuals of violence that mirror that of Pasolini's Salo-minus the body mutilation and coprophagia- the imagery of the plantations and South are as vibrant as a Gainsborough painting, which emphasize the beauty and evil of the world.

First, let's talk about the beginning. The opening two or three scenes served no purpose other than to confuse. It first seemed as though he was a slave, and then he became free living in New York, or he was dreaming. Obviously that was not the case. The part where he wakes up and then starts to have sex with the woman next to him is also very unclear. It seems like that was just thrown in there with no context at all. There was no explanation of the scene or why it happened, and there were no later ramifications from it. It was a noteworthy event that was just a passing scene. 
Except for the opening scenes, the movie has no other serious flaws. There were some issues with the casting (namely Brad Pitt and Paul Dano as John Tibeats). For the most part though, the acting was superb. Clearly, Chiwetel Ejiofor was brilliant. Michael Fassbender and Lupita Nyong'o (Patsy) were great.
It is somewhat disappointing that his legal endeavors were not in the film. It would be just as interesting to see his frustration with the laws at that time that prevent him from attaining justice. 
The ending was rather anticlimactic as well. He goes through 12 years of pain and suffering, and all but loses hope of ever seeing his family again. When the moment finally comes when he sees them again, it was not particularly poignant. It was brief, and only moderately emotional. It left much to be desired.
The movie did not do well at all at keeping track of time. It only once, I believe, states the date, and that was at the beginning. This may not be a problem, but it also never shows any lapses of time or signs of aging or changing of seasons. The entire movie takes place in the summer. Never once did it show cold weather. When it goes from one scene to the next, it could be later that day, the next day, the next week, the next month, or even the next year, it is very unclear. By the time he was freed, it only seemed like he had been in slavery a few years, rather than 12.
The sound effects when a slave was struck (kicked, slapped, whipped, etc.) were unnecessary and over the top. They were so clearly artificial, like you would expect in a super hero cartoon. It detracts from the realistic, raw violence that was going on.
Overall, the movie did well to show the suffering and frustration Solomon endured while he was a slave. It highlights the stark abuse of slaves from their owners, even to the point of being unsettling. It does a great job of adapting an interesting story into a fantastic film.

Kidnapped and sold into slavery, Solomon Northup's right to be a free man in pre-Civil War New York is cruelly stolen from him by a network of white man intent on keeping slavery alive. There are subtle indications throughout as to when the hatred towards him began, the events which led to him being marked out as a man whom white men wanted removed from his "free" status and demoted to the rank of property. As an entertainer and family man, Solomon was living his life the right way and was becoming a pillar of his society. I can only be thankful to him that he manages to escape and tell his story and that it took a man of immense intelligence and uncluttered vision to bring this story to the big screen. Steve McQueen III is hence arguably the most important film director operating in the Western world right now. Every element of Northup's journey is sinister, from the ripple of the waves upon which the slave boat travels to the trees and reeds which decorate the New Orleans swamp and surrounding areas of the plantations to which were taken. McQueen's ability to allow the camera to linger where necessary and to conduct events which are just outside of our vision add power to an already emotionally overwhelming narrative. Much of what Solomon and the other slaves endured is relevant to the black experience today. The film works as a warning to black people that many tolerate us but very few actually regard us as equals, capable of the same level of ingenuity and deserving of the same level of respect. Chiwetel Ejiofor has been an outstanding talent in his art for at least a decade now, delivering breathtaking performances on stage and on screen and he proves to be the perfect man for this most difficult and haunting of roles. A serious high quality film about slavery and its consequences had been long overdue until 12 years a Slave arrived, suitably following shortly after the fantasy of "Django Unchained" and the nobility of "The Butler". Every element of the slavery of black people, to which we have become accustomed through years of watching and reading are touched upon in some way here, displaying McQueen's keen eye for detail and significance. I feared a personal emotional breakdown when my date to see this film drew nearer but I left empowered and thankful in the knowledge that Solomon, and all the other unfortunate human beings who suffered such wrongs due to hate and disrespect, paved the way for people like me to continue the noble fight against oppression and spitefulness whether mental, verbal or physical. I would suggest that my viewing of Steve McQueen's second film, "Shame", with its unflinching account of sex addiction, and its pitfalls, prepared me for 12 Years. A masterpiece and landmark film, 12 Years a Slave may not receive the awards I feel it deserves but it is one of the most important films we as a human race have produced and its power will never die.

I will be honest. Twelve years a slave is not the easiest of movies to watch. Nor should it be, because its only goal is to cast an unflinching glare on the institution of slavery, perhaps the darkest stain on our nation's history.
	At no point does it try to shield viewers from the horror it is exposing, but neither does it fall into the realm of sappy tear jerking. It simply shows the truth of slavery, which is that it was an inherently brutal and cruel institution base on fear and the complete control of another person. Solomon Northrop discovered this firsthand when he was lured from his comfortable life in New York and sold into bondage by men he thought were his friends. 
	Chiwetel Ejiofor portrays the horror and bewilderment Solomon felt upon the realization of his captivity and his grim determination never to accept his state with stoicism and restraint. At time it may seem that he- and by extension the film- lacks emotion, but this is represents not a lack of emotion, but rather numbness, alienation, and repression of his rage and anguish. It's only when you look closer that you see his despair, loneliness, and profound homesickness. Solomon's repeated maxim is that you cannot let yourself be consumed with despair; for then you are lost and your master has won. 
	Just as Ejofor shows great restraint in his acting, the film shows admirable restraint in not portraying all white Southerners or even all slave owners as vicious evil men, while still not apologizing for their actions or letting anyone off the hook. Master Ford is a decent and surprisingly kind man for a slaveholder and is clearly uncomfortable with the more inhumane aspects of the institution. Yet he paternalistically believes that it is enough to be a good master, and when Solomon's life is threatened the best he can do is to sell him off to a man with a notorious reputation for harshness and anger. 
	And Master Epps is a harsh and angry man. Played by Michael Fassbender with intensity, barely contained fury, and not a trace of mercy or humanity, he is every bit as hatable as Cotton Candy from Django Unchained, yet far more believable. A sadist and an inveterate racist, he believes that his every misfortune is the fault dark skinned chattel and that the lash is the solution to every problem. Besides his propensity for using his fist and the lash against his slaves, he also shows 'favor' to his favorite slave woman by directing his affections towards her. And his is the kind of affection that is not only imposed against her will but violently forced upon her. The kind of affection which fills his wife with jealousy and hatred the girl. The kind of affection which makes a woman wishes she was dead.
	His cruelty is exceptional even by the standards of the time, but even when it not overtly brutal, the slave's life is one of toil and degradation. It's a life of long days working in the hot sun, of debasing yourself before any white man, of being subject to your master's every whim.   To survive a man learns to keep his head down, to never stand up for himself or let on that he knows as much as he does. And he does it out of fear. Twelve years never lets the viewer forget that the entire institution of slavery is based on fear of violence and death. Fear so strong that it breaks a person, makes them go about their work while a man hangs from a tree, even whip their fellow slave lest they be in the same place.
	Nor is only the slave who is affected by the evils of slavery, though he bears it the hardest by far. Seemingly gentle men are made callous by their participation in the peculiar institution, even as the suffering they cause, directly or not, eats at their conscience Even in the midst of hypocritical self pity, a white cotton picker shares a nugget of truth; whipping other men day in day out for a living doesn't sit well with a man's conscience. He either eases his guilt with excuses or numbs himself with drink, because any man with a heart knows deep down that slavery is a vile and inhumane practice.
	This is a lesson that Twelve Years never lets the audience forget, though some may wish to. Even the happy ending is at best bittersweet, because when the nightmare is over and he's a free man again, it still doesn't make everything right. He will never get those twelve years back, so much has changed in his absence, and while he regained his freedom, the other slaves on the plantation don't have theirs. It's a depressing thought, but this was a depressing reality, and one we should all be painfully aware of.

"12 Years A Slave" is based on the real story of Solomon Northup (Chiwetel Ejiofor), a free black man living in New York, who is abducted and sold into slavery in Louisiana. It challenges the viewer to consider both the individual life of Solomon Northup, and use his story as a springboard for a serious discussion on slavery, given that screen time is spent entirely with the victims. Indeed, it is a brutal, unflinching portrayal of the torture inflicted on slaves in 19th century America. It is definitely hard to watch (some people left our screening during a particularly brutal whipping scene).Most actors get very little screen time. Paul Giamatti and Sarah Paulson are seen for a few minutes, but are both great, as are Benedict Cumberbatch, Michael Fassbender  (as evil slave-owner  Edwin Epps), and Brad Pitt. But the real star is Chiwetel Ejiofor. His performance as Solomon is unforgettable and very Oscar worthy.

Steve McQueen is one of the best directors working today. He made Shame which is probably one of the best movies of the last 10 years, and the very solid political drama Hunger. All his movies, even Shame, are about characters who are enslaved in some way or another. So its hardly surprising that he chose to make a movie about American slavery. 

      Some people have complained that there has been too many movies on the topic of slavery, but I really don't think many have the same raw power that Steve McQueen and his cast have accomplished here. It's a pretty harrowing look at the cruelty people are capable of. By linking the theme of slavery with one mans frightening tale of injustice, the movie is an unflinching and brutal account of historic events.
 
     The performances are outstanding. Chiwetel Ejiofar gives a wonderfully commited performance as the stoic hero Solomon Northup, a black man from a privileged backround, who was kidnapped and sold to work on a plantation in New Orleans in the 1800's(the movie is based on the true-life memoirs of Northup). For a movie like this to work you need an antagonist who is interesting, not just a one-eyed depiction of cruelty in the south. Michael Fassbender gives a predictably brilliant performance as Edwin Epps. He is a racist, tyrannical sadist who treats his slaves(or as he calls them his ''property'') with all possible cruelty. But he is also a complex, mercurial character. His character has the stuff of a great oppressive villain. He is religious and preaches about justice, yet sees no contradiction in his own wicked actions. He is threatened by Northup who is physically superior and more intelligent. He is also madly in love with one of his own slaves, Patsey (Lupita Nyong'o). In her debut performance Nypng'o is a revelation. There is a very strong supporting cast, including Paul Giammati, Benedict Cumberbatch, Sarah Paulson and Brad Pitt.

      The movie tackles the grim subject of slavery with integrity and is unabashed in its message of cruelty and justice gone awry. It's wonderfully filmed by McQueen. The shots of the southern landscape are at once gorgeous and gothic. This is a very satisfying and accomplished piece of cinema.

12 Years a Slave director Steve McQueen is on those authors whose movies will be remembered for many, many decades. This movie, just like Shame and Hunger, goes beyond the masterful aesthetic of the picture and camera to a sober, solid and honest drama about a free man who is kidnapped and sold into slavery on the United States. 12 Years a Slave embodies by nature the characteristics required to be considered an award winning movie, that is sure, but the movie goes a lot further and disconnects itself from that award aura. The north-American slavery theme is not a recurring one in cinema, even if the recent Django Unchained walked those steps one year ago. McQueen proposes a well paced movie that chooses feeling over gore, atmosphere over shock. The movie develops and gets better over time, presenting a lot of well written real characters that end up being shadowed by Chiwetel Ejiofor and Michael Fassbender's unbelievable performances, only matched by Cate Blanchett's Blue Jasmine this year. 12 Years a Slave is not an easy movie to sit through, nor is it a particularly hard one. It is, above the drama, a contemplative movie that respects the audience. This is not a candy to chew on, but a gourmet dish to look at before tasting. Cinema at its best level, and probably the best movie of 2013.

Firstly the gripes, which is why this is a four-star "very good film" and not a 5-star "masterpiece"
Solomon Northup, the freeman but son of a freed slave. lives in a very posh house with clothes, manners and nuclear family to match . After he is kidnapped and returns 12 years later, his wife and family are still living in upper middle-class dignity and wealth... Umm, I don't think so, Mr McQueen.  I guess the filmmaker is trying to get us to identify with the humanity of the victim as if he were "one of us", but poor people and poorly mannered people are just as much people, and the film  half-falls into the trap of suggesting that the real offense lies in the fact that before he was taken and enslaved, Solomon was RICH and SUCCESSFUL!  Oh dearie me.....
Gripe 2 is that Solomon is so very lovely, and there's hardly a character flaw to be seen, so his character comes over a little lightweight and fantastic, which is a shame. Horrible stress and suffering may bring out grace and maturity in a person, but usually that is after the childishness and rage have surfaced first, and there is little on show here of any character progression, not only in Solomon, but the other characters too. There are  some not-so-nasty white men, but perilously little character progression. 
BUT.... this is a very good film. It is well directed with Steve McQueen's trademark good judgement of showing the dilemmas involved within difficult and contentious issues. The story is well paced, well scripted even if the characters are static . There are moments of stillness and beauty here which counterpoint the violence and inhumanity effectively -lovely place-shots of Swamp Cypress and the still evening atmosphere.
 The film makes its point about the inhumanity of slavery by some telling scenes- the separation of a mother from her children at a slave auction;  naked  slaves being examined by potential buyers; brutal flogging by the sadistic plantation owner of his sex-and-cotton-picking slave Patsey for leaving the plantation without permission to garner herself some soap; Solomon ,  overcome by a desire  to run when he is first trusted to leave the plantation and fetch supplies, only to stumble onto two escaped slaves being lynched by the posse; perhaps the most powerful  scene is when Solomon is just saved from a lynching after he retaliated against a white overseer but is left strung up with his toes just touching the ground. As everyone awaits the plantation master's return,no-one dares to release him, and  the other slaves come out of hiding in their shacks to carry on as normal in the background, as Solomon tip-toes in the mud, barely able to breath. The contrast of the quotidien  with the horrific and violent makes a powerful impact. 
One irony stood out for me- Solomon is quietly biding his time, believing in hope that an opportunity will eventually come his way to get word back to his "people" up North to rescue him. But when Patsey requests that he help her "escape", by assisting her suicide, he declines as the deed is beneath him. Perhaps his self-preservation is all to him, as it must be so often when people find themselves in peril. The irony is completed when he has to administer the flogging himself at gunpoint, which he chooses to do, rather than be shot. We don't see any remorse or compunction over this incident, strangely. 
So, comparing to the rash of slave movies recently, I would suggest that 12 Years a slave stands above the rest. It illustrates the human cost of the obscenity of slavery. Not as worthy or populist as Lincoln, not a cartoon like Django Unchained, not as removed as Amazing Grace. Perhaps no one film can cover a subject so big, that is still  as relevant as ever in our world where de-humanisation in its many guises is rife and often unseen by the masses that perpetrate the offences.

His style of an unflinching, often static camera becomes more important to the drama than ever before, and the visceral power of ugly images is made striking as it is often set against the beauty of a shamed landscape. Indeed, there is at least one scene here that may well go down as classic, and be talked about as people did of Omar Sharif's entrance in 'Lawrence Of Arabia'. Other moments of long-held shots where the changing expression of an actor thinking is equal to any dialogue they could be given prove very brave and affecting.

The film manages to examine the fact that the slaves were not the only victims of the atrocity, which is impressive, and the the whole piece carries with it a weight of obvious importance and care given to a vital story that should be seen by all. That said, there is some over-scoring in the first act, it is arguably a little plodding at points, and an odd casting of Brad Pitt in a role which may have been more befitting of an unknown is a tad distracting, so it is hard to give it a full 5 stars. Certainly not an easy watch, but a typically bold piece of cinema from an ever-uncompromising artist.

Having the ability to cinematically re-tell a chapter of history has expanded rapidly in this generation. The majority of bio-pics and historical-dramas feature a story with oppressive contents; however, there are the odd few true stories which depict a touch of hope within humanity. 12 Years A Slave tells a story of pre-Civil War America that represents the brutality of slavery whilst within it, introduces Solomon Northup's extraordinary and touching tale during enslavement. Following in similar footsteps to Steven Spielberg's Schindler's List and Roman Polanski's The Pianist, 12 Years A Slave certainly does provide enough visual persuasion of 1800s American slavery whilst also becoming a fantastic bio-pic filled with sublime performances from its ensemble cast and breath-taking mise-en-scéne.

Although slavery in America occurred in the 19th century, for Hollywood to illustrate and promote an oppressive piece of their history may have been difficult. Still, the aim was to interpret American slavery as it was at the time. Last year we saw Django Unchained, a slight historical twist of slavery in the US but 12 Years A Slave more realistically portrays a brutal reflection, especially the attention to detail in moments of violence and abuse. Furthermore, slavery in 12 Years A Slave is centred primarily on Northup's personal experience in which the whole concept becomes both disturbing and inspiring. Similar to the representation of the Holocaust in Schindler's List and Nazi-invaded Poland in The Pianist, Northup's 12-year odyssey of enslavement exposed inner faith, which is the key to a bio-pic told within a hostile environment.

Prior to directing 12 Years A Slave, Steve McQueen had only made two features - Shame and Hunger, both of which are low-budget, British independent films. In their own ways, both have been sadistic projects from the perspective of its protagonist. In that sense, 12 Years A Slave and its contents became prominent to McQueen's directorial style and subject choice. 12 Years A Slave became less independent than McQueen's previous works and had consequently become a high-standard film, with a higher budget and more Hollywood-y touch to it. At the same time, it still maintained the perspective of Northup within the dark and raw surroundings. Similarly, while the subject is oppressive, the actual production of 12 Years A Slave was beautiful, particularly Sean Bobbit's cinematography who occasionally highlights the natural landscapes; therefore, enhancing the realistic touch of 1800s America. 

Throughout his career up until now, Chiwetel Ejiofor has been 'that actor' who made regular supporting appearances behind central stars. However, Ejiofor leads the pack in this historical-drama with a superb breakthrough performance. Similar to Adrien Brody's performance in The Pianist, Ejiofor reflects Northup's clear family-minded, sensitive nature whilst exhibiting the horrors of slavery. We observe many African-Americans in 12 Years A Slave but Northup becomes the black male slave as his journey of torture, pain and sorrow illustrates a clear understanding to viewers from just one man's viewpoint. Nevertheless, Ejiofor has finally had his breakthrough role and deserves to be an Oscar contender. Meanwhile, Lupita Nyong'o makes her acting debut in an outstanding performance as female slave Petsey. Like Ejiofor, Nyong'o's performance is a representation of gender within American slavery and her role impressively interpreted the vulnerability and innocence of women during enslavement as well as the pain, cries and pure fright.

Michael Fassbender returns for the third consecutive time with Steve McQueen. Following his previous critically acclaimed performance in Shame, Fassbender shines once again as the sadistic plantation owner Edwin Epps. Fassbender has portrayed cold, bitter characters in the past and this became advantageous to his role in 12 Years A Slave. He superbly reflected the cold-hearted, sinister mannerism of Epps; therefore, honestly depicting the cruelty of Caucasian plantation owners towards their slaves. In addition, Benedict Cumberbatch makes a decent appearance as William Ford, another plantation owner but more benevolent than Epps. Paul Dano also gets some screen time as Ford's abusive and incredibly racist carpenter. Being arguably the most racist character in the entire film, Paul Dano brilliantly enhanced further realism among their treatment of black people during that period. As a result, it has become his greatest performance since There Will Be Blood or even Little Miss Sunshine.

Whether based on real-life events or an original screenplay, the cinematic representation of slavery is bound to raise curiosity and occasional controversy, especially when there's slavery involved. 12 Years A Slave marvellously depicts to viewers how America was in the South during that period, which was enhanced further by McQueen's superb directing, excellent performances from particularly Ejiofor, Fassbender and Nyong'o. McQueen's latest is as energetic, drama-wise, and is not far among Schindler's List and The Pianist in terms of expressing human drama through historical facts. Nevertheless, 12 Years A Slave may be a stomach-turning film but there is no doubt it is one of the most powerful bio-pics of this generation and will be a strong contender for Best Picture.

I liked the concept of looking at slavery from the perspective of a free man kidnapped into slavery.  It allowed a greater empathy as we could both relate to his situation and view the plight of those borm into slavery through his eyes.  There was a real opportunity for this to be a truly great film, but whilst it has some very powerful scenes, ultimately it fails to deliver on its promise.
I think there are 2 reasons for this.  Firstly, it is just too long for the material it contains.  There are scenes which are too drawn out.  For instance a scene near the end when Solomon just looks vacantly at the sky for some considerable time.  Presumably this is done to emphasise his despair at his plight - but we know that.  The unnecessary dwelling and the slowness of pace don't quite lead to boredom but they do give a sense of irritation that a story waiting to be told is not being told.
The second point is that the film focuses strongly on Solomon's relationships with his white slave masters and much less so on his relationships with his fellow slaves.  Ironically the fact that the interaction between Solomon and his masters is so well done (particularly the beautifully crafted character of Epps) only serves to emphasise lack of focus on the other slaves.  The message this gives is that Solomon empathises more with his white slave masters than his fellow slaves because they, like him, were born free men.  That is not to say Solomon has no empathy for the plight of others (the scene where he is forced to whip Patsey shows that he does) it is just that this aspect of his slavery is not really explored.  Perhaps this is intentional and is a comment on his attitudes as a free born black, but if McQueen feels that Solomon's character sees himself as a free man first and a negro second then his relationship with his fellow slaves should have been explored further.
So whilst this is undoubtedly a very good film on a number of levels the lasting impression is one of disappointment that the opportunity has not been taken to make this a great film.

It soon became clear that there would be no exciting escape attempt or mutiny, just a grim round of work, beatings and weird relationships. This was a strange plantation to be kidnapped to! As a piece of historical re-enactment it failed because it confused the crime of owning black people as slaves with less common mental illnesses as displayed by Michael Fassbender's psychopathic slave-owner and his equally disturbed wife. Their hatred and violence tended to work against the aims of the film by making their ghoulish behaviour seem too excessive to be true or at least generally true of slave owners in those days. 12 Years a Slave caught my attention as one of the most highly acclaimed films of 2013, in what was mostly a dreary cinematic year. But Steve McQueen is a great film director and the cast is full of talented names, so I simply had to see it.

12 Years a Slave has a truly passionate atmosphere which proves that Steve McQueen truly has his hear in the effort of telling this story. It opens with beautiful cinematography shot on some strongly vibrant locations with plenty of colour to symbolise the opportunity and life that the protagonist Solomon Northup has, and soon after it becomes very dry and monochromatic to change the feel of the film to a more grim and intense film. It soon becomes clear that Steve McQueen has used his strength as a film director to render 12 Years a Slave as a visual experience, as well as an emotional one. 
Steve McQueen's directional style is great because of his detached method. He takes a step back instead of a claustrophobic method, because instead of getting so up close and personal that you feel like you're experiencing the horrors of Slavery yourself, Steve McQueen's method explains to you that you will never feel the horror that these people have felt. Steve McQueen takes the most real path and still manages to stay true to Solomon Northup's account of events, and he depicts the horrific drama in such an intensely powerful way without ever going excessive. Arguable, 12 Years a Slave is uncomfortable viewing for some people, but it's that kind of experience that needs to happen so that the story of Solomon Northup is told. And it's execution of his story emphasises simply how he is a hero merely because he survived. That is a hell of a thing, and it works it to maximum effect.
And the script of the story is excellently convincing in its handling of 19th Century language, particularly in terms of specific language terms such as racial slurs. The way the script handles the word "N*gger" is very well done because it implements in so smoothly that it becomes just another word and therefore enhances how the viewer perceives the time and setting that 12 Years a Slave is happening in. The production design manages to perfectly capture a feel for the 1841 timeframe that the story is set in, and the costumes add to the convincing aesthetic qualities, so 12 Years a Slave proves convincing in all areas, and has a gentle pace to it.
But what it so powerful about it is the fact that it has such a strong theme of nihilism. Whenever hope comes by in 12 Years a Slave, it is picked off bit by bit until it lies dead on the ground. It gives off the real sense of hopelessness that enslaved human beings have been forced to face the darkest and most hopeless life available to them. So 12 Years a Slave is an emotionally gripping and gritty story which benefits from a constantly intense atmosphere which rides the strength of an impeccable musical score, great visuals and strong direction combining the sufficient script with the incredible cast.
Chiwetel Ejiofor is perfect in every conceivable area as the man portraying Solomon Northup in 12 Years a Slave for one precise reason: he never slips up ever so slightly. If you watch him closely, you can see that every inch of him physically believes that he really is a man forced into slavery. The amount of intensity in his physicality is immense and shockingly powerful, and he shows off just what the true extent of being an actor is all about. He completely embodies his role and the identity of his character is lost as his spirit dissolves so that viewers can see him from the same perspective that slave traders do. It is an intense experience, and Chiwetel Ejiofor makes it one lead by an incredible performance. I was mesmerised by the skill of acting in Chiwetel Ejiofor's soul and 12 Years a Slave is unforgettable if for nothing else than simply for his flawless lead performance as Solomon Northup.
Michael Fassbender has never looked so intense, or as darkly evil as he has in 12 Years a Slave. The antagonistic nature of his character Edwin Epps is intensified by a burning rage within Michael Fassbender which is so hot that the anger comes out on the surface so much that it seems like he actually has a hate for African-Americans. I mean obviously he doesn't, but he so flawlessly convinces viewers that he does that the product is almost too shocking for viewers to handle. His performance is definitely one of his best and the product of his performance is so powerful that he more than earns an Academy Award nomination for Best Supporting actor, he deserves it. I believe that it is his single greatest performance of all his career in 12 Years a Slave. 
Lupita Nyong'o makes a name for herself in 12 Years a Slave because she pours such a sad and passionate strength into her performance as Patsey through simple characteristics of acting which show off just what it is to be a great actress in such a heart-wrenching film. Some of the time she finds the ability to single-handedly dominate the emotional drama of the story with great performance strength, and so she makes a great addition to the cast. I don't believe that she had enough screen time to earn her Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress, but the strength of her acting skill in her few scenes is very effective.
Benedict Cumberbatch is interesting to see for any fan of Sherlock since he's in a role incredibility different yet still manages to nail the character head on. It is never easy to determine whether his character is a good man because he is both a friendly person to Solomon Northup and a slave owner at the same time. Benedict Cumberbatch easily walks the thin line between both elements and does it with natural skill where his accent never comes out and his acting skill simply flourishes naturally.
Brad Pitt does the same thing in his brief role. His voice alone makes him a genial presence and his delivery of his extensive lines are done excellently. Brad Pitt makes a terrific impact in his brief appearance in 12 Years a Slave and it makes the film a more enjoyable experience.
The issues with 12 Years a Slave are minor, but still present. 
For one thing, the high quantity of nihilism and sadness can prove emotionally wrecking for viewers or dull to the less patient crowds. And its pretty consistent in repeating itself until the end with few surprises coming along. Essentially, since the formula for the slavery drama has been set in motion long ago, 12 Years a Slave is mostly a predictable story which piles pessimism and nihilism up and up until the mountain is too high to climb. The first time I watched the film I was overwhelmed by that and felt emotionally manipulated, but Re-watching it a second time made me realise the beauty of the film is its melancholy. It holds no restraints in telling its story of sadness and it tugs at the heartstrings with such intensity. I will never feel the full effect of slavery as I never will experience such a victimised situation, but I can't the closest to feeling it as I possibly could thanks to 12 Years a Slave.

Solomon Northup is a free African-American man living in Syracuse, New York.  A talented musician, a loving husband, and an admirable father. He is introduced to two men who act astounded at his ability to move them with his music. On a trip he is taken on to do performances, he is betrayed, kidnapped, and sold into slavery. With no idea how it happened, he demands he be let go. He pleads to his holders that he is a free man, but his new owners think it's nothing but lies. Soon Solomon is going by the name of Platt, working the field in the hot sun, forced to hide his real identity from everyone. Over the 12 years he serves a slave, he is sent to work for many different owners at different plantations with what appears to be no end in sight.

Steve McQueen has crafted a powerful, haunting drama here. The story is unsettling, but there is no sense turning a blind eye to a story that couldn't feel more real, especially with how McQueen brings it to the screen. The direction and cinematography is top notch, and the movie is carried on Chiwetel Ejiofor's shoulders throughout. He provides an amazing performance, as does everyone involved. Lupita N'yongo provides a heartbreaking performance, and Michael Fassbender channels such hate and evil, it's hard to see nothing but Edwin Epps, the plantation owner. These actors dissapear into their roles, making it feel real. Going into early 2014, it's hard for me to see 12 Years a Slave miss at the Oscars. It is exactly what the awards looks for.

On another note, is the violent aspect of the film. It feels real, and fills you with despair as you watch innocent people get beaten on. It adds a whole new layer of emotion to this film. A lot of people talk about how brutal and graphic the violence is, but I don't agree as much. The situations and the acts are brutal and horrific, but in terms of what the film shows, its hard to watch, but not to the point where I couldn't. The only complaints I have for 12 Years a Slave, is that it can be quite slow. That's not a fault of McQueen, for a story like this really couldn't be told any other way, and especially couldn't have been told better. While I say this, I gotta say by the end it was hard to believe 12 years of Solomon's life was depicted in the film. It feels like 1 or 2 years, not nearly 12. By the end, you can see the grief instilled in his face and the grey in his hair, but there was not much way of knowing how long it had really been. Other than those gripes I may have, it is a great drama that is sure to be the biggest player at the Oscars.

It was a hard movie to watch, though the filming/photography was superb.  It laid bare the complicated and wounded human psyche.  As I watched the suffering inflicted upon the slaves -- the whippings, the humiliations and cruelty, the dark shaming -- I could not but compare it to the Crucifixion.  Only this seemed like the Crucifixion magnified thousands of times.

There was the fundamentalist religion of the slave owners.  Their need for some divine justification for the ugly predicament of entitlement and blindness that they found themselves in.  Their own suffering and confusion at the darkness of their own souls, which they could not seem to find their way out of.

There was the music.  The Negro Spiritual - a beauty as consoling as Gregorian chant which rose up out of human suffering itself.

It's hard to know what to make of a single human life - its capacity for suffering and cruelty, as well as its capacity for joy and love.  How to make your way through the unique maze of human life that is given to each of us.  What's going on here?  What meaning is there in this suffering and struggle for justice?

On the way home I stopped at Whole Foods for some things for a soup that I want to make tomorrow.  I noticed the very special beauty of the young Black boys who were bagging my groceries.  No doubt descended from slaves.  We've come a ways from those times of slavery, I suppose, but I still believe that the root of slavery lives on in the prisons of this country. Underground, hidden.  Whatever is at the bottom of this evil has not yet been exposed.  Perhaps this movie is a beginning ...

Steve McQueen not only provides a gritty and brutal look at slavery and the emotional story of Solomon Northup, but he also makes this an unforgettable journey with his pristine direction.

Praised as "unflinching," but it's not. Not in its exploration of the reasons God-worshipping people could be so inhumane (there is no such inquiry), nor in its dispassionate display of the mental and physical torture endured by the slaves. What the admirers reference is the extended shot of Solomon Northrup dangling with a noose around his neck. But the scene (and the rest of the film) is as distant as the slaves who mustn't offer Solomon any assistance.  For all the inhumanity on display, director McQueen and screenwriter Ridley fail to provide the resonant humanity that Northrup's story deserves and needs. The memoirs convey an aching for his wife and children that is absent here, and the movie plays like a series of agonizing experiences that stir up moral outrage but don't adequately dramatize Northrup's horrific plight.

The story is about a musician living a calm and free life in Washington who is kidnapped and sold as a slave to a cotton plantation in the South. He is subjected to the worst treatment and humiliation imaginable. He longs for his wife and 2 children who do not know where he is. The story follows his plight through his slavery and a few of his fellow slaves. I will not reveal the ending.
Directed by Steve McQueen there are many disturbing scenes of grotesque violence. However the scene that steals the film for me is the scene towards the end where Solomon's gaze shifts from off screen to looking straight into the camera and stays there for a full 45 seconds to one minute. This powerful gaze is almost staring into the soul of the man whose dignity and freedom have been stripped from him.
Ejiofor gives an excellent account of himself. Fassbender is diabolical as the sadistic master who inflicts so much horror on his "possessions". Cumberbatch injects some warmth as a more benevolent master.
McQueen allows the camera to settle on the beautiful southern landscapes contrasting the sounds of nature with the horror of the victims of slavery. The horror is unflinching and he allows the camera to remain on the atrocities, stifling the viewer at times. There is no exploitation of violence here. This is a worthy masterpiece in many respects reminding me of films such as Spielberg's Schindler's List, Polanski's The Piano and Kubrick's Spartacus. 
McQueen's ending is a hopeful one but what I remember is that we should never go back to the horror of these times again and the violence,war and racism are ugly stains that are difficult to erase.

What is remarkable about 12 Years a Slave is not that McQueen refused to shy away from the horrific historical reality, but that so much of the Anglophone press found this (utterly right and correct) decision remarkable. Yes it is brutal viewing, slavery was a brutal thing, but to say it is 'hard to watch' is doing it the sort of disservice no one would think of for The Pianist or Schindler's List. It is eminently watchable, because it is brilliant cinema, and much of that brilliance comes from refusing to compromise on the the disgusting truth of slavery. It should be required viewing in every American middle school history class. It should enter the cultural lexicon the way the 1970s miniseries 'Roots' has done. It is a brilliant rendering of history, artfully shot, well acted and set to a typically superb Hans Zimmer soundtrack. And like all good history, it forces the audience to come to terms with the truth.

Say hello to the big Oscar contender and GRAVITY's biggest competitor. This is not another movie about slavery, it's THE MOVIE about slavery - and there may not be another one like it ever again. Here's the irony, the film's director and lead actor are not American, but British. Sometimes I guess it does take someone - or a group - from outside a bubble in order the see the true picture for what the situation really is - or was. 
That being said, we're given the true nature of what slavery was really like, and it's done with incredible care and precision by director Steve McQueen. There's not a frame or a cut in this film that resembles any kind of "flash" or "effect" for entertainment. Simpley, it's just subtle observation - nothing more - and that's all that is needed. Period. McQueen lets the occasional horrific brutalities speak for themselves on screen simply by doing one thing... keeping the camera rolling from one angle, but knowing exactly when to cut away - depending on the situation - before it becomes too much for the viewer. In other words, the film can be a tough one to swallow at times, but its respectful for the viewer by not letting the pieces be too big that you'd choke. The ensemble cast is magnificent here, each well-known and unknown actor perform their own parts with the best of their realistic abilities - never going over the top - no matter how intense some of them turn out to be. You expect to be angry at the scenes you will see in the film, but it surprising that it happens at the most subtle of scenes as compared to the ones you'd expect. For instance, when a slave is nearly hanged by a vengeful white man (PRISONERS' Paul Dano again!) he is saved by the owner's assistant, but left to hang there while standing on his toes in the mud because of an "ownership loophole" in "the system". What boggled my mind was how the camera keeps rolling on the same shot as the other slaves carry on around him - pretending as if nothing was happening - trying not to draw attention to themselves. While watching the film, the audience's biggest outcry came from one line spoken by the wife of the most sensible of slave owners (displayed here) following a slaved mother who was recently separated from her children for good. It was meant to be said with great sorrow when she days, "...It'll be all right. You're children will soon be forgotten." These scenes are examples of why this film stands out from the others. Further on, for the film's most intense sequence, Steve MqQueen pulls off a similar trick-that's become an Alfonso Cuaron (GRAVITY) signature move - by achieving a long one-take tracking shot to secure the reality of the beast that some of us are as humans to each other. I expect for this film to be nominated for almost every category possible at the Oscars obviously except for Best Visual Effects which is the Oscar that will be easily won by GRAVITY (and what a battle at the Awards it will be between these two films!). Hans Zimmer provides an incredibly subtle score, but his most haunting since Terrence Malick's THE THIN RED LINE. 12 YEARS A SLAVE is a film that must be seen by everyone around the world - especially in this country. No excuses America!

"12 Years a Slave" is not for the faint of heart.  Let me reiterate: This is a rough movie and it should only be approached in the proper mindset and with emotional preparation.  I am so glad that this autobiography has been revived and put onto the silver screen as it expresses the need to suppress bigotry and racism.  It goes beyond Civil Rights awareness and shows a need to leave racial tension in the past by graphically depicting one of the darkest chapters in our nation's history.  Although I am not a history expert, it is interesting to read that Dr. Emily West, specialist in the history of US slavery, has been quoted as saying that she has "never seen a film represent slavery so accurately."   To me, that is the seal of approval on this opportunity to view untainted history.  The film is so honest in its approach to the pure sadness of the situation, much like "Requiem for a Dream" or "The Passion of the Christ."  The heart of the film lies in the raw, life-like acting from its cast.  Chiwetel Ejiofor is a shoe-in for the Best Actor Oscar.  He gives one of the most vivid performances that I have ever seen, progressing from a strong-willed free man that will not be treated as a slave to the resignation of what he has become.  The slow breaking of this character is symbolized through his violin as every last shred of humanity is stripped away from him and he is left completely empty and void of his will.  His performance is matched by Lupita Nyong'o in the role of Patsey, who seems to be the leading choir for the Best Supporting Actress Oscar.  I was not sold on her performance until the whipping scene.  Most actress would interpret this scene with extreme duress and pain but Nyong'o approached it with resignation and exhaustion.  It told so much of her character - tired of the physical and emotional abuse, tired of living.  This role is quite an accomplishment for an actress in her first feature film.  These two are supported by seasoned actors who add different perspectives to this look at slavery.  Paul Giamatti is the slave trader who viewed it solely as a business without any emotion attached, Benedict Cumberbatch brings the perspective of a master that treated his slaves with respect, Paul Dano is the racist who wanted to cause trouble for the slaves, Brad Pitt is the white man opposed to slavery, and Michael Fassbender (nominated for Best Supporting Actor) gives the extremist view of slavery being sanctioned by the Bible (though I feel that this was a bit exaggerated to create more drama).  John Ridley's screenplay does an amazing job of taking this man's life and the people that he encountered and representing all perspectives of slavery while maintaining historical accuracy.  Adding to the realism of the film are the southern plantations on which they filmed, beautiful but filled with terror.  It is amazing how we become desensitized to the powerful images as  the film progresses (particularly hangings), and that we even grow to expect them.  The two most difficult scenes of the film are the most important and the most impressive.  First is the hanging scene.  This still shot is unrelenting as we are forced to watch this man slowly suffocate for minutes.  It transports us into the position of his fellow slaves who must just walk by, helpless to lend aid to him, and gets particularly rough when you see children playing in the background as if this is a common sight.  Even worse is the aforementioned whipping scene.  I won't spoil the scene but it is sure to leave an image that you will never forget, nearly uncut as we see the pain inflicted on a slave over something so trivial as wanting to bathe with soap.  Complete with a haunting theme by Hans Zimmer, the raw emotion runs throughout this film from start to finish, saving the most poignant and emotional scene for the end.  "12 Years a Slave" is incredible and when you are ready, it may change your life.

Perspective is always valuable ; it's impossible, really, to say now which of the films of this era will stand the test of time. The greats only become truly apparent much later. What we can say with some degree of certainty is when we've seen something genuinely outstanding in this day and time; when a film's subject matter, artistic contributors, global context all come together with perfect synergy to mark out a film as truly essential. I rarely say that people must or should see a film; our tastes vary, what we need in a night at the cinema might ebb and flow, our individual levels of the appropriateness of difficult content is never universal. We can guide as to quality, but we should be very slow to glibly say that everybody should see a film for fear of wearing out the expression, breeding apathy and cynicism rather than engagement with great art.

With the scene thus set, let's make this abundantly clear: everyone should see 12 Years A Slave. We can't say for now if it will become an all time great - though my personal feeling is that it will; we can say with conviction that it's easily the best film of recent years. It is perfectly directed and shot; the performances are uniformly strong without ever falling into the awards-bait trap of drawing attention to the performer; the story is conveyed clearly and moves quickly - this may be a film about important, urgent themes, but it's no worthy issue film. It's a story with characters who breathe deeply and fully. Despite the awful events played out before us, there's dignity, intelligent insight and perfectly judged moments of wit and humour even in the middle of tragedy and suffering.

The story is the true one of Solomon Northup, a free black man from New York in 1841 who is hoodwinked by people apparently keen to make the most of his musical talents and finds himself shipped to New Orleans, losing his name and spending 12 years as a slave. The film is based on the book Northup wrote after he'd gained his freedom, carrying with it a simple lack of sensationalism which refuses to flinch from realities we'd much rather avoid. The casual verbal hand-grenades of the n***** word; people as property; casual violence out of nothing; sexual abuse. It's not these, though, that really compel me - as haunting and brilliantly conveyed as they are. I was left reeling instead by the normality around the violence and brutality. A scene where is man is left hanging is disturbing for the brutality of the act, for sure; more shocking still is how long the camera lingers on it, letting us see just how long life carries on as normal whilst a life is gradually snuffed out. Will we look away before someone intervenes? Which would we have done? Several times director Steve McQueen (only his third film) lets the beautifully composed camera shots linger far longer than would usually have been allowed, the better to take in the detail and the context, for reality to imprint itself in our minds.

At the centre of it all is an astonishing performance from Chiwetel Ejiofor as Northup. It takes a special actor to carry such subject matter and not disappear beneath the weight of it or mug to the camera. His performance is note-perfect; as the camera lingers on him for what feels like an age at different times we see a gallery of emotions across his expressive face, movement barely perceptible but real and unmissable. One remarkable scene after a burial hones in on Northup's grieving, angry, silent face as those around mourn and worship with the beautiful gospel cadences of Roll Jordan Roll. He's too angry, too lost to sing; tears hang on the brink of falling. He's barely containing himself. Until he sings, first quietly then with ascending volume, his hands finding the clapped rhythm. Anger isn't pushed down; it's transfigured into worship to find a deeper and truer reality than the awful facts of the situation.

Looking for faults, it would be easy to see Brad Pitt's character, a moral voice and agent of hope, as a white rescuer. I don't know the facts of the story - the book is on my 'to-read' pile - but it would have been equally unhelpful, I think, to portray every white person in the film as racist abusers. His is, like all the supporting players, a well judged and fleshed out part. That's one of the many strengths of the writing in the film; no line is too small to get right. A distraught mother forcibly separated from her children hears a simple but unforgettable eight-word reply, delivered with such run-of-the-mill dispassion that it drew audible gasps of shock from the audience of which I was part. There were several moments like that - perfectly under-stated, delivered faultlessly, shocking enough to  result in voiced disbelief.

Do not fall into the trap of presuming that this is a film to simply endure like bad-tasting medicine because it is 'good for you'. It is good for you. but only because it is, like life, laced with beauty and hope even in the darkest moments. It will live you reeling; if you engage with it properly you can't be the same person at the end. It's not lecture or treatise, however; instead it's a story, a real one, with flesh and blood and soul.

You really, really, really should see this. There is no good reason for it not to win every award, (if Steve McQueen wins the Best Director Oscar, he'll be the first black man to do so - how very appropriate, should it be so); no rational explanation for anything else being the film of the year or decade. Where it sits in film history we'll know in due course.

In the end awards and instant reaction don't cement a film's legacy. For now, whilst we wait, you should simply see it and let it change you.

Once again Hollywood waves its sanctimonious wand over history with this glossy movie about slavery in the United States. Like a self-righteous teetotaler telling off an alcoholic, it is a sentimental, holier-than-thou piece that challenges you to criticize it or ´you're a racist too´. Following in the footsteps of Django it uses the excuse of history and a worthy theme to justify gratuitous scenes of violence. 

The film begins in the home of the central character, Solomon Northop, a free black man, who lives a genteel life with his family in New York. The director is clearly eager to get to the gory bits though, and within the first ten minutes Solomon has been kidnapped, enslaved, and the audience is cringing under a close up of his contorted face during a twenty minute whipping scene; the first of many to come.  

 

The film continues in this vein, as we follow Solomon's journey through an array of increasingly evil slave-owners. There is a segregation of personality in the film, with most of the black characters being good and moral and the white ones evil. Surely it is as patronizing and insulting to assume personality is dependent on colour as it is politically correct. At least the same cannot be said of gender, the white women are as evil as their male counterparts. However no film about slavery is complete without our token good white guy, and Brad Pitts rises to the occasion, strolling in bearded and ready to play, once again, the hero. 

 

One does wonder why Solomon doesn´t send a letter under his ´mistress´name on one of his frequent forays to the shop. (Of course, his one attempt to run away is thwarted when after two steps he stumbles on a lynching scene). Perhaps the point the director is trying to make is that Solomon is too broken and scared to do this. He is too proud, however, to pick the cotton quota demanded by the sadistic slave-owner. A necessary contradiction perhaps, as this allows more whipping scenes as he is punished daily. 

 

Or why, instead of trying and failing to write a letter with a blunt bamboo stick and watery juice, he doesn´t simply use the candle end and stain the paper instead. But it is not a film for the details. Nor the historical overview. 

 

It is two hours of increasing brutality, culminating with a horrendous scene where one girl is whipped until her flesh is exposed. Everything about 12 Years screams Oscar: period setting, heavyweight cast, topical subject matter with historical context and, the cherry on top, a Hans Zimmer score. Much like Lincoln last year, this is the "traditional" (read: safe) Best Picture nominee which the Academy loves to dote on and, although I don't put it in the same league as Gravity or Captain Phillips, I can see why it's become the favourite to win the biggest award in Hollywood. 

Firstly, the acting is nothing short of amazing from all involved. In his first major lead role, as Solomon Northup, a free African American who is kidnapped and sold into slavery, Chiwetel Ejiofor wisely opts against histrionics in favour of a subtler, more impactful blend of gritty determination and soul-destroying vulnerability. He's surrounded by a range of top-notch supporting turns - including Benedict Cumberbatch, Paul Giamatti, Brad Pitt, Sarah Paulson, Paul Dano and newcomer Lupita Nyong'o - with Michael Fassbender delivering yet another tour de force performance as ruthless slave owner Edwin Epps. 

Then there's Steve McQueen's unmistakable style behind the camera, which, after Hunger and Shame, has been subdued slightly to ensure this drama is his most accessible work yet. McQueen employs his trademark long, lingering shots to powerful effect, notably during two unrelenting scenes of a near-hanging and a lashing. McQueen's oblique camera work and point of focus was, for some, cause for frustration in his previous two films, but here it only emphasises the dire circumstances these slaves endured and adds to the bleak atmosphere. 

Not quite as monumental as the awards buzz would suggest and certainly not without flaws, 12 Years is nevertheless a worthy and highly recommendable motion picture, which admirably and honestly tackles a shameful portion of America's history.

An excellently crafted film with a less than stellar story arc. 12 Years a Slave was both a painfully raw, unvarnished piece of cinema and a stunted, surprisingly uneventful experience. Nothing really happened. He had it good, he had it really bad, then he had it good again. That's basically the entire premise of the film. With a post credits' caption letting everyone know what happened to the man after the events we had just witnessed which, usually, is a good thing to part a film with, but here felt like an extension of the uneventful grandeur we had just seen. He was alright, he didn't get justice, and then he disappeared and probably wasn't alright anymore. I enjoyed everything that I saw but it was what was lacking that made the movie a less than excellent experience for me. I would have liked to see more development of characters like Ford, Bass, and Mistress Epps, and I would have really liked the drama not to have been so heavy-handed. I think we got the idea that shit was really bad about 1/5th of the way into the film, but we kept getting hit with the same terribly unfortunate sentiments. It lost its shock and awe value less than a third of the way in. It could have easily retained that shock factor for the atrocities committed on the screen had it brought us nearer to the characters. 12 Years a Slave (2013) - For those of us familiar with the TV series "Firefly" and saw the film "Serenity" you can rejoice in seeing a certain leading man finally get the attention he deserves in this harrowing motion picture. "12 Years a Slave" stars Chiwetal Edjiofor as Solomon Northup, a free African American in the 1800's and family man. Through a series of cruelty, Solomon winds up suffering the ultimate torture of living as a slave to various plantation owners for over a decade despite his freedom in society. This film directed by Steve McQueen captures the utter brutality and despicable nature of human beings at their absolute lowest and shows a glimpse into a time never to be forgotten based on the memoirs of the actual Solomon Northup.

The one thing you will hear over and over again that I will repeat myself to open this review is that this IS NOT an easy watch. This movie is uncomfortable and often difficult to watch but because of how masterfully it's handled, you will never want to look away. If I was to never see another film set in this awful time in human history, I would be relieved in knowing that I saw the greatest/clearest capturing of it on film in "12 Years a Slave". Not only is this film a masterpiece of its class but it is absolutely essential and should be documented in the archives for educational purposes for future generations. 

With all of that praise aside, I cannot honestly say that everyone will want to (even if they should) see this movie for all of the reasons mentioned above.  It's harrowing in nature and through an entire cast of powerful performances; it becomes one of the most engaging, raw and powerful movies of last year (2013). Chiwetal Edjiofor is sensational in this movie and thankfully is being honored by nomination at the OSCARS for his portrayal of Solomon Northup. You as a viewer, you fight alongside Solomon through every unjust and cruel endeavor he must suffer throughout the 2 hr 13 minute long running time and ultimately rejoice in bittersweet sorrow upon the films conclusion. The victims and incarnations of the unspeakable evil that took place in the 1800's are played by a laundry list of great actors/actresses along with some other supporting roles worth mentioning including Lupita Nyong'o, Brad Pitt, Paul Dano, Paul Giamatti, Benedict Cumberbatch, Sarah Paulson and last but certainly not least Michael Fassbender. The absolute stand-out of this lot is Michael Fassbender, whose turn as the plantation owner Edwin Epps displays the utter disgust and evil of men in this time all through his villainous performance.

This is a drama that shouldn't be missed but ultimately will be for a lot of people because of its subject matter. Steve McQueen crafts a movie that truly captures the ugliness of mankind but still manages to make a great looking film despite that. It never goes too far into gratuitousness or pushes its audience too far but it also doesn't pull any punches either. I absolutely recommend seeing this movie but you really need to mentally prepare yourself for the emotional blow that's to come post end credits. It's an eye-opener and likely a movie you will never want to see again (I sure don't) but it is a necessary viewing for everyone in my humble opinion.

An emotional and heart wrenching tour de force from director Steve McQueen.  With the antebellum south as a backdrop the, the drama is very historic, but the focus always stays on the personal struggle of what life likely consisted of for a slave.

Based on the true story, Solomon Northrup (Chiwetel Ejiofor) is a free black man living with his wife and kids in upstate New York.  He is respected in the community.  One day he meets two men who befriends him.  They have a nice dinner with plenty of drinks.  The next day he awakes in a bare room, chained to the floor.  The next day he is on a boat on his way to a Louisiana Plantation.

He ends up with an cruel and egotistical owner (Michael Fassbender) who freuently abuses his slaves.  Solomon is trapped, but never gives up hope that one day he will be able to prove that he is a free man.

The movie is harsh and vast, but what I liked the most was the quiet moments when things get very introspective.  The beauty of the southern scenery contrasts with the cruelty throughout.

Add flawless performances to it and you have a great film.  It does have a few moments where it drags a bit, those moments lead to rich sequences.  One of the best films of 2013.

We only really see one subtly hinted at in the movie. It is as though the director has allowed his camera to just linger on the moments when abuse is occurring giving us time to empathise with the horror - but for the rest of the movie there's a rather rigid and repetitive telling of the manner in which slaves lived and worked. I get the feeling that there must have been a lot more depth to Northup, particularly after the movie finishes with some brief facts about what he did following his freedom from slavery. I would have liked to have seen the movie shortened by about 30 minutes with some of this other history being explored.

Chiwetel Ejiofor is excellent as Northup with a lot of this pain being expressed as the camera moves closeup to his face. For me, one of the most compelling scenes occurred when Northup was left to hang from a tree, just high enough to reach the ground with his tiptoes, suffering for hours as people just went on with their everyday activities around him. It was quite shocking.

The supporting cast is also very good, especially Benedict Cumberbatch (Ford) and Michael Fassbender (Edwin Epps). The weakest character is played by Brad Pitt (Bass) who was also one of the producers of the movie.

The soundtrack was interesting, particularly in the first half of the movie with quite a raw and "disturbing" texture as the backdrop to the events. The cinematography was stunning. In fact, I would say that browsing through stills of some of the scenes would be quite stunning. It's a shame that that same artistry didn't spill over into the overall structure of the story.

This a movie worth watching because it's important to remind ourselves of the horror of slavery. However, it felt overlong and didn't have the potency I had hoped.
