Director Steve McQueen made an explosive art house debut in 2008 with his first full-length feature "Hunger," a shockingly realistic portrayal of a UK detention center for political prisoners during the 1980's. Michael Fassbender was also noticed due to his strong performance as an IRA activist going through daily torture. McQueen continued his co-operation with Fassbender three years later in his second feature "Shame," a psychological drama about obsessive sexual behavior. The film was met with praise equaling that of "Hunger"

Now McQueen has tacled a tricky project: the film adaptation of Solomon Northup's 19th century memoir "12 years a Slave". And praise is again in order. The director has abandoned claustrophobic settings but not the claustrophobic emotions of "Hunger". His lyrical take on visual storytelling has grown accordingly: the hot light of the cotton fields, the gold of the evening sun, the silence of the Deep South; all beautiful but deadly. The cinematography focuses on halted moments and is in no hurry. McQueen still knows the power of a long take. I was often pleasantly reminded of Terrence Malick. Hans Zimmer's score adds to the beautiful but hopeless air, althoug I have to nitpick and point out that Zimmer recycles Cobb's theme from "Inception" almost note to note.

But back to the book and why it's such iconic and a difficult one to adapt. Northup was a free black man, a carpenter and a musician, who was kidnapped and sold to slavery. He spent 12 years of his life pretending to be uneducated and ignorant in the harshest of conditions, getting sold from owner to owner, experiencing heinous acts and witnessing worse. His memoir has represented the deep shame of slavery for two centuries, and is again current as human trafficking is getting more attantion in the western world. It's about time we got a film that addresses the history of human slavery so directly. It's a rare central subject of analysis in cinema, one I instantly connect only with Lars Von Trier's haunting "Manderlay".

As a movie "12 Years a Slave" is a devastatingly uncomfortable experience. Rarely is a movie so very effective and shocking in such a realistic way, rarely does a movie make you feel so concretely. This film is even more potent than "Hunger," which was another excellent but uncomfortable cinematic masterpiece. Fassbender acts again, this time as the main antagonist, and boy is he good as a sinister slavelord with a destructive obsession for a young subject of his, Patsey, played brilliantly by Lupita Nyong. The same depth can be found to some extent from all the actors. On the pages of a script many of the characters would come across as absolutely demonic, but McQueen's intimate directing and the actor's layered performances give them dimensions and vulnerability. It's truly unique how a character can perform acts so hideous you feel physically ill and still come across so that you recognize something in those actions that makes it impossible to simply hate them.

The protagonist himself, Solomon, is probably the character with least depth in the film. He is a straightforward everyman, honest, humble and a silent survival. Chiwetel Ejiofor offers what I can only call a standard Oscar performance. But it's a damn good Oscar performance. His face conveys raw emotion with grace; the character becomes the outlet for the viewer's emotions quite directly; there is no voiceover, but Solomon becomes the narrator through his face. The character is human in the most classical of ways as we observe him in situations of relentless dehumanization. His tormentors are human through a more modern angle, their humanity is animal, fearful, weak and also sadly relatable.

Movies that handle a strong subject matter always run the risk of ending up as understatements or then succumbing to manipulative melodrama. "12 Years a Slave" kind of falters both ways, so that the lapses end up compensating for each other. The overall sense here is a bit detached emotionally, which might make the most painful scenes all the more powerful. McQueen underscores just a bit at times, but all the wordless analysis is subtle and rich enough to make one forgive a few moments where too much is being said in stead of being shown. This is definitely never an easy film, however you look at it. It's emotional torment- as it should be- and also a bit slow, even though every moment deserves to be shown and thus experienced. This isn't an entertaining piece per se, but it captivates, affects you emotionally and keeps on processing within your mind.

12 years a Slave is a film about a man forced to confront the schizophrenic nature of the culture, country and times in which he lives. In the North of America, Solomon Northup is a "free" man. But in the South of the country, his skin colour marks him out as a slave. He lives a "free" life as a violinist with his wife and family in pre-Civil War New York, untroubled by the brutalities of the slave trade in southern states, until two business associates kidnap and sell Northup like cattle.

Enslaved for 12 years, Solomon must come to terms with his own silence and duplicity on the enslavement of other Africans in America. As he struggles to free himself and return to relative 'safety' in the North, the film examines notions of collective silence and the physiological damaged caused by both emotional and physical violence.

There are moments when the face is not even shown thought the actor is crying (just his sitting body with an over the shoulder shot). This is riveting, painful and hard cinema at its best. With really tight shots of an expressive face, it shows the life and injustice of a slave through subtle glimmers and glimpses. The whipping scenes are stronger on the audience than passion of the Christ, the portrayal of slavery more real than any other movie I have seen and yet, it is commercial. Freedom, life, friends, the ability to make your own decisions, these are all things we take for granted in this life. But what if you were stripped of all of that, without a moments notice, forced to live under a false name, currently being sold and made to do unspeakable things. I'm under no illusion that we, in this day and age are not aware of slavery and the racial horrors that not only followed it but were a precurser to it. The topic, brought into public eye again with last years Django Unchained is yet again brought to our attention, however this time its real, its in your face and it doesn't shy away from making you feel like you should, shocked and appauled. Solomon, a family man in the 1800's and quite the violin player is double crossed one day and imprisoned, before begining his 12 year journey of being traded as a piece of meat between masters on the good ol american countryside. Its wonderfully acted, the cast is a healthy one, yes some big names appear, if only for 1 or 2 scenes but they fill the screen with such life and attention that its worth their inclusion. This would all mean nothing though without the tear jerking performance of Chiwetel Ejiofor, and boy does it hurt, watching him cope with his surroundings has you on edge and completely rooting for him. The script is brilliant and rolls off the actors tongues so easily and freely you become completely engrossed from the get go. The real star of the show however is McQueen, his entire style of film making and long drawn out shots, blended with his tender intricacies make this film completely hypnotising to watch. During my showing a lot of people walked out, especially after one lashing scene that will make your eyes soak up in seconds. Even though its a differing style from Django Unchained Mcqueen just gets it note perfect from the get go, making you hate yourself for being part of a race that could do that to people. Im not taking anything away from Tarantino's outing, however if ever there was a film to open the flood gates and make people care about one another more than ever, its this. A wonderful and agonising film from begining to end and I couldnt recommend it highly enough.

Brutal yet elegant, 12 Years a Slave is a beautifully rendered punch to the gut about the most shameful chapter in American history. Though the film brims with memorable characters, the show ultimately belongs to Ejiofor, who upholds the character's dignity throughout. Other stars such as Brad Pitt, Alfre Woodard, Benendict Cumberbatch, Paul Dano and even a cameo from Paul Giamatti deliver performances that will stick with you. The effects are clear in 12 Years a Slave's most harrowing sequence, where Epps forces Solomon to administer seemingly endless lashings upon Patsy's back. 12 Years a Slave is by no means light entertainment but it provides a more worthwhile cinematic experience than about 90% of what's out there and the impressions it leaves aren't easily dismissed or dispelled. This revolving door of graphically rendered brutalities might feel like its own punishment if not for an array of astonishing performances that's practically a one-stop Oscar-nomination shopping spree. It's the unhappiest happy ending I've ever seen, a moment that makes you weep not just for this one man who found his way back to freedom, but for all those men and women who never knew it in the first place. This is impressive filmmaking, but it is not easy to take in. VERDICT: "Instant Classic" - [Positively Acclaimed Reaction] Usually I give this rating to a movie that I believe is absolutely outstanding and has little to no flaws in it. People are too busy judging this movie based on the subject matter.  There are so many problems with this film in terms of story and character development that, if looked at subjectively, you will see that is is a poorly made film.
a)  The Characters. This is the biggest problem.  Every character is one dimensional.  The Black characters are helpless victims while the White characters are evil for the sake of being evil with no rationale behind their actions.  But the one good white character (Brad Ptt) is so generic and bland that even when he does decide to help Northrup, it is so uneventful and unexciting.
Even the white villains who abducted Northrup could have been salvaged by showing that their motivation was money.  A small cut away of them talking about needing another slave to make more money, or being told to do so by a slave trader.  Instead we just have two white villains who are evil for the sake of being evil and have no depth their their character.  And it wouldn't take much to write that in there.
b) The Story:  We already know by the title that he is a slave for 12 Years.  But we don't FEEL that.  Northrup is with his family at the beginning, but there is no real development of his familial relationship.  Then he is abducted maybe 10 minutes into the movie (very quickly).  And he is gone for 12 years.  But we don't feel that.  We cannot tell the passage of time.  Then he goes home after being freed and sees his family.  All of his children are grown up and we basically see all new characters.  There are not idiosyncrasies or traits that are reflected in the adults that they used to have as children.  And it wouldn't take much.  Imagine how more powerful it would have been for him to see these adults who used to be his kids, have a hard time recognizing them then seeing one little type of smile that his daughter has, or a thing she does with her hair, and then it clicks with him and he gets more emotional.  
Add to that the husband of his one daughter.  Sure, we don't have a room of people that WE as an audience don't recognize, but now let's add another New character.

I could go on and on about this movie, but the biggest problem is this.... While we sympathize for Northrup.....we don't Empathize with him.  We don't feel what he is feeling...and if the movie were made better we would feel his loss.

Este es un film que adapta la novela autobiográfica de Solomon Northup, publicada en 1853, que ya previamente había sido adaptada en un filme para televisión, bajo el título de "Solomon Northup's Odyssey", en 1984 con el actor Avery Brooks en el papel estelar. Pero sin duda es ahora con la película llevada a la pantalla grande y nominada a múltiples Oscares, y ya ganadora de varios Globos de Oro, que la historia verídica de Solomon Northup es conocida por la audiencia en general. Es una pena que una novela publicada en 1853 tarde 160 años en lograr el interés de la industria del cine para ser presentada. Y es que supongo que es más fácil para los Norteamericanos producir infinidad de filmes sobre los horrores del Holocausto Judío en Alemania, que admitir que en su propia tierra, sus antepasados fueron igualmente de sanguinarios y crueles con la gente de raza negra, y me agrada que en el filme tomen un momento para mostrar a indios, ya que sin duda ese es otro episodio oscuro donde los indígenas ni siquiera fueron esclavizados sino básicamente exterminados y recluídos en reservas. Y es que a veces no es fácil de asimilar que aunque ciertamente las fuerzas armadas Norteamericanas fueron el factor clave para la derrota del Nazismo, aún en los Estados Unidos se practicaba abierta segregación, que aunque en las legislaciones ya tenían derecho al voto, en la realidad, inclusive en el ejército eran asignados a escuadrones aparte y en algunos casos a labores, que aunque esenciales para la defensa, ciertamente no eran misiones que les asignaban a los soldados blancos. Y aunque ya ha habido excelentes ejemplos de la esclavitud en los Estados Unidos como la épica miniserie "Roots" basada en el libro del mismo nombre, es aquí en "12 Years a Slave" donde toman un ángulo que no todo mundo conocía. Ya que aquí muestran que los esclavistas no solo se conformaban con traer a la fuerza gente de raza negra del Africa para usarlos como esclavos, sino que además secuestraban gente afroamericana que eran libres en estados del Norte, para ser llevados a la fuerza y bajo documentos falsos para ser esclavos en los Estados del Sur. El filme presenta un uso excepcional de la fotografía, tanto por sus ángulos como las decisiones de tomas y su duración. Un filme que permite que el actor Chiwetel Ejiofor demuestre su control en escena y echarse la cinta al hombro y volverse definitivamente la estrella del filme. Pero igualmente, el filme posee un elenco impecable donde actores como Michael Fassbender, Sarah Paulson y Lupita Nyong'o comparten la solidez de actuación en este filme. Y con grandes cameos de luminarias como Benedict Cumberbatch, Alfre Woodard, Paul Giamatti y Brad Pitt. Lo único negativo, por llamarlo así, sería que el filme es muy cruel y duro de ver en ciertas escenas evocando sentimientos similares como cuando se ven cintas tales como "The Passion of Christ" donde sin duda es necesario mostrar lo que realmente ocurría, pero no deja por ello de ser duro de ver y asimilar. Pero claro, eso es parte de la intención del filme para evitar que algo así vuelva a ocurrir.

When I first saw the trailer for 12 Years a Slave, I thought, "this looks good, maybe even great, but it's nothing we haven't seen before." Then, on my way to the cinema, I started mentally listing great movies about slavery... and quickly realized that most standout films I'd subconsciously categorized as "slave movies" aren't, in fact, about slaves. Glory? Black soldiers fight for freedom. Amistad? Would-be slaves never reach the plantation. Amazing Grace? British politician abolishes the slave trade. Lincoln? American politician abolishes slavery. NONE of these admittedly incredible movies actually depicts slavery in all its brutal ugliness, and what's more, they all star white folks, with black people in supporting roles. 12 Years a Slave takes us where no big-budget film has gone before - straight into the gut-wrenching realities of slavery, not as a bystander, but as a victim, and ultimately a survivor, but never a conqueror. This is an integral piece of American cinema that should be required viewing in every US History classroom, period.

Praised and favored for all possible awards, 12 Years a Slave is an extraordinary, brutal and depressingly emotional movie. Depicting in almost documentary way the darkest part of the slavery period in the US, it is an extremely challenging and uneasy movie to watch. It does not impress with an amazing escape story, but with graphic portrayals of cruel characters, ruthless habits and the tragic lives of Afro-Americans during the slavery period.

Almost entirely based on the true story of Solomon Northrup, 12 Years a Slave goes back to 1841 when the free-born Solomon, living in Saratoga with his wife and kids, is kidnapped by slave traders and illegally sold in slavery in New Orleans. With a new name and no hope to regain freedom, Solomon's life becomes a daily struggle to survive. In terms of a story development and getting free again, 12 Years a Slave is far from being an adventurous movie. On the contrary, it is a delivery soaked with brutality, violence and hopelessness.

Director Steve McQueen has focused himself on depicting the life of Afro-Americans as slaves in the deep American South as well as beliefs, understandings and way of thinking of their enslavers. Every single character in 12 Years a Slave is an embodiment of particular stereotypes and groups of people. Chiwetel Ejiofor is simply terrific as Solomon Northrup, disturbingly honest, vulnerable and yet willing to survive. Together with Michael Fassbender they are one of the reasons why this movie is so engaging. Speaking of Fassbender and his third collaboration with Steve McQueen (after Hunger and Shame), his brutal and ruthless characterization of the Edwin Epps is mesmerizing. An embodiment of a whole social sub-group his delivers a performance that would irritate every stomach. To some extent Fassbender outshines Ejiofor thanks to Steve McQueen's skilful depiction of the way of thinking and reasoning of slave owners during these years. What is even more shocking is the frightening, stone-cold performance of Sarah Paulson as Mistress Epps. In the very few scenes she is involved in; it is her female coldness, lack of compassion and humanity that truly will shock you.

As a whole, it is the way Steve McQueen portrays a world that seems so distant and illogical to us, that creates the feeling of being utterly uncomfortable while watching his delivery. Apart from the graphic scenes (the whipping of Patsey was completely unbearable for me) it is also the logic and reasoning; the points of view of slave owners shown in the movie that shock. From our post-modern point of view that society and period would seem completely unacceptable, but Steve McQueen manages to show a world in which modern thinking is non-existent, in which slavery, brutality and the worthlessness of human lives are a common sense.

12 Years a Slave has definitely been slightly overhyped, but given the fact that it was shot in only one month it deserves all the standing ovations it could get. A movie which would test your senses and emotions, it constitutes Steve McQueen as one of the directors-to-follow and getting some Oscar Awards are just a matter of time. With 9 nominations it could be considered a favorite in the Best Motion Picture, Best Editing and Best Adapted Screenplay. Definitely a must see !!!

Emotional thriller based on a true story. Set in the 1800's, a  young man named Solomon is tricked into slavery and taken to New Orleans to work picking cotton and building huts, being forced to leave behind his family in New York. He is treated poorly throughout his ordeal, taking whippings and being fed on as little as possible. But Solomon never gives up hope, trying to help those around him. In particular fellow slave, Patsey. 
Chiwetel Ejiofor gives a stunning performance as Solomon Northrup and deserves all the acclaim and awards coming his way. To tap into the emotion Northrup must have been feeling cant have been easy but you really feel his suffering at times. Michael Fassbender also as evil plantation owner Edwin Epps is on fiery form, you really do hate him in this. Lupita Nyong as Patsey, Epps' "favourite" slave is brilliant, surely a difficult role to play and its not always easy to watch but she is also captivating.
Overall, 12 Years a Slave is something of a classic. It's not always easy to watch, but that's not the point, it's about one man's story of pain, suffering, hope and love, it's a great, emotional and powerful story and one thats told brilliantly.

Brutally realistic, brutally difficult to watch, brilliantly constructed and superbly acted, '12 Years A Slave' is an incredible film. Although the subject and theme of slavery and black rights has been explored increasingly in recent years with the likes of 'Django Unchained' and 'The Help'-both excellent films, '12 Years' avoids the possibility of being a film on the subject which will fade into obscurity by breaking the boundaries of its subjects and delivering a masterpiece onto our screens.

Telling the story of Solomon Northrup, a freeborn black man in pre-civil war America, who is kidnapped and sold into slavery it is clear from the start that the film is hardly going to be an easy sit down and tune out film. I cannot recall many other films which have left me feeling physically sick after some sequences and uncomfortable to watch. Yet those sequences are essential to creating the experience of viewing the film, showing the audience just a tiny snapshot of the lives of slaves and the horrors they suffered. 

Although certain brutal sequences stand out the overall feeling and tone of the film is steeped in a dark, sombre and menacing mood, created perfectly by the incredible acting abilities of Chiwetel Eijofor who, along with McQueen regular Fassbender, steals the show. There is no doubt that Eijofor deserves the Oscar for his efforts and constructing a real life character whose experiences would be hard to recreate without insulting his memory. Fassbender's tyrannical and psychotic portrayal of slave owner Epps is physically terrifying, whilst the supporting cast give fantastic performances in the vast variety of roles they perform-especially Lupita Nyong'o's devastating portrayal of Patsey which left me in anguish and sorrow as her character experiences life at the hands of Epps and his mistress.

McQueen's directing abilities have already been well established with both 'Hunger' and 'Shame', productions which have pushed the limits of independent dramas and shown that McQueen is, even after three films, one of the best British and global directors of his generation. '12 Years' pushes his dramatic boundaries further, creating the gutwrenching picture which thoroughly deserved the BAFTAs for Best Film and Best Actor for Ejifor. With a supposed HBO series in the works I look forward to more from McQueen.

To say that I enjoyed '12 Years A Slave' would be an unfitting word to the horrific experience it was to watch. Although the ending of the film is somewhat obvious and some inspiration is expected, the film follows a downbeat ending, offering little hope nor shedding any light (in keeping with Northrup's book), of the lives of Patsey and the other slaves following Northrup's departure. Inspiration is muted to say the least. Yet the purpose of '12 Years A Slave' is not to offer inspiration but to realistically explore the life of an American slave. It is tragic and hard to watch but it is a film which should and must be watched, not just for the technical and creative achievements it makes, but for the story it tells.

An incredibly powerful film, 12 YEARS A SLAVE is an effectively somber rendering of slavery based on an autobiography penned in 1854 by Solomon Northup, resident of upstate New York and family man, who survived a kidnapping that led to him being sold to a vicious plantation owner.  The film proficiently recreates a time and place in which conviction, when simplified, was very much black & white.  The outright injustice is glaringly and irritatingly blatant, quite difficult to watch at times.  Yet there's is no other way to tell such a harrowing story.  The very last minutes of the film act as the much needed catharsis to two hours of visceral infliction that sets the film's tone from the very start.

It is extremely intense and well-acted, but, as usual, I have to assume the book does a better job telling the story, as the filmmakers seem more concerned with shoving atrocities in our faces than the actual plot, which is really what is most intriguing. It is undoubtedly well-done, but I certainly don't want to see it again.

Steve McQueen has created art with "12 Years a Slave." Art that tears your heart out, stomps on your soul and crushes your spirit; Art that fills your senses with sounds and images that makes up for lack of touch, taste and smells; Art that almost makes you forget the ugliness of human nature when juxtaposed next to the wonder of mother nature; Art that reminds you of the infallible ability of human beings to rationalize self-interest. 
However, because it is art, it does not (perhaps by intentional decisions) address slavery as a current dilemma that plagues that world, nor does it address the reality of people born into slavery because of the focus on the film's protagonist. 
I do not think there is some grand social commentary here, just a beautifully jarring film through a former artist's eyes that recognizes the cruelty of slavery's past from the perspective of Solomon Northup.

It becomes obvious wherever he goes that he is a cut above the norm but this has various drawbacks for him throughout the story.

Nel 1841, Solomon Northup viene rapito a New York, dove vive libero assieme alla famiglia e si guadagna da vivere suonando il violino, e viene deportato come schiavo negli Stati del sud, in crisi di manodopera per le difficoltà sulle rotte negriere dall'Africa. Per raccontarne il lungo incubo prima di ritrovare la libertà, l'inglese Steve McQueen cambia alcune coordinate del suo fare cinema e, quasi a volerlo far intendere subito, utilizza più di una parola nel titolo: si tratta di un film più corale rispetto ai precedenti, che sono dedicati allo scavo psicologico di un solo personaggio, non c'è Fassbender come protagonista assoluto e, soprattutto, la scrittura è affidata a qualcun altro. E' difatti di John Ridley la sceneggiatura costruita sulle memorie di Northup - che sapeva leggere e scrivere, anche se fu costretto a nasconderlo nei suoi anni di schiavitù - finendo però per essere l'anello debole del lavoro: pur non essendo in nessun punto davvero piatta, la storia non sorprende davvero mai e rende meno efficace l'impatto complessivo. Impatto che, invece, beneficia dell'accuratissimo lavoro della regia sull'immagine: se McQueen conferma la sua bravura nel costruire le inquadrature filmando un profondo sud opprimente dal punto di vista fisico e psicologico (il direttore della fotografia è il fido Sean Bobbitt), il regista inglese dà il meglio di sé nella rappresentazione della fisicità umana, in perfetta continuità con le sue opere precedenti. Si tratta di corpi sofferenti, con in primo piano piaghe sulla pelle che riflettono quelle dell'anima, e di volti che non si vergognano di esprimere i sentimenti - come dice esplicitamente Eliza in una delle tante scene in cui si piange come fontane - raccontando i pensieri che stanno dentro gli sguardi. L'orrore infinito della schiavitù sta nella sgradevolezza dei personaggi interpretati, in piccole ma significative parti, da Paul Dano e Paul Giamatti, oltre che nella gelida cattiveria della signora Epps di Sarah Paulson: se pare vacillare la coscienza di Ford, il primo padrone di Solomon - Benedict Cumberbatch esce di scena troppo presto -, la ferocia del secondo, Epps, la compensa abbondantemente. Nei suoi scomodi panni, l'attore preferito di McQueen, cioè Fassbender, disegna con grande profondità il ritratto di un uomo apparentemente senza sentimenti, violento con più di una punta di sadismo e alcolizzato, rubando se non la scena quantomeno l'attenzione rispetto al resto del cast: ne è testimonianza, fra le altre, la lunga sequenza - girata senza interruzioni con la macchina da presa che segue gli attori - della fustigazione di Patsey. A tener testa a cotanta interpretazione, c'è quella di Chiwetel Ejiofor nel ruolo del protagonista: l'attore inglese, sulle prime dubbioso, coglie al meglio l'occasione della vita rendendo con efficacia prima lo spaesamento di Solomon e poi la sua determinazione a uscire dalla trappola in cui l'hanno ficcato senza piegare (troppo) la testa. Accanto a lui, si fanno ricordare in special modo due figure di donna di una tragicità se possibile crescente, ovvero l'Eliza di Adepero Oduye e la Patsey dell'esordiente Lupita Nyong'o, la cui addolorata performance le ha ben meritato la nomination all'Oscar (corrono per la statuetta anche Fassbender ed Ejiofor, oltre al film e al regista). Piccola, ma decisiva per la liberazione di Northup, è invece la parte di Brad Pitt, che però compare nella lunga lista dei produttori, a testimonianza del fatto che lo sforzo realizzativo è stato notevole per quello che, a tutti gli effetti, è un 'filmone': eppure, malgrado la meritoria denuncia (non va dimenticato che la schiavitù esiste ancora), la notevole partecipazione di tutti quanti, le emozioni comunque suscitate anche grazie alla colonna sonora di Hans Zimmer alternata ai canti di lavoro nelle piantagioni, '12 anni schiavo' fatica a colpire nel profondo. Per carità, si tratta sempre di un film che sta tra il buono e l'ottimo, ma forse il fatto che sia tutto chiaro ed esplicito rende impossibili gli angoli bui e i momenti indefiniti che congiurano perchè, ad esempio, una pellicola pur non perfetta come 'Shame' si piazzi nell'animo dello spettatore e cresca con il passare del tempo.

Beautifully shot, impeccably acted and meticulously recreating the atmosphere of a 19th century slavery ridden nation, 12 Years a Slave ultimately plays it a bit too by the book for such a controversial topic. Director Steve McQueen has by now become an expert at portraying stories featuring tormented characters, yet now at his third effort he seems to lack one important element that made Hunger and Shame such moving experiences: passion. 
We follow Chiwetel Ejiofor's Solomon through his agonizing journey of slavery, yet it all feels so impersonal, it's as if we're watching a play made up of quite disjointed episodes, as he passes from owner to owner, straightforwardly moving towards a calculated and expected bittersweet ending. McQueen's trademark long, single takes are ever present and expertly crafted as always - that whipping scene near the end alone is a powerful example of masterful filmmaking. 
The performances are all around great, yet in the end it's still Fassbender that stands out from the crowd. Mainly because he is portraying the only character from which you get the feeling that there's something more to his actions, unlike most of the other characters, who somehow feel like archetypes that only serve to move the story forwards. We don't really get to see what makes them tick, or if and how they develop throughout the story. Regretfully, this also applies to the main character. As we pass from one story ark to another, we meet the big names in the cast, Paul Giamatti, Paul Dano, Benedict Cumberbatch. And they all do a great job, but it all falls apart when we get to Brad Pitt. That has to be one the worst castings of the year, as it's just Brad Pitt playing a Brad Pitt deus ex machina, and for those moments he's onscreen, he just pulls you out from the whole experience. 
At times it feels like a safe, Oscar bait feature, while at others its visceral direction and powerful performances are a one-two punch straight to the heart. Despite other moments, when it feels so focused on depicting the journey through carefully crafted scenes, yet it forgets about the characters and leaves us emotionally unengaged. But all in all, 12 Years a Slave is a great cinematic experience and a great depiction of a crucial era in American history.

Such a heartbreaking, sad movie. Besides the discrimination the movie much more highlighted the selfish desire and greed of human, and in conclusion, the humanity. 

The story is what we have already realized so it's not surprising, but what made it marvelous was how the movie showcased the story as well as addressed the condition of slavery. The movie maximized human drawbacks and the suffering of black people to upset us and then gain our sympathy, get us into the movie by the cinematograph, the song and the score (which I highly praise this movie for) and then bring up the cruel reality. 

One of the unforgettable scenes was when Soloman (played by Chiwetel Ejiofor) was being hanged at the back yard and the filmmaker applied an establishing shot to show us the reaction/ POV of the people surrounding Soloman on the suffering of Soloman. From this shot, I could see the ruthlessness and cold-heartedness of human as well as the helplessness and fear under the circumstance. Also, black people being hanged were not uncommon at that time. We could see there were child playing at the yard though Soloman was being hanged. Combined with the choking sound of Soloman, this scene with this shot was unbearable, making me really uncomfortable coz I think as a human, no one can bear watching someone suffered and not do anything. Apparently, the director is well aware of that so he brought audience a "torturous" scene like this to let us get into the movie to experience what they had been through because as an audience, we really couldn't change anything but only watching. Sadly, you would lament with signs coz there was no way out for the black people at that time. They might be selfish but they had no alternative. If they were going to interfere, they might lose their lives. Accordingly, the adult chose not to involve and the innocent kids were going to enjoy being alive.
Speaking of the song, most of them were sung by the characters together in order to demonstrate their restraint, tolerance and solidarity (which helped to present the contrast between the selfishness and warm-heartedness of black people).  However, there was a song sung by Tibeats (played by Paul Dano) showing discrimination. The lyrics with the tone and the growing speed he sang disgusted me very much. It is the most uncomfortable song I have ever heard so far, but this song helped to maximize the suffering of black people and human's flaw besides the visual. In term of the score, when it was on, it touched me so deeply and I quickly drew into the role and was moved to tears.

In front of the camera, the shining point is the supporting roles, especially Michael Fassbendar as a sick bastard, Edwin Epps. His brilliant performance reflected the misery, the anger and particularly the fear the black people were facing. His acting enabled me to walk into Soloman's or other black peopl's shoes to perceive what they had been through. Frankly, he really horrified, and meanwhile amazed and impressed me a lot.

However, there was a blemish. This good movie had a solid beginning but its ending was quite slipshod.  It's too rush to end the film with a saint (Bass played by Brad Pitt) who shared same belief with Soloman helping to free him. I think its suddenly out of the rhythm of this movie. It seemed like the movie suddenly ended. It's quite rough actually.


All in all, I had strong feelings on almost every scene, which naturally led us to walk into the characters' shoes to understand their intention, perception and motivation, either positive or negative. 12 years a Slave is sorrowful movie from the beginning to the end (even the survival would not light us up after Soloman suffered through the cruelty) and it raises the human right issues. We all deserve to have equal right, to be treated equally so we should never give up fighting for ourselves, or others.

El director Steve McQueen, luego de las abrumadoras experiencias cinematográficas llamadas "Hunger" (sobre las huelgas de hambre en Irlanda) y "Shame" (sobre la adicción al sexo), nos trae esta obra maestra basada en las memorias del violinista Solomon Northup, quien en 1841 fue engañado y vendido como esclavo. His wife is everything a plantation owner could want and yet he covets, borderline obsesses, for a slave girl. The ultimate power on his land, at times he is weak. This character rides a wave of chaos and Fassbender delivers. Lupita Nyong'o is great in a subdued role as an abused slave. Ultimatly director Steve Mcqueen under utilized his phenomenal cast. Benedict Cumberbatch is not given a chance to display his acting chops and Paul Giamatti, who is scary good, is only on screen for about five minutes. Mcqueen had some miscues that truly kept this film from being great but his raw take and some exceptional acting still made it very good.

Well, I'm not about to call this the 'feel good movie of the year' but I could call 12 years a slave one of 'the most emotional, thought-provoking and at some points, distributing movie of the year' Steve McQueen has put together a film that while yes, it does tell a story, the movie is more about showing a slice of history. In some aspects, the movie is not a total flow-and what I mean by that is that you come out of the movie with a sense of "did I really watch a story"?, which one usually thinks of when they see a film or "was I watching a documentary"? Actually, it was a little bit of both and it was simply amazing.

At the heart of the film, an African-American who lives in the North and who is free gets hoodwinked and ends up back in the South where he is now a slave. Over the next 12 years, Solomon Northrup-who has his identity totally changed is passed around from on owner to another with no regard to him being human. Solomon learns to "accept" his slave identity since that seemed to be the way he survived as he quickly discovered that when his did try to tell people who he really was, all it brought was consequences, so he did what he had to survive till eventually Solomon finally found a confidant in Bass and finally achieved his goal of getting back to his family in the North.

The rest of the cast is amazing and very believable in capturing the times, the emotions and the way of thinking. While I observed that some of the slave owners might have been not as harsh as others, make no mistake about it, owners had to show their resolve no matter how they try attempted to show any hint of compassion. Ironically, the slave owners were pretty much followers of the literal translation of the bible, so I wonder where did the bible and GOD condone one human owing another?

Yesterday, I went to see 12 Years a Slave in anticipation of tomorrow's Academy Awards show. It's about a freeborn man kidnapped into slavery. On NPR I had listened to commentary about certain scenes in the film that were somehow emblematic of slavery and its brutality in the pre-Civil War United States. But aside from that, I knew very little as to what to expect. But to my surprise, the violence depicted was rather mild compared to movies like Amistad or even Django. Sure, there are hangings, lashings, and much verbal abuse with a Southern twang. But the majority of the emotional pull is in the protagonist's (Solomon) anguish over losing his family. Lots of quiet scoreless closeups of him to elicit sympathy and longing for his dignity to be restored. The actor, played by Chiwetel Ejiofor, did a fine job, but there are better performances.  Michael Fassbender is once again brilliant; this time as an evil plantation master. He's an actor of enormous talent (and beauty imo). But the standout act goes to Lupita Nyong'o for her heartbreaking film debut as an abused slave. The film had been nominated for 9 Academy Awards. And I'm almost certain, Lupita will win for Best Supporting Actress. (Because Jennifer Laurence just won last year and  her role this time around doesn't carry much sympathy value). In terms of the technical production aspect, there is not much to say, other than noting some bucolic shots of the lush Southern landscape. The score is worth mentioning for the fact that it is subtle and sometimes even absent from the screen. Good choice, as music can overpower or draw too much attention to itself. Here, it allows the story to unfold without telling you what to feel on cue. And what you feel is ultimately a faint sorrow about the injustices of the past. How humans can be so inhumane. We've come a long way, but you get the sense that the hurt (and the hate) still linger among the Spanish moss and the winding rivers.

A lot of expository depth is certainly picked up along the way as this character study progresses, but that's mostly with the lead Soloman Northup figure, who, even then, is given only so much immediate background development, as most supporting roles' characterization feels somewhat forcibly placed, sometimes seemingly for the sake of simply reinforcing thematic depth, rather than dramatic depth, with only so many layers, and therefore only so much subtlety. A common mistake that these films make is ironically dehumanizing its characters, both protagonistic and antagonistic, in order to get the full range of effectiveness out of themes dealing with the dark depths to which a human can plummet, and while this film's characters are well-portrayed enough on paper and in the performances for you to get a fair grasp on their depth, much of the effectiveness of this drama goes diluted by a thinning of characterization within both the brutal slavers and, to a lesser extent, the helplessly enslaved that sometimes, dare I say, thins subtlety, no matter how much Steve McQueen charges his directorial interpretation of a sometimes thin script with, well, maybe a little too much thoughtfulness. Speaking of black heritage, McQueen has his "roots" in dry art filmmaking, and while this film is quite a ways away from being the tedious bore that was McQueen's artistically misguided and atmospherically cold "Hunger", there are occasions in which McQueens gets to be, maybe not questionably offbeat, but a touch too chilled with his thoughtful storytelling, which is piercing when it works, and all but, well, dulls when it doesn't, as it often does once material's momentum lapses. Clocking in at about two hours and a quarter, this film runs a length that I was looking forward to seeing handled, hoping that it would be used to extensively flesh out a narrative with this much depth and dramatic potential, yet what you end up with is much too much meandering fat around the edges that drags out the film, whose seemingly tight length is secured by the moments in which writer John Ridley rather awkwardly rushes through the narrative - whether it be its exposition or its set pieces - in an attempt to make up for lapses in tightness. Really, the pacing inconsistencies, while always glaring, aren't initially that big of an issue, but before too long, pacing problems become the film's biggest issue, as it leaves the final product to gradually descend into empty focus, dragging along as not much more than an aimless study on set pieces without a sense of progression, until you're left with not much to do other than think about the film's other shortcomings, subtle though they may be. This subject matter is sensitive, not just because it's so emotional and important, but because it has a dramatic potential that can either soar or be disappointingly betrayed, and while the final product is by no means a disappointment, its expository shortcomings thin depth, while pacing inconsistencies thin focus, until the film finds itself dragging along, losing momentum, until the excellence that it could have and sometimes does achieve is lost. No, the film isn't as good as they say it is, and yet, boy, it sure is still mighty good, and for all its thin spots and unevenness, it consistently compels, resonates and even haunts, particularly aesthetically.

Needless to say, in order for this subject matter to be sold, the era in which its narrative vehicle is set needs to be sold, and art director David Stein, realizing this, goes all out in using Adam Stockhausen's production designs and Patricia Norris' costume designs to restore the distinguished setting of mid-1800s America a manner that is practically lavish in its intricacy, and goes further polished by Sean Bobbitt's outstanding cinematography, whose tastefully subtle emphasis on lighting compensates for a lack of color flare in establishing a haunting visual style that goes topped only by the film's musical style. Hans Zimmer is arguably the greatest score composer of the modern film industry, so of course I was thoroughly excited to see just how he would interpret this, his first major artistic project in quite some time, and let me tell you that if nothing meets my expectations every step of the way, it is Zimmer's absolutely outstanding musical performance, which is richly dynamic in its themes, each one of which is graced with tightly composed and emotively executed compositions whose aesthetic and narrative are both breathtaking. Whether they be somberly atmospheric compositions inspired by Zimmer's work on "The Thin Red Line", or stylishly intense modernist compositions, maybe even innovations in the usage of improvised instrumentation, most every piece that Zimmer orchestrates is outstanding, both by its own musical right, and as a particularly effective artistic compliment to the selling of the depths of a story whose tellers, to be honest, aren't are consistent in their doing justice to this subject matter. Aimlessly uneven and somewhat thin in its layering, the storytelling could do so much more with this subject matter, but the shortcomings cannot obscure the considerable potential of this important story dealing with the depths of the struggles faced by the enslaved, which could have been made into an excellent film, but is still crafted into a compelling opus, partly by highlights in a script by John Ridley that come in the form of anything from sharp dialogue to fearless set pieces, in addition to more genuine bits of characterization that bring life to the drama's human depth, though not as much as the powerful performances. As solid as this talented cast is, I had my concerns that dramatic material would be written too thinly for this cast to milk its genuine depths for all its worth, yet whether it be because material is realized or simply because the acting is just to doggone inspired, most everyone - whether it be the Paul Dano as a slaver who is sensitive over his power, or Benedict Cumberbatch as a guilty slaver, or Michael Fassbender as a terrifying man who is more Godless than he thinks he is, or Sarah Paulson as a frustrated and emasculating wife of a man who would rather fulfill his physical desires with a woman she considers no more than a disposable tool - has a time to shine devastatingly, and that particularly goes for the emotionally overwhelmed Lupita Nyong'o, as well as for leading man Chiwetel Ejiofor, whose charismatic, intense and altogether penetratingly layered portrayal of a once-free man struggling to keep hope alive in the midst of horrors beyond his wildest imaginations makes him both an immersive avatar for the audience, and a worthy lead by his own right. Ejiofor carries this film, while everyone else proves nothing less than worthy of backing such a remarkable lead performance, and it really is an enthralling experience seeing just what new heights in dramatic acting will be hit next by this esteemed cast, and yet, the performance that truly secures the final product as engrossing in most every other regard is that of Steve McQueen, whose inconsistencies in pacing beget an inconsistency in effectiveness, of course, until the final product finds itself not quite inspired enough to soar towards its potential, yet nonetheless inspired enough for McQueen to prominently utilize scoring and style in order to bring depth to his thoughtfulness, whose audacious attention to dehumanizing brutality - whether it be violent, or degrading, or even sexual - and humanizing heart captures an intensity that is often truly a challenge to withstand, and is sometimes moving (The ending is particularly penetrating), with heights in emotional resonance that provide glimpses of a more realized, perhaps even upstanding drama. Were there more consistency to the realization of McQueen's clearly ambitious directorial efforts, the film really would have stood out, rather than fall shy of being all that strong, at the least, yet they never lose their inspiration, and no matter how much the drama leaves you, or at least me with much to be desired, the patient are sure to be rewarded by this harrowing portrait on humanity as something both corruptible and respectable.

Overall, the film, through blanding atmospheric dry spells and glaring inconsistencies in narrative structuring, gradually loses momentum that was limited to begin with by expository thinning, until the final product falls pretty decidedly short of outstanding, and yet, through excellent art direction by David Stein, handsome cinematography by Sean Bobbitt, great score work by Hans Zimmer, a generally sharp script by John Ridley, strong acting, - especially by Lupita Nyong'o and Chiwetel Ejiofor - and inspired direction by Steve McQueen, "12 Years a Slave" still stands as a thoroughly rewarding and sometimes dramatically devastating portrait on a dark time of corruption and dehumanization in American history.

This movie is about the unfortunately true story of the life of Solomon Northup.  Shot in around 1841, in the Pre-Civil War United States, Solomon (played by Chiwetel Ejiofor) lived with his wife and two children in Saratoga, New York.  Solomon's freedom is stripped from him when he is tricked and kidnapped into slavery.  The plot of the movie depicts the epic tale of his hardship experience as a slave for twelve years.  

Solomon's will-power to survive is moving.   When Solomon crosses-paths with an apologists, his life takes another turn, this time for the better!

John Ridley did a brilliant job writing the screenplay, based on the autobiography by Solomon Northup.  This film is not something you read about your history textbook, for it is still considered a taboo topic in America.

The film has an all-star cast - Chiwetel Ejiofor, Brad Pitt, Lupita Nyong'o, Benedict Chumberbatch, Paul Dano, Michael Fassbender, Paul Giamatti...

Steve McQueen, the director stated that everyone deserves not just to survive but to live. This is most important legacy of Solomon Northup. McQueen dedicated the film to all the people who have endured slavery and 21 million people who still suffer slavery today (as  of 2014).

So after all the Oscars hype I decided I needed to catch up yesterday, and what better place to start then the film that won best picture! I'd heard that 12 Years A Slave was a great flick, but I wasn't sure if it would be good enough to nudge Gravity out of best picture glory. First up, the performances are amazing. Kenyan actress Lupita Nyong'o shows that she knows the score and deservingly was awarded an Oscar for her efforts. It's taken me a while to warm up to both of these guys, but Michael Fassbender and Benedict Cumberbatch both showed up to give it their all for this shoot. You will hate Fassbender's character by the end of the movie. But it is Chiwetel Ejiofor who carries the film, playing the lead: Solomon Northup. It's funny he barely says anything throughout the whole thing, you can see it all in his face and eyes, the horrible things that his character has to endure. Director, Steve McQueen captures all of this expertly. The hell of being a slave is shown in a confronting yet tolerable way. McQueen holds some shots just that little bit longer then normal, making you squirm in your seat. You almost feel the pain of the characters on the screen. Brad Pitt has an interesting cameo, but I can't help but feel that he probably cast himself as a 'good guy'. And although he does it well, with his producing credit stamped on this one it seems that he would have said 'this is my role'. I would have rather seen him in a more difficult 'bad guy' role like Fassbender's. 12
Years A Slave is a very powerful film and deserves all this awards hype, but I don't think it is better then Gravity. I have seen films like 12 Years A Slave before. Many films. Where Gravity is more original. But honestly I think that Prisoners was the best oscaresque film of last year and was appalled that it wasn't even nominated for best picture. Oh well. Go see 12 Years A Slave at cinemas if you can catch it, but don't worry if you don't. It'll be just as good on DVD. Dallas Buyers Club review coming up next!

Film fans have a very love-hate relationship with the Oscars. We love them, or at least put up with them, because they are a means of getting the general public to see more adventurous, unusual or sometimes challenging films, and they form the perfect icebreaker for film-related conversation. Likewise, we hate the Oscars for being a bad advert for the film industry, being out of touch, smugly self-satisfied, and usually getting it very, very wrong.

In this manner, Oscar buzz has to be handled the same way every year: acknowledged, but taken with a pinch of salt, in the knowledge that the best picture probably won't win Best Picture. This year, however, is different, because for once the Academy got it right. 12 Years a Slave is a truly transcendent piece of film-making which cements Steve McQueen's burgeoning reputation, and is perhaps the most deserved Best Picture win for a decade.

In the past, films which have explored the subject of American slavery have tended to be from the white man's point of view. Films like Amistad, Lincoln and Amazing Grace have noble intentions and often a lot of talent behind them, but they tend to view slavery as an issue that noble-minded, morally-upright white men must resolve, in opposition to less noble-minded, morally-upright white men. In doing so the people whose cause they claim to be championing are unduly and often unintentionally marginalised.

McQueen's film, by contrast, is told very much from from the slaves' point-of-view. It's very easy to put this down to his status as a Hollywood outsider: being a British director who started out as a visual artist, one could argue that he brings an objectivity to the subject that no American filmmaker could have done. As compelling as this argument may seem, however it does ignore both the transatlantic nature of the production and McQueen's own ancestry, which includes many victims of slavery.

More important than McQueen's background or status is his sensibility, which is key to the film's success. He has a recurring interest in dehumanisation or the abuse and degradation of the human body. Having handled starvation in Hunger, and sex addiction and attempted suicide in Shame, he now gives us the commodification of human beings into property, and the physical abuse given to slaves in the form of lashes, attempted hanging and rape. The film is deeply emotional but also disturbingly clinical, a very rare trick to have pulled off.

McQueen establishes this approach with the opening shots: a cold open on a sugar cane plantation in media res, and then a sex scene between two slaves which is the very definition of unsexy. We see our two participants in close-up, moving slowly against each other but with not a shred of joy or love on their faces. In doing this, McQueen shows how slavery strips people of their humanity, to the point where even the most sacred and joyous of acts have become empty and devoid of meaning. Like Naomi Watts' masturbation scene at the end of Mulholland Drive, sex has become the act of those who are hollow, desperate and defeated.

Much of 12 Years a Slave looks at the means by which people become institutionalised into slavery. The film goes to great lengths to show how hard it is to escape being a slave, with Solomon Northup being robbed of his identity and becoming little more than a portion of labour that can be bought, sold and mistreated at will. Much of the film is concerned with the brutality inflicted upon the slaves by their masters, and as in his previous work McQueen never pulls any punches.

Even by the standards of a generation raised on so-called 'torture porn', 12 Years a Slave is an incredibly brutal film. It's arguably the most violent mainstream film since The Passion of the Christ, the difference being that the violence doesn't drown out the deeper message, as it does in Mel Gibson's work. The characters are so well-written and sensitively portrayed that every violent act perpetrated against them carries great weight and brings the appropriate response of repulsion. The scene where Patsey is repeatedly whipped is one of the most flinch-inducing moments in modern cinema.

Scenes like this reflect the film's nuanced understanding of how the power relationships between masters and slaves are structured. It acknowledges that hard power in the form of whippings and rape were not enough to guarantee obedience; slaves were also institutionalised by adopting the customs of their masters. By behaving like their captors, and being rewarded for their obedience, their desire to rebel and escape is steadily eroded, much like the prisoners in The Shawshank Redemption.

This is played out in the film on at least three occasions. Firstly, we see Solomon play his violin at a dance for Mr. and Mrs. Epps: the joyful tunes he played as a free man are honed into the respectable, formal melodies of which they approve. Secondly, we see Shaw's plantations, where slaves are treated like country ladies, being plied with tea and cakes to make them accept their lot in life. And thirdly, in Patsey's whipping, where Epps invites Northup to beat his own kind, forcing him to embrace and appropriate the very form of violence that would be used against him.

The film is also very interested in the hypocrisy of religion. Christians were very prominent in the abolitionist movement later in the 19th century, and yet both Ebbs and the more moderate William Ford use scripture to justify their actions. Ford leads his slaves in services and prayers in his gardens, while Ebbs views an outbreak of cotton worm as a plague from God. Both men see slavery as their Biblically-sanctioned duty, something which in Ebbs' case extends to abusing them as well.

In lesser dramas, these characters would be painted in broad strokes as blind, deluded morons who should be ridiculed. But both McQueen's direction and John Ridley's fantastic screenplay constantly invite us to question things more deeply, and challenge our own beliefs in the process. Both Ford and Ebbs' behaviour are perversions of Christianity, neglecting Christ's teaching of compassion and forgiveness in favour of out-of-context Old Testament brutality. But we are still invited to view them as flawed men rather than dismiss them as madmen, no matter how easy that would seem.

12 Years a Slave is centrally a story of survival. It avoids falling into the trap that Schindler's List did, namely attempting to fashion a heroic story out of circumstances which didn't deserve it; in the words of Stanley Kubrick, "Schindler's List is about success. The Holocaust was about failure." Northup does very little that could be considered heroic: he doesn't liberate his fellow slaves or challenge the system to its core. He is very fortunate to survive, based upon the people he meets, and when he is swept off he is forced to leave Patsey behind.

On top of its thematic richness and brilliant storytelling, the film looks absolutely splendid Sean Bobbitt has collaborated with McQueen on both his previous films, as well as lending his eye to the underrated Byzantium. At times the plantations on which Northup works have a distinctly lyrical quality, reminiscent of the best work of Terence Malick. But as with Byzantium, there is plenty of room for harshness amongst the lavishness, and McQueen never lets the beautiful colours dominate proceedings or sanitise the violence.

The performances in 12 Years a Slave are very hard to fault. Chiwitel Ejiofor is amazing in the lead role, rivalling his performance in Dirty Pretty Things for its emotional depth and sensitivity. Newcomer Lupita Nyong'o thoroughly deserved her Oscar; she makes Patsey a complex, wounded lady who never fails to break our hearts. Michael Fassbender continues his winning streak with McQueen, turning in another powerhouse performance as Ebbs, and there is good support from Paul Dano and Benedict Cumberbatch, as John Tibeats and William Ford respectively.

12 Years A Slave is an utter masterpiece and a worthy winner of the Best Picture Oscar. It is a fantastic, mesmerising creation which is at turns a gruelling endurance test, a profound mental stimulant and a powerful emotional drama. McQueen's status as a great director of our time is assured, as is its status as an essential piece of filmmaking. It is, quite simply, astonishing, and a shoe-in for the best film of the year.

I've been underwhelmed at the cinematic output of the last year in general, and by no means is this a bad movie, but at no point did I feel like I was watching something that should be deserving of a Best Picture award. As someone who loves historical movies, I really wanted to like it, and I went into it assuming that I would. The acting was tremendous, particularly by Nyong'o and Fassbender, but the storytelling and direction of the plot in general was lacking for me. Instead of a fluid story line developing, it seemed more like it was a collection of scenes featuring the slaves being sadistically tortured that were jumbled together and then abruptly wrapped up as Brad Pitt inserted himself heroically [note: sarcasm] into the movie as a form of deus ex machina to save the day as the enlightened white guardian angel. You could take half of the scenes in the middle of the movie, arrange them in some randomized order, and it wouldn't feel that much different than what the final product turned out to be. Steve McQueen, the director, comes from a background in performance and video art, a field where performers typically seek to shock the public rather than try to put together a cohesive story or message, and I think that's exactly what the intent was here. At certain point it seems like you're watching a snuff film or what others have called "torture porn". There are great performance and great scenes, but instead of the movie being greater than the sum of its parts, it's vice versa in this case. The fact that slavery was a horrific blight in our country's history doesn't mean that a movie about it should be able to skate to a Best Picture Oscar on shock value alone.

I never thought that I would use a Tarantino movie as a source of moderation when it comes to gratuitous violence, but I found that to be the case with this movie. "12 Years..." was basically a bunch of horrible things happening and nothing really progressing or materializing until Brad Pitt comes in and saves the day at the very end. For a movie all about enduring hardship the ending seemed too easy. It's good, but not the momentous cultural masterpiece that it's being portrayed as.

There's an interesting argument to be made over, as Slate magazine called it, "The Hero Problem" in American cinema. As brilliantly crafted as McQueen's vision of Solomon Northrup's story is, there's a schism between what an audience can or cannot digest-- how far can you take things before they become too ugly to comprehend? How low is too low for our battered protagonist? These are difficult issues, and perhaps a Hollywood film can't ever illustrate the incomprehensible horrors of slavery-- but then again, how could anything? 

Regardless, I think McQueen tackles the issue as well as anyone could. He deftly approaches the morally corrosive nature of institutional racism (a problem America still struggles with in different forms) in a brutally frank manner that is still accessible. Ejiofor and Nyong'O are absolute standouts among the cast, and Fassbender is strong even though he gets a bit hammy at times. My biggest issue with the film was the sore miscasting of producer Brad Pitt in a small but crucial role. Pitt is a great actor, but he's totally out of place here (I really would have rather seen his casting reversed with Garret Dillahunt). 

All things considered, this is essential viewing.

I've never really been the biggest fan of Steve McQueen, but I'll never deny his ability as a film-maker.  Every single film he has made has been brilliantly produced and crafted, and 12 Years A Slave is no different.  

The true story of Solomon Northup is quite incredible when you think about it.  A free man who was tricked and kidnapped and then sold into slavery, separated from his wife and kids for 12 years.  It's hard to imagine stuff like that actually happened, but it did quite often.  I'd say the strongest quality of 12 Years A Slave is how accurately it portrays such a barbaric and inhumane period of history, especially that element of kidnap.  The scene where Solomon wakes up in a dark cell and finds himself in chains for the first time is a very claustrophobic sequence, and it only gets worse.  In fact the film is so gritty and realistic when it comes to portraying oppression that by the end I felt as though I needed to wash myself because I found it so skin crawling.  

Another great positive is how well the film is actually made.  The cinematography is beautiful throughout, the sound design is something I especially thought was done well, the dialogue sounds very authentic and every actor seemed to bring their A-Game.  Chiwetel Ejiofor is faultless in the lead role which makes me glad because he's an actor I've admired for a long time, and it seems he's finally getting to a point where he can show his ability.  Michael Fassbender steals the show for me though.  As always, he's amazing, and he really shows how good he is in 12 Years A Slave as he is asked to play a truly disgusting character and you're constantly praying he catches a well timed bullet to the head at some point.  You have to give credit to the director for all the great performances, however.  Steve McQueen definitely knows how to get his actors firing, and it's not surprising at all considering he makes films that are essentially character studies.  His films revolve around his actors, and even though he makes sure every other aspect of his films are just as strong, without those central performances everything else would be hollow.  

Despite all the praise I'm heaping onto it though, I can't give 12 Years A Slave more than 3.5 stars.  For me, a big part of the ratings I give to films depends on my own personal enjoyment when watching them, and while I can recognise how well the film is produced, it's not a film I particularly enjoyed watching.  There's only so much brutality, oppression and despair I can take, and there's almost 2 and a half hours of it in here.  Yes, I'm aware that the whole point of this story is to communicate those very things to the audience and to show the extensiveness of it all, but I have a limit.  I also didn't feel like the film took place over a 12 year timeline.  Nobody really visibly ages until the very end when Solomon returns to his family to find his children have grown up, other than that the film felt like it took place over 8 months or so, so I think the passage of time isn't something that's particularly well done.  Brad Pitt also has a small role that I didn't take to.  He's only in it for around 10 minutes or so, maybe less, and when big stars like him are cast in such small roles it acts as a bit of a jolt and takes me out of the film.  All I could think was, "Oh, there's Brad Pitt...and he has an awful beard.." and by the time I'd gotton over that he was long gone and the film started drawing to a close.  It's a minor personal inconvenience I'll admit, but I don't understand why they couldn't cast an unknown to play that role, the film wouldn't have suffered from it. 

Overall;  a harrowing depiction of slavery and the primitiveness of it all.  Top-notch production values and the actors turn in brilliant performances.  But it's not really an enjoyable experience and is definitely a one-time watch only.  It ends in a sudden fashion and I didn't feel as though the passage of time was represented as well as it should have been.

	'12 Years a Slave' is the unflinching depiction of American slavery that took home the Oscar for Best Picture this year, as well as numerous awards at other shows. It is, unquestionably, an important film: there is so much racism and denial still present in today's world that slavery demands to be understood and appreciated. But the film is so absolutely miserable and harsh, with no happiness or hope presented, that its horrors become like planes in open sky: they might as well be motionless.
	Many people will tell me that there was no happiness in this time, that this is accurate depiction: they may be close to correct. But what about 'Schindler's List'? A masterful depiction of humanity's darkest hour, made thoroughly watchable by hope that pulses all throughout it. A tragedy with a beautiful story at its centre, it shows us the worst of mankind, but never loses faith in mankind's ability to be great. It is uplifting and inspiring even as it is educational and harrowing.
	Or what about 'Grave of the Fireflies'? A gorgeously animated story of WWII in Japan, it remains one of the most devastating films ever made. Its simple, powerful images are impossible to cleanse from your memory afterward, and the relationships between the characters are authentic and affecting. It is because of the simplicity of a boy's love for his sister that the film is so destroying, so grounded in emotions we know and can appreciate. Inhumanity is best presented alongside humanity, and 'Grave of the Fireflies' understands this perfectly.
	In this sense, '12 Years a Slave' is a failure. It is a horrible watch: the terrible inhumanity in the story is not offset by any true development of character or positive theme. Those who suffered under American slavery, one of the worst genocides in the history of the planet, deserve to have their story told, and for this I applaud the film. But they also deserve to have their story understood, and no true understanding can come from a film that simply regales us with the harsh truth of slavery. Understanding must from mature contrasts, appreciation of the scope of human emotion, and tenderness, three things this film conspicuously lacks. I sincerely hope that someday soon there will be a film about slavery so emotional and affecting that we finally have some context for this darkest hour in our continent's history: until then, the planes will hang lifelessly, and '12 Years a Slave' will be the best that we have.

Steve McQueen, with his third directorial outing, crafts a powerful social commentary/biopic about slavery, a topic that's been covered through almost all mediums rigorously, but none is quite as commanding as "12 Years a Slave". 

Now, a quick glance at McQueen's filmography can make even the coldest person sigh a sigh of sorrow ("Hunger" or "Shame" anyone?). It's a no brainer that McQueen has delivered dismal films and quite honestly, "12 Years a Slave", which is based on a book named, you guessed it, "12 Years a Slave", is no different. You will be uncomfortable. You will squirm in your seat. You may or may not cry; I'm not judging the macho men out there. It's all a testament to McQueen's incredible expertise in concocting narratives with absurdly palpable emotion. The techniques don't feel cheap, overused, or a ploy to simply stir the audience's heartstrings. McQueen delivers an incredibly powerful narrative -- nothing more, nothing less.

Which is another reason to commend McQueen -- he solely leaves the narrative power to the actors and screenplay. I've always had issues with Chiwetel Ejiofor after his disappointing performance in "Children of Men" or "Four Brothers". But after seeing the quieter moments, as he stared off into space in despair, that's when I knew that this is his best performance to date. McQueen trusted Ejiofor. He was unafraid to leave the camera rolling as Ejiofor conjured up emotions of grief and hurt. And what more can I say about Michael Fassbender? Though I've got to admit that he couldn't quite hold up a Southern accent, he was captivating nonetheless. But the real power came from behind the camera -- Steve McQueen himself. He directed "12 Years a Slave" masterfully, orchestrating and juggling different emotions one after the other. As a result, the ending brought a tear to my eyes, a first for a movie, ever. Yes, I admit it. Don't hate.

A great achievement on many levels, 12 Years a Slave a stirring, emotional journey. Bolstered by a castful of powerful performances, what appears to be the journey of a single man becomes a reflection of society as a whole.

Based on a memoir written by its protagonist, 12 Years a Slave follows Solomon Northrup as he gets torn from his life as a free man and put into the brutal system of slavery in antebellum Louisiana. This straightforward plot allows for a deeper delving into of what characters and situations we have, a nice change from the globe-trotting blockbusters that are so prevalent nowadays.

Stylistically, the film is unblemished. A bright, unfiltered view of 1850's Louisiana adds to the realism. The brutality that was so common in that time is kept just out of the screen, with the camera glancing over, rather than lingering on it, leaving its results painfully up to our own interpretation. What does get shown onscreen is subtle. The little spurts of blood flew out from whippings, yielded a greater effect to me than the massive geysers of the stuff as seen in 300 and the like.

Most importantly, this tale about a single man and his struggles becomes an exploration of many sides of society. We see some of the slaves submitting to survive while others rise of in defiance. With the slave owners, more interesting dynamics occur. With Benedict Cumberbatch's Ford, we see a sympathetic and caring man who blinds himself to the inherent evil on which he stands. Epps, portrayed by the brilliant Michael Fassbender, gives us true, pure evil, who exploits anything and everything for his own, selfish gain. The contrast between our primary characters is also stark. Patsy is broken and on the verge of giving up, while Solomon refuses to forget what he had before. All of these characters create a fascinating collage of beliefs and mindsets that are still relevant today.

In the end, we get a unflinching look at the brutal world of slavery. It is a reminder of what people have been through and what people have triumphed over. But the most significant and heartbreaking part of this film is when it reminds us of how people are.
