Slavery is one of those territories that is blatantly tiptoed around and only ventured into by few, as if a vociferous outburst of indignant voices was expected. Film, too, deals with it rarely, dotting the map of cinema with several entries worth dwelling on, including Steven Spielberg's 'Amistad'. Quentin Tarantino ought to be sidelined despite his ferocious claim to be a trailblazer in the matter. The assumption behind this could be the inherent nature of violence, today exponentially inoculated with the help of entertaining, visually arresting imagery in a sad attempt to ensnare the attention. Slavery is inevitably tantamount to brutality imprevious to such methods, because its heart lies in the lurid abyss of the worst of what a human can be, which is a picture difficult to watch for anyone. The discomfort, however, may be a source of strength, depending on the director. Steve McQueen presents his take on slavery in '12 Years a Slave'.

Referred to by the director himself as the 'Pinocchio tale', the film leads a story of Solomon Northup - an educated, amiable and demure man who lives with his family in prosperity and happiness. It is only later when he is brutally stripped of his life and deprived of his name by merciless traders who sell him into slavery that the harmony abruptly ends for twelve years. The servitude to slave owners, from the meeker one being Ford, to the most savaged and twisted Edwin Epps, finds him as a watchful observer who strives to retain his dignity where there is a shortage of it. The struggle for survival ensues, despite the overbearing force of despair and despondency.

The film is pungent with a heavy, relentless surge of difficult images. Apart from the violence itself, the challenge of watching resides in the sheer shock of Solomon's experience, the well-known subject strikes as bare, acutely unknown and compelling. To defamiliarize slavery and unveil its sordid nature in order to restore it its harrowing sight seems like the greatest attainment of the film. As ghastly as the tale may be, the narrative unfurls in cruel, albeit calm and sedate tone, constantly forcing the viewer to plunge into the total lack of hope and tragedy. Such propensity to steep the viewer in this world owes a debt to the story itself that delivers a direct, realistic to the core experience. Criticism of its violence, therefore, seems ill-judged, especially once one views it as an intrinsic servant to credibility and justice done to the film's hard, but still requisite truth. Furthermore, there is a potent human element in the form of Solomon's inner perspective. His genuine good-heartedness and a well-rooted sense of right and wrong engage in a swirling dialogue with the brutality to produce a central emotional conscience - a rarity for a film today. His attentiveness, intense presence and restrained words remain a piece of silent storytelling that is unabashedly authentic and never strives to be turgid or pretend to be something it is not.

A powerful story deserves a talented cast, a case in which '12 Years a Slave' is no disappointment. The challenge and demands of the lead role require an intense performance that is rife with difficult issues to digest. There is not much to be said in terms of Chiwetel Ejiofor's role other than he delivers Solomon's portrait on screen with an effort, devotion and focus that induces admiration and deepest respect for his commitment. There is no doubt a role like this calls to invigorate all of an actor's capacities. His fellow actors do not lag behind in their equally steadfast performances, many of whom deserve a praise, including Lupita Nyong'o and Benedict Cumberbatch, but another Oscar-worthy work has been lauded as Michael Fassbender storms through the story with his seething with rage, repellent and vile Edwin Epps. All the characters sear deep into memory, simply because their creation is conjured not only by a unique story, but by a clear vision of the director.

Many may conjecture film media is a transmitter of a shadow of reality, a purported illusion of the tangible. The question arises whether its purpose is to elevate from the daily drudgery, produce pleasure, or heal. This picture aims to leave its spectator utterly spent, mentally wrought and emotionally drenched. The potency of such an experience corroborates what staggering an illusion it creates, or rather how deeply the world of the screen may weave itself tightly around the audience's collective mind. The reconstruction of a true story finds itself shattering this elusive wall of artificiality. The story is delivered, ripe with meaning. Steve McQueen's films are hallowed for such a meticulous, although painful study of the subjects he chooses, and his latest picture seems the most successful so far.

This year's Oscars were a curious test of courage for the academy to acknowledge the film's value. Thankfully, the outcome in the form of The Best Picture award was more than satisfactory. Still, even if this had not happened, no harm would have been done to '12 Years a Slave'. Suffice to say we now have a film that already joined the canon without the need for anybody's approval.

So, to be honest, this could work the same if we were watching a documentary. The fact that this is a historical film doesn't mean they couldn't have added real character and development. I would have much rather preferred a story a-la Philomena. It's interesting that the film is an adaptation of the book by Salomon himself. So why not make a film telling the story of him writing the book and remembering, this way making the tie between the audience and the characters a lot stronger. What we feel for Solomon we don't feel it because we care for him, we'd feel the exact same thing for any other human being the writers would've decided to put on screen. Take out ultra violent scenes and, let's be honest, the film is not that jaw dropping. It's the most common film ever. If we're talking slavery, The Butler or Django are way more INVENTIVE at least. That's what makes 12 Years a weak film, how unoriginal it is. The just literally took Solomon's story and adapted it to the screen. And really, please be honest with yourself, his story is not THAT heroic or touching or moving. I think Brad Pitt as producer had much more to do with it's acclaim than it's actual greatness. It's the typical Hollywood film previously digested for the audience. On the other hand, I can't help comparing this to it's biggest adversary on this year's Academy Awards, "Gravity". Built up as one of the most highly anticipated films of the year, 12 Years A Slave gives the audience powerful, remarkable and heart-wrenching story of a freed slave (Solomon Northup) from Upstate New York who is abducted and forced to endure the inexplicable horror that is slavery for 12 years. 

Although I probably would have preferred someone like, perhaps, Jamie Foxx or Cuba Gooding, Jr. to have played the lead role, but I guess Chiwetel Ejiofor did a good job, just I felt his character was just holding back something - holding back the raw pain and struggle seen in Lupita's performance. However, it's not a bad performance, just not the right style, I think, for this kind of picture.

As the film has already won Best Dramatic Picture at the Golden Globes, it's safe to see it'll probably win at the Oscars too for Best Picture. Despite American Hustle winning Best Musical/Comedic Picture, The Academy only rarely tends to route for a comedy as the best film of the year. 12 Years A Slave has everything an Oscar-winning movie has come to symbolise: a film based on either factual event or real person, cameos from renowned stars (Brad Pitt, Benedict Cumberbatch, Michael Fassbender, Alfre Woodard), quite long, and really makes you think how god damn luck your life is compared to the fierce hardships of America's black peoples all those years ago.

Needless to say the stunning performance by Lupita Nyong'o in her feature film debut was absolutely stunning and beautiful. I think the scene that does it for us is she demands just the basic right to be clean with a pathetic bar of soap as a reward for collecting more crop than any slave (man or woman) does each day. Even her character "Patsy's" eyes tell a story of pain that no amount of education, textbooks or words can bring to light - especially for white people. It's almost as if this isn't a picture, almost as if it's actually taking place at the time it's so powerful and remarkable. The harsh treatment of Lupita's character by the jealous master's wife speaks volume to the fact that not only man can be violent and physically abusive. The harsh, and almost unwatchable whipping scenes of Patsy by her fellow slave (Solomon Northop) was just brutal and left me face-palming and out of breath for a good few minutes. 

As I write this view the day after the Golden Globes in which I was surprised that Lupita did not win. Instead the award went to Jennifer Lawrence for her "cameo" performance in American Hustle. Don't get me wrong I love Jennifer in Silver Linings and Winter's Bone, but her performance in American Hustle is nothing more than an extended cameo and arguably the weakest (although it is convincing) performance in the whole picture. Anyway even though Lupita didn't win over the HFPA and maybe not the Academy (given their track record for snubbing many black nominees), she, undoubtedly, won over my heart in this story.

12 Years A Slave is arguably overblown, but inarguably strong on performances, especially Chiwetel Ejiofor. Apologies if I come off offensive, but once you've seen one film dealing with racism and slaves, you've seen them all. They all have different stories, sure, and this film tells a very solid one, but you also go into it knowing a lot of what to expect and half certain of how it's going to end. It may be called 12 Years A Slave, and the "12 years" sure adds an impact to the situation... being slaved for TWELVE years... but the 12 years in the film flip by fast... are you sure it wasn't 2 years? Not intended as a joke, just a very noticeable oddity, but of course this was based on actual memoirs and the film only has so much time to show "12 years". Anyhow, the film sticks out solely for the performances and it's disturbing, but fairly honest portrayal of the abuse of black slaves in the time period. One scene in particular which will not be spoken (you'll know it when you see it) hits you hard, and it does it well. 12 Years A Slave won't offer an insight on a time in the past you didn't already know about, but it does grab your attention and make you feel and care strongly for the injustices portrayed. It's the small moments and specific performances that make it ultimately memorable.

This is one of those films that will stick, with me at least, I don't know about anyone else, for a long, long, long time.  An absolutely incredible film that showcases slavery in about as unflinching and ugly a manner as is possible.  And, quite frankly, that's the way it should be done.  It should be done in a way that makes people uncomfortable and sick to their stomachs.  I think that's the only way to truly tell a story about slavery/racism.  Because, and this isn't something exclusive to this side of the world, even if some parts of the film are dramatized or modernized, that some people would like to forget their past.  And I believe that people shouldn't be allowed to forget their past.  I don't mean these people should be shamed every time someone gets a chance, I don't mean that at all.  We have no control over what happened in the past and we shouldn't be penalized for something we can't control.  What I mean is this idea that people have that nothing bad ever happened in the past.  We have to keep the horrible, ugly, and disgusting truth of slavery and racism alive in order for it to not become a reality again.  Those who don't know their history are doomed to repeat it, as cliched and corny as that sounds.  And the film tells this story in as realistic a manner as possible.  Of course, not everything is going to be as the film presented it, but it wouldn't surprise me if this is the most accurate portrayal of slavery out there.  It's disturbing and unflinching, but it's incredibly powerful stuff and an indictment on the people who did these horrible things to these people while using the bible to try to justify their actions.  Yea, I realize that Christianity also had its part in abolitionism, but it was also used, or at least the bible's scriptures, were used to justify horrific actions.  So yes, while Christianity had its positive effects on the end of slavery, it also had some very negative effects as well.  So the film focuses on that dichotomy of how could someone, who theoretically follows Jesus' teachings, also think it's ok to own people and treat them as your property.  The film doesn't focus on the positive effects Christianity had on ending slavery, because it's one man's story and the horrible things he faces while he's forced to be a slave, even if he was a free man, he had no way to prove it.  Chiwetel Ejiofor absolutely knocks it out of the park here with an absolutely incredible performance.  Quite frankly, I thought he should've won the Oscar of Matthew McConaughey.  It's not that I think he got robbed, it's just that I think Chiwetel delivered a more powerful performance than Matthew did.  Matthew still deserved to win, but Chiwetel deserved it just a little bit more.  Lupita Nyong'o is absolutely outstanding in this film, just tremendous.  She's got incredible presence and delivery for someone that has had very little film experience.  She's done this film, a short film, and a miniseries.  Yet, she stole the show here with her emotionally wrenching performance.  And she's part of one of the most disturbing scenes in recent memory as Solomon, forced by Epps, has to whip Patsey for going to a nearby plantation on her day off, or the day of Sabbath, in order to get some soap to clean herself with.  The scene itself is incredibly disturbing as, for the most part, you only see Solomon whipping her and you hear the sound of her screams.  Then, after Epps takes over for Solomon, the camera cuts to Patsey's back as Epps whips her a couple more times and it is absolutely sickening to see the damage.  It's quite the powerful image...especially when you know that this really did happen, and that outrages me.  Anyway, this is a tremendous film.  It's the type of film that should be required viewing.  Fabulous performances and an unflinchingly brutal look at slavery make this one of the best films of last year.

As for the rest, I didn't notice much substance worth retaining, the melodramatism ended up distracting and was counter-productive in the sense that it deprive this work of some power of persuasion. This dramatic language has been used and re-used many times in cinema, to the point where it has become insipid, now it is a glaring artificialism difficult to cover up if the work is not smartly done, the illusion that things flow naturally is to weak to prevail. In my opinion this movie would be more interesting if the sentimentalism and urge to shock weren't so "in your face", or rather, predictable and higher prevalence was given to an analytical perspective. I also think that the contrast between free man and slave could have been more accentuated, I was a bit surprised to see how fast one situation turned into another, I expected more development of the main character as a free man to have time to know him more deeply and emotionally relate, this would give more impact to the whole experience. Technically it's excellent and has great emotional impact which aids to the reflection about slavery more thoroughly, but looking at the cinematic merits, I see little beyond a competent but vulgar film with little appeal to re-watch after the first view... nothing new here. I think the greatest merit of "12 Years a Slave" is the emotional impact, which, according to each one's subjectivity, will dictate how accomplished or rewarding the overall experience is and whether or not this movie is elevated to something bigger than what it really is. I found the vulgarity of the cinematic paradigm to degrade the overall impact this movie made upon me. The most brutal scene in this movie (the poor girl is whipped to near-death) is what I'll retain in my memory for a longer time, I think it's a brilliantly made long shot and condenses the essence of this movie pretty well. There's some good acting, though I found the supporting performances from Benedict Cumberbatch (The Hobbit: The Desolation of Smaug), Paul Giamatti (Turbo), Paul Dano (Prisioners), Sarah Paulson (Mud), and particularly Michael Fassbender (Prometheus) more impressive than that of the lead by Chiwetel Ejiofor (Salt), the Oscar-winning supporting performance of Lupita Nyong'o, and the two underwhelming turns from Alfre Woodard ("True Blood") and Brad Pitt (World War Z).  It marches through all the tropes of a movie about slavery and racism, but makes sure to throw in there a few Biblical quotes that are out of context, just to go a step further in painting the whites as evil.  It's not a terribly engaging story beyond the white guy bad, black guy good.  Even though it tries to paint a few whites as tolerable, they're just the tokens. Oh, and the whole build up around Nyong'o's character is shortchanged entirely in the end.  Honestly, as despicable as he was, Fassbender's character was the most nuanced.  Pitt's was just laughable.  And now, my biggest complaint of the film - I love Hans Zimmer (The Lone Ranger), but his score for this movie felt like scattershot cabbaged from 'Sherlock Holmes'. Chronicle of Solomon Northup (Chiwetel Ejiofor), a free black man from New York who got kidnapped and dragged into slavery in 1841. Steve McQueen ("Hunger", "Shame") is a great director who has proven to be quite eclectic with only three films to credit (tackling hunger strikes, sex addiction and now slavery) and his collaborator in all three movies, the underrated Michael Fassbender gets probably the flashiest role of his career playing a classic villain as Northup's second master, plantation owner Edwin Epps, who is anal about how much cotton his slaves pick and has the hots for slave Patsy (Lupita N'yongo). Nyong'o is a tour-de-force in a relatively brief role (that is astoundingly her film debut) - while she starts off silently enduring the abuse of her master and the wrathful envy of his ruthless wife (Sarah Paulson in a solid villainous role), she gets to demonstrate a wide emotional range leading up to a key climactic scene where Epps orders Solomon to whip Patsy. That scene, in addition to one where Solomon is left hanging for nearly a day after getting into a fight with a carpenter (Paul Dano) while in possession of his first owner, the kind-hearted William Ford (Benedict Cumberbatch), is one of the movie's best two. The first scene is long and perfectly conveys the dreadful sense of time that Northup must have felt. Like the latter scene with Patsy, it puts us right there with him - you will feel the discomfort and the pain. Ejiofor is very strong and carries the movie well. His character is by no means an empathetic slave - he is a survivor who tries to make the best out of his situation and is keen on freeing himself at the right time. He manages to portray that strength and show weakness and vulnerability at the right moments. The only thing is that key supporting players tend to outshine him. This is definitely one of the best movies about slavery (but I wouldn't call it the "Schindler's List" of slave movies). Adapted to the screen by John Ridley from the 1853 memoir of the same name by Solomon Northup. Winner of 3 Oscars: Picture, Supporting Actress (Nyong'o) and Adapted Screenplay; Nominated for 6 Others: Director, Actor (Ejiofor), Supporting Actor (Fassbender), Costume Design, Editing, Production Design.

Dare I say the frontrunner for the most overrated film of 2013? All the rest from the Oscar pile hovered around the 4 star mark but this really did not meet expectation. Many may have rated this highly purely on its serious context. Perhaps there was a subconscious fear that if they did not publicly applaud it then it would be a sign of them trivialising the issue. On the contrary, I feel even more inclined to voice my disagreements with the film's direction since they had a very strong premise here to produce a epic but, in my opinion, failed. 

One of the biggest problems I encountered was the tempo and flow of the story. Scenes were short and skipped ahead to one shocking incident to another very quickly without any sufficient link to a developed story arc. There was no natural progression, no time to linger on the mental and physical anguish of the slaves after each event. If it wasn't for the title, I would never have realised the film's timeline spanned anywhere near twelve years. It resembled a play in many respects. Most scenes were close-ups on only two speakers, the language sounded like that of Shakespearean origin while the background and other characters often served as little more than props. This could be a personal preference but I did not find this approach effective and would much rather a Scorsese or 'The Godfather' style with extended scenes and in-depth character studies. Another remarkable element was the lack of character development. No real connections were established between the audience and any of the slaves (only knew the name of one other slave).  Even the main character could have done with some productive monologues to keep the audience up to date with his mental transition during captivity. Michael Fassbender proves the most engaging as the fierce plantation owner but he could be reasonably accused of hamming it up a touch. As depressing as they may have been in nature, this limited the emotion behind the more horrific scenes.  

The imagery is powerful and there are moments which will stay in viewers' memories for a while, the last whipping scene in particular. In spite of this, the director chose the wrong angle to adapt this book onto the big screen and consequently the '12 years a slave' was not done the justice it deserved.

Twelve Years a Slave is an adaptation of the 1853 memoir of the same name by Solomon Northup, a New-York state born free Negro who was kidnapped in Washington D.C. in 1841 and sold into slavery. He worked on plantations in the state of Louisiana for twelve years before his release.
It is depressing, sad, annoying, frustrating to watch what Solomon Northup (Chiwetel Ejiofor) went through his 12 years as a slave. A great performance by Chiwetel Ejiofor whose act of bewilderment, despair, anguish, trying to survive is just outstanding. There are moments when with no sound and little movement, he projects what hopelessness looks like. His 12 years of unthinkable abuse, backbreaking labour, fading dreams of happy family, desperateness to figure a way out to his freedom...every act moves us. The brutality, dehumanizing acts of the masters make it so tough to even look at the screen.

Ford (Benedict Cumberbatch) as a cotton plantation owner is shown as humane yet ineffectual who eventually sells Solomon to the vicious, drunken Epps (Michael Fassbender), another cotton plantation owner. Epps is ruthless. The screen timings with him in the frame are like an unbearable demonstration of misery in movement.

Another applauding performance has come from Patsey (Lupita Nyong'o) who is vocal about her grief, a young slave, victim of Epps' barbarous and insane ways. She is raped and beaten by Epps, who is also a cause of envy to Epps' wife who feels that Epps has an eye on her.

I was actually moved by lot many scenes in the movie. Mother's pleading not to separate her from her two children, still all three being sold to different masters creates a lump in the throat. Solomon strung up by the neck for a transgression and his toes are barely touching the dark plantation mud as he dangles, near-dead under the scorching sun. Another disturbing visual is merged with this i.e. children are playing in the background, other slaves are going ahead with their chores since they fear that if they would help Solomon, they would lose their lives. Patsey somehow manages to give him little water. The psyche of the slaves, their surrendering to the fate one side and the heartless brutality of the masters / overseers on another side are very well captured. The night Patsey comes to Platt (Solomon's identity as a slave), asking him to kill her is a scene of unbearable pain, particularly as Platt turns his back and Patsey sobs into the night. Male / female slaves with their bleeding back after being beaten up (almost to death) choked me. Solomon just wanting to rush with officials who came to free him (following Bass -Brad Pitt's) efforts, turning back to give a warm hug to Patsey is so overwhelming.    

It depicts the dark chapter of slavery in American History. It is beyond one's imagination the kind of suffering the slaves faced. A complete shame to humanity.

Steve McQueen as director is adept with his articulation. Though the title says that Solomon would be slave for 12 years, McQueen and John Riddley makes us feel that it could be forever. Sean Bobbit (Cinematographer) has given great aerial shots which are so effective in making us bewildered, disoriented, and a complete lost feel along with the protagonist.

12 Years a Slave isn't easy to watch since it not only unfolds the tragedy of Solomon in particular but it also depicts the tragedy of such countless souls who lost the biggest gift of mankind- the freedom.

The movie that won the best picture Oscar, did it deserve it? I am here to answer that question. I think it didn't deserve the award, before you start hating me, let me explain. For a human drama, I didn't care for any of the characters. I know they are based on real people; I just did not care for any of them. Different reviews say that this was more of an experience, about slavery in The Unites States of America. To be fair, there are many documentaries that show you how it was in this time frame. The reason I did not care for the main character, is because the movie does not give me a reason to care. The only reasons I found were; he has a family, he was free and now he's not. The last reason is used a lot in this movie. The main character is always crying out, yelling, I was a free man. This does not make me care more about him. The reason I didn't care for the supporting characters; the other characters weren't shown enough for me to care. This has nothing to do with the actors. The acting is great; they deserve their nominations and wins. The dialogue is great, it's very real, and it sounds nice. It makes it sound very sophisticated, and gives an emotional depth to the movie. It does look great, the cinematography is wonderful. It's directed great, despite me saying I didn't care for any of the characters; there are some very emotional scenes I got choked up in. The movie does show the brutality that the slaves went through. That's what this movie is trying to do, and it successfully does that. That's all this movie does, is show us what the slaves went through. Steve McQueen, the director, tries to add substance to something that doesn't have anything to show for. There were better movies in 2013, I did not think this should have won. Would I recommend this? Not really, not because I did not think it was as good as other people thought, but because it's not an easy watch. Most people might not want to see all the violence in this movie. If you want to see an Oscar movie, because you're a film buff, by all means go ahead. If you're not a film buff, it really is your choice if you want to sit through this.

It doesn't take long watching this film to see that Director Steve McQueen isn't going to pull punches on graphic language and brutal scenes telling this painful, but true story.  The audible gasps from the audience throughout the movie are proof that McQueen succeeded in capturing the injustice, inequality, human suffering, and death that remains the darkest chapter of our nation's past.
     
An educated northern black man is taken from his family and the free life he was living in pre-Civil War America, turning his world upside down. In a blink of an eye he's bought and sold to southern slave owners and renamed.  However unjust and misplaced his circumstances are, this new slave, Solomon Northup, must immediately struggle to survive while keeping faith that someday he'll return to his family and a freed life.
     
The brilliance of this Oscar-nominated 'Best Picture' (9 nominations overall) is the patience it takes to describe the cruel and savage treatment of slaves.  It clearly illustrates how a northern black man with his "freedom papers" and an education had a different life than one without in the South--who was left to be viewed as "property".  The film is an emotional, intense, and raw look at not only black men enslaved by powerful white slave owners, but also from the perspective of black women and children who were victims of the same human suffering and died.  Lastly, we catch a small glimpse of the differences between northern whites and slave owning southern whites that becomes a precursor to the Civil War years later.
     
'12 Years a Slave' is a profoundly solemn and shocking film that will make viewers uncomfortable and sad-and rightfully so.  A powerful film such as this one is as necessary to acknowledging our history's faults as it is to making a film touting America's success stories. To do anything less would allow all who suffered during those unbearable years to be trivialized or, worse, possibly forgotten.  This chapter of our nation's history is very difficult to watch and yet impossible to forget; both equally important to understanding our past and our present.  When we forget who we are and the missteps we've made, we're more likely to move backwards and repeat our mistakes.  This is a 'must-see' movie that will leave you wanting to make sure that never happens.
     
Grade: A

A star for the performances and another for the cinematography. Everything else about this film is a miserable experience. It is discouraging how lopsided the positive to negative review ratio is, creating monstrous hype that surely disappointed many expecting Roots 2.0 or at least a film that's half as good as Glory. Both of those are considerably better works that serve to better humanize slave characters while actually being entertaining.

In a pre-Civil War time, there were people who would abduct free black men who lived in the north and forced them into a life of slave labor in the south. The evil, evil south, half filled with raging, sadistic, one-dimensional cartoon villains, the other filled with white knights who sympathize with the plight of the slaves but usually do nothing about it. This may have been a true story and it sounds like an interesting one, but the entire focus of the movie was for the protagonist, Solomon Northup, to be miserable. Maybe the film just resonates with people who have an extreme sensitivity to white guilt, but I am completely bewildered that this is being called an "important" film. It's supposed to be entertaining, isn't it? Do you really need to see actors pretending to whip each other to reaffirm your belief that slavery is bad?

The film tends to linger on things for a very long time. Beatings, an almost hanging and the like, they just go on and on in an attempt to milk the feelings out of you. For me, for what could have been a great story, they focused on the wrong thing and made the plot extremely thin (man is captured, man is a slave, man is miserable, man is freed) and proceeded to pad it out. By the time you reach the end, you don't really get a sense that 12 years have passed. It feels more like 2 Hours A Slave. The resolution is all too quick and rushed to feel satisfying, giving me a sense of, "Oh, now it's over."

They really dropped the ball on how Solomon was written. While the audience is definitely made sympathetic to him, there is nothing else to the character. He's a father, a husband, extremely intelligent and prefers to keep his head down and bear it in order to survive, rather than rebel or take risks. But that's everything you'll ever know. Contrasted to the aforementioned villains and other characters, it only makes him seem more boring.

The villains are on the loopy, angry side, sometimes coming off as campy, as the actors chew into their roles like taffy. On the other hand, there are three white male/knight characters played by Benedict Cumberbatch, Brad Pitt and Garret Dillahunt, who seem more complex and rounded. They have palpable, conflicting feelings as they fraternize with Solomon. Each time you see them, you think, "Okay, here we go, this nice white guy's gonna save him finally, hurray!" It becomes a case of the protagonist becoming a passive object, a male damsel in distress who is completely helpless, while white men steal every scene to either physically and mentally subdue him or give the audience hope that rescue is a possibility.

A terse text epilogue sums up the more interesting story: there was a trial for the men responsible for his abduction. Why THAT wasn't filmed is a missed opportunity. I wanted to see Solomon as he readjusted to life as a free man. I wanted to see justice at the trial. I wanted to know more about the abduction operation, especially in order to see it being dismantled. But I suppose if all they wanted to show was how being a slave is terrible, they certainly succeeded in that regard. Too bad it's manipulative and obvious.

Directed by Steve McQueen (Hunger (2008) and Shame (2011)) and adapted from Solomon Northup's 1853 memoir by John Ridley (U Turn (1997), Three Kings (1999) and Red Tails (2012)). This is a harrowing and heavy-going look at slavery in the Deep South before it was abolished in America, sort of like the anti-Django Unchained, because this is REAL. However, it's so compelling and moving to watch. 1841, and free negro Solomon Northup (Chiwetel Ejiofor) lives and works in Saratoga Springs, New York. But he's tricked into going to Washington D.C. where he's imprisoned and sent into slavery where he's sold to plantation owner William Ford (Benedict Cumberbatch), and they manage to get on well, but after Solomon attacks's Ford's carpenter John Tibeats (Paul Dano), who in turn tries to Lynch him. But, Ford see's Tibeats off, and to protect Solomon, sends him to work with cotton plantation owner Edwin Epps (Michael Fassbender), who is brutal and very racist. Solomon tries to survive, but an encounter with Canadian Bass (Brad Pitt) might be his salvation. It makes you angry that stuff like this went on in the Deep South, but throughout the film, there's an everlasting glimmer of hope that our hero will escape from this hellish life and get home. McQueen gets the best from his cast, and it's not an easy film to watch, but it's a very thoughtful yet upsetting and painful history lesson.

If you are one who grew up in the United States and progressed through the american school system, than the institution of slavery and therefore 12 Years A Slave's plot-points should be very familiar.  Just about everything we learned in school has some screen time in Steve McQueen's adaptation of Solomon Northup's 1853 memoir; from picking cotton at whip's end and finding respite in song to the passive cruelty of the scorned plantation owner's wife, its all here.  But if you were to think it nothing more than a textbook on celluloid you would be mistaken. 

12 Years A Slave takes all these familiar teachings and infuses them with something even the best professors cannot, empathy.  Through the magnificent performances by 12 Years A Slaves' talented cast, the film cuts through the elements everyone expects from the picture to grasp something special.  It is not only through the film's horrific scenes of violence that we understand either, many times the camera just lingers on characters engaged in no work and sensing the phycological hell they endure from not knowing the location and health of their loved ones, or simply the anguish of knowing all is lost. 

Perhaps the greatest aspect of the picture might be the fact that 12 Years A Slave is very much it's own film.  With all the violence and psychological horror that was an everyday hurdle for slaves, the picture could very easily had evolved into another Schindler's List, and while the picture does indeed have it's share a graphic violence and psychological torment, when the credits roll, the impression the picture imparts feels less violent and more emotional than Spielberg's holocaust drama. 

12 Years A Slave ultimately uses it's relatively unique source material to lay bare the inhumanity of one the darkest chapters in american history.

Prior to 12 Years a Slave, Steve McQueen had already established himself as a powerful name in discomfort cinema. Where "Hunger" dealt with the desperation of IRA prisoners and "Shame" explored the outer limits of sex addiction, his new film comes about as close to a literal gut punch as you can get.

Among the most overt features of the film is the extent to which violence is portrayed. Gore has a firm place throughout, and the audience is often shown nauseatingly graphic depictions of whipping and beatings. One standout scene even manages to out-do Mel Gibsons "Passion of Christ" extended whipping scene by a substantial margin, and the pain of the recipient is almost palpable through the screen. While these moments are disgusting, they are often made made far worse by the context in which they're placed. Nudity is frequent, and often used with artistic skill to make us feel uneasy, especially given the backdrop. Music underscores the tone well, and Hans Zimmer once again provides a fitting soundtrack which is occasionally bolstered by clever audio design.

One of the most impressive things to note about the direction of the film was it's simplicity. The most harrowing scenes are the ones in which very little is going on. Elements, with no exceptions, are placed with intent and clear purpose. The result is that although scenes are often long, you would be hard pressed to find any excess or filler throughout the movie, something increasingly rare as directors cram more content into the same space.

As a result of the very simple camera work and framing, on top of the sheer length of many shots, 12 Years a Slave often feels quite voyeuristic, and you'll likely want to look away from the screen as McQueen stubbornly refuses to cut away from the abject suffering. It's a window into a real persons life and draining as it is, you'll feel compelled to continue watching purely for Solomon Northup's character. This is among Chiwetel Ejiofors few lead roles, and he is unnervingly convincing in every second he spends onscreen. The majority of its supporting cast, including Michael Fassbender, Paul Dano and Benedict Cumberbatch are similarly intelligent in their portrayal of distasteful, demeaning and frequently debasing characters. As expected, they all display extraordinary talent in conversation, but also do a surprising amount in silence. Facial expressions are often far more profound in meaning than any words exchanged, and Ejiofors in particular takes advantage of this to great effect.

Unfortunately, the movie is not without fault. Sarah Paulson plays Mary Epp with a harsh single toned menace which, while not totally out of place in the landscape of the film, is nevertheless severely outclassed by a group of simply better actors. Brad Pitts appearance also seemed like a misstep, as although in truth his acting was acceptable, the cameo was simply distracting for me, although if you can see past him being Brad Pitt in his scenes you may disagree. Frankly, just like in my Captain Phillips review, I also have to mention the blatant recycling of Zimmer's "Time" theme from "The Thin Red Line" and "Inception". Although this will be no issue for a casual movie goer, for fans of Zimmer's work recognising this riff several times throughout the movie will likely be distracting.

But these are minor quarrels which in truth you would have to be intensely pessimistic to hold against the film, especially when it does so much right. From the frightening violence to the electric acting, it's easy to run out of adjectives to describe the emotional rollercoaster which 12 Years a Slave invariably is, but it is a movie which you should subject yourself if for the acting alone.

It's hard to talk about a movie that shows us "what the true horrors of slavery was like" for a few reasons. Most importantly, no movie is going to be able to do such a thing. The horrors of America's shameful institution cannot be recreated or reenacted in its inhumane entirety. The second is that a goal of eloquently showing the true impact of slavery is hard to do on such a macro scale. Which is why director Steve McQueen chooses to instead show the terror inflicted on one individual specifically, Solomon Northup (Chiwetel Ejiofor).

Northup is an atypical hero for a slave-era story: he is educated, he is relatively affluent, and he is free. When he is taken from his family, kidnapped and transported to the deep south, he is thrown into a world that he is uncomfortable in. Beyond the obvious discomfort of his new shackles is the anxiety of having been stripped of his identity. Solomon is to be known as "Platt", he is encouraged to keep mum of his ability to read and write, and many hint that his talent with the violin could become his undoing. He is not just in a new environment; Solomon is a new person, and not one of his choosing.

12 Years a Slave is a dramatic look at race, but it stands contrary to many attempts by Hollywood to surgically extract your tears from their ducts (Lincoln, The Blind Side, Crash). Instead, McQueen is content to lay the matter before us in a calm manner, and let us decide our reactions. This becomes especially obvious during the most terrifying of moments throughout the film. First, a shop owner named Theophilus Freeman (Paul Giamatti) sells slaves with the playful exuberance you expect at your neighborhood Verizon store, hardly lending a thought to the horrors that lay ahead for his "merchandise." Next, a plantation overseer (Paul Dano) welcomes his new crew with a light rendition of a shocking ditty aimed to both crush the spirits of the new arriving slaves as well as to discourage their attempts at escape. Daily lashings on plantation owner Edwin Epps' (Michael Fassbender) land are carried out routinely after the cotton yield is counted, and these happen with little fanfare or mercy while the world marches on, refusing to notice the pain being inflicted. The most excrutiating attempt at calmly depicting the many horrors of plantations during this era has to be the long shot of Solomon strung up on a tree, toeing his way to saving his own life--McQueen and cinematographer Sean Bobbitt (often a crew-member of McQueen) create a sequence you won't soon forget.

Where 12 Years a Slave forces its seriousness onto the medium is the score. Many sequences were joined by an intimidating accompaniment, specifically in the most unnerving of moments; indeed the first time the music stands out is Solomon's trip on the slaving boat, which brings him to his horrifying destination. The score remains an important and smartly-used element of this powerful film.

Chiwetel Ejiofor's performance followed the blueprint set out by McQueen. He was forceful when necessary, and didn't exhaust his thespian background to a fault to try to reel in our empathy. Instead, the subtlety written (and performed) in his interactions with his surroundings bought our appreciation. His terror as he convinces his master that he had no intent to run away will make you hold your breath, and is a critical moment of brilliance by both Ejiofor and Fassbender.

McQueen's greatest triumph is to introduce a much exhausted topic in American culture, history classes, and cinema, and reinvigorate it with a fresh sense of realness and terror (to clarify, the topic of slavery is not exhausted, merely the dramatic recreation with the intent only to shame and not to learn from our past). Much can be said about his attempt to introduce a hierarchy within the ranks of slaves (those who were born slaves vs. those who were kidnapped like Solomon). But of course, this isn't a new concept. This is a step the director takes to be authentic to all aspects of this dark time in American history.

What results is a genuine, gut-wrenching, mesmerizingly exceptional look at an inhumane era.

Brilliant, intense, and profoundly indigestible. The tale of Solomon Northup, a free black man living with his family in the free North (New York), before being unexpectedly stripped of his freedom beginning his 12 torturous years as a slave, is an unforgettable one. This awe-striking movie tugs at the emotional fabric holding the audience together and challenges them over and over again with wave after wave of enough tear-jerking moments and graphic violence to fully engage each and every eye on screen for the duration of the film.

Bleak is the default tone throughout Steve McQueen's acclaimed (Academy Award - Best Picture) masterpiece 12 Years A Slave. Solomon Northup, portrayed by Chiwetel Ejiofor, is forced to endure the will-breaking horrors of slavery in the 1840's South after being drugged at a dinner which he was invited to under the pretense of being offered a job playing violin in the circus. As Solomon awakens from the night before, he finds himself chained signaling the beginning of the calamitous journey that will forever leave both Northup and the audience changed.

More misfortune would befall Northup after his improbable journey lands him in the clutches of one of the south's most barbarous slave owners in Master Epps, portrayed by Academy Award nominee Michael Fassbender. An unfortunate sequence of events thrusts Northup into the arduous challenges of surviving the South's most wicked slave owner in Fassbender. Northup's ability to endure the harshest of will-breaking conditions for twelve agonizing years, is what takes him from free man, to slave, to hero. The metamorphosis that Solomon experiences is one that the audience will not soon forget.

This movie is as real of a depiction of the master and slave dynamic as there has been in cinematography. With a film that centers itself around a plot with this much pain and suffering attached to it, it would have been impossible for McQueen to depict the dehumanizing nature and woeful strife of the slave era's violent past, without authenticating those times down to the bloody detail. McQueen embraces this challenge for 134-minutes while catching the subtle nuances that underscore the master and slave dynamic. Fassbender's wickedness garnered well-deserved Academy Award buzz, while costars Academy Award nominee Chiwetel Ejiofur and Academy Award winner Lupita Nyong'o also breathed believable life into McQueen's characters.

Steve McQueen's 12 Years A Slave, simply put, is the the best slave movie ever made. I do not want to categorize this project, as I think it deserves praise beyond its 'slave movie' designation; however the movie itself serves as a 134-minute fictitious snap shot of what slaves had to endure during a very dark time in American history, and this movie's importance will be immortalized thanks to McQueen's brilliance. While hard to digest at times, 12 Years A Slave earned every bit of gaudy 96% critic rating on Rotten Tomatoes and the veneration from the Academy bestowed was well deserved for this graphic masterpiece.

The 2013 Oscar race was a tight race. A very, very tight race. My personal favorite to win was Gravity, and American Hustle was deep in the talks for a shot to beat out all the other films. To be honest, though, there was always one thought out clear front runner in the race: 12 Years A Slave. Throughout the Best Picture race, 12 Years A Slave was always thought to take the win. Gravity, maybe, could beat it out, but it was still pretty far behind. 12 Years A Slave's profound message is clear simply through the title itself, and a movie hasn't been this powerful since Schindler's List. It was obvious it would sin the Best Picture, even with Lupita N'yongo grounded to win her Oscar and Steve McQueen and Chiwetel Ejiofor  the frontrunners at one point in their categories. So clearly, 12 Years A Slave was big and won Best Picture at the Oscars. Now, it's time to understand if it was deserved of Best Picture or not. It definitely was. 

  12 Years A Slave was a 2013 drama film directed by Steve McQueen and written by John Ridley based on the book of the same name written by Solomon Northrup. It stars Chiwetel Ejiofor, Lupita N'yongo, Michael Fassbender, Bryan Batt, Brad Pitt, and many more. Steve McQueen's direction is what made the film strong and hard to watch. It's also what made it the best movie of 2013 according to many critics. His direction was unique, excellent to watch and used a beautiful score and great cinematography. In total, his direction was great and he perfectly portrayed this story like no other.

  The acting was also very good in the movie. Chiwetel Ejiofor was a bit off as Solomon Northrup, looking as if he conveyed only one emotion throughout and nothing else. I wish his character could convey more diversity in emotion, but other than that it was a real good performance. Michael Fassbender was my favorite in the movie, for he played a ruthless villain like no other. He was intimidating, hateful, and pure evil. He was amazing in his performance, and every emotion he conveyed was spot on. In my opinion, it was the best performance of 2013. Lupita N'yongo also gave a stellar performance, being a very broken slave who is heavily abused by Michael Fassbender. The best female performance of 2013 as well, I definitely thought she deserved the Oscar over Jennifer Lawrence. All the other actors did great in the film, and in total, I thought it was one of the best acting ensembles I've seen in a while.

  The writing by John Ridley was also very good. It perfectly portrayed the horror of America's darkest time, and he wrote Solomon Northrup's life without any holding back. I felt the only problem with the film though was the utter lack of humor. I wish at least one piece of dialogue in this movie was funny, at least adding a bit of lightheartedness. The problem was, the darkness throughout the film got a bit annoying, rather than horrifying to watch each time. Other than that, though, Ridley adapts a great film and provides for one of the greatest stories of the past decade.

 12 Years A Slave in the end is a masterful film. Only Chiwetel Ejiofor's lack of emotions but sadness and the utter devoid of any lightheartedness in the film. The acting though was great from everyone and the direction from Steve McQueen stellar. The writing completely carried a lot of the film, and helped viewers understand the horror and pain in this time of America. In total, 12 Years A Slave is brilliant and a great film, and the best film about America's darkest time in history. And it deserved so much more then Best Picture. 9/10.

12 Years a Slave is a 2013 historical drama film and an adaptation of the 1853 slave narrative memoir Twelve Years a Slave by Solomon Northup, a New York State-born free African-American man who was kidnapped in Washington, D.C., in 1841 and sold into slavery. 

Chiwetel Ejiofor gives us one of his finest jaw-dropping performances by taking on the helm as the lead actor while Director Steve McQueen (III)  (Shame, Hunger) directs the movie with a Brilliant Cast consisting of Brad Pitt, Paul Giamatti, Sarah Paulson, Michael Fassbender and Lupita Nyong'o. While the movie can be slow at times - the storyline, the cinematic script and the unpredictable editing give this movie its true flavor. One day, two men offer him a job in Washington D.C., Northup agrees but once they arrive the two men drug him and he wakes up in a slave pen about to be sold into slavery. The film follows Northup in his 12 years as a slave with different kinds of masters and bearing all kinds of atrocities but never losing hope to see again his family. 
With such a delicate and strong premise, this film needed a strong script, directing and performances in order to succeed as an artistic picture and fortunately has them. But not only this film has amazing acting, it counts with a bold direction by Steve McQueen which give us long and hard to watch punishment sequences, striking visuals and the real misery the slaves endure enhance by the phenomenal acting; it has an amazing adapted screenplay that does the source material the justice it deserves, the story, most likely, gets some sentiments from the audience without using cheap ways to get some tears out of you, beautiful locations and a well done pre Civil War atmosphere.
A deserved winner of the Academy Award for Best Picture, a film that will hook you and will make you cheer and/or cry by the time the credits roll thanks to its direction, script and spectacular performances but is not a comfortable experience. However, come Osar time, the film that reigned supreme earning the coveted Best Picture award was 12 Years a Slave. A film that originally appeared to me as another political tear fest of seeing how black slaves were oppressed and feeling bad about being white (don't get me wrong, I have nothing against black people but sick of the politics behind it all) actually has a deeper meaning here when you see the brutal torment of our main character, Solomon Northup, in particular that pulls the movie through as something to emulate as deserving of it's nomination and later victory in Academy Awards.
The film takes place in what is assumed to be the Antebellum South where Negro salves pick cotton and perform other grueling outdoor tasks for their white masters. Our main character is thrown into the mix while trying to prove he is free and getting no sympathy in return, being whipped and worked to death, told not to escape lest his life be not spared, and even being forced to whip a young Negro girl much to his heartbreak and dismay.
The emotions are crystal clear and the film totally engulfs itself in the experience of slaves at the time. If you are weak at heart, or any other weak constitutions, I suggest you skip this one. This is the uncensored abuse in full bloom, constant whippings, hot sun, grueling work, bitter cruelty, the whole nine yards. You feel the pain watching this movie, and I think that's the heart of this film. Which like I said works to it's advantage, but I do wish they focused more on the narrative. The first hour or so focuses on merely the experience of the slaves. They work, they sing (very nice singing), they have families, they feel weary and hopeless yet committed. And while that's intriguing, I got more invested in every scene that showed Solomon's struggle. He wasn't supposed to be one of "them", an aspect to this brutal story that would have made this film stellar to me if it was brought out more. He gets his redemption at the end, he has conversations about it, but everything else is drawn out around him that it's fighting for room. Another nitpick I have is the titles on screen that tell of the setting of the movie and what became of Mr. Northup after he was finally freed. The font was incredibly small, and illegible without a magnifying glass. Maybe it's just me, but that was really distracting. Fundamentally, this is a good movie, even if it's not your favorite movie of the past year. It's emotionally resonant and tones down it's agenda enough to grab a broader scope than perhaps originally intended.

A truly great movie is one that stays with you long after it is ended.

A truly great movie is one that stays with you long after it is ended. The emotions and story unshakable; hours, days, weeks and 12 Years A Slave is such a film. From the moment the film opened on the first scene I was racked with anxiety. Not having read any reviews for 12 Years A Slave, I only knew it was fearlessly honest about the story of a free man from the North, kidnapped and sold into slavery in Louisiana.

Such clear purpose and vision could only produce a story of unwavering fortitude such as this. Steve McQueen, the director, is an artist and true visionary for his unflinching portrayal of Mr. Solomon Northup's story and the unending brutalities and injustices encountered by those in slavery. The knot that persisted in my stomach from start to finish is a direct result of his firm ability to never look away. I felt compelled to honor those who had endured such unspeakable horrors that were once their life by watching and also not looking away, likely Mr. McQueen's goal. From the moment Mr. Northup is sold, as Platt, you hopelessly seek out for some person to be a refuge as he fights to survive. The story is beautifully told, never allowing you to fully become immersed in the slave's life, never truly forgetting the freedom that was once had - with the use of flashbacks and remarks reminiscent of a previous life. No scene is wasted, no filler, no false emotions spurred from music, just the hard truth of one man's life. The saddest truth is Mr. Northup's story is unremarkable in comparison to thousands of other men, women and children forced and born into slavery.

Every actor deserves not just a nomination, but an award, to honor their brave and ultimately successful choice to take on such an insurmountable task of each role. Chiwetel Ejiofor, Michael Fassbender, Lupita Nyong'o, Sarah Paulson, Benedict Cumberbatch, Paul Dano, Adepero Oduye and the countless actors who I failed to list or those who played minor roles were impeccable and steadfast and a direct contributor to the movie's achievement.

If you are emotionally mature enough to endure such a dramatic, honest and truthful story then I implore you to set apart a day and watch 12 Years A Slave. A day is necessary to allow yourself to process such a magnificent film that is truly in a class of its own surpassing all other films released this year.

I do understand if you do not, as the movie was incredibly difficult to watch.

A horror movie in all respects -- except for the usual overt trappings of the genre.  For example, instead of creepy music, we get the dramatic cues of the typical Oscar-winning drama.  This was really the only drawback for me. Director Steve McQueen already displays the terrible realities of slavery: the brutal physical torture (hard labour but also whippings, sexual assault, and lynchings) and the chilling psychological torture (being separated from family, not knowing whether to vie for positive treatment from the master and be judged for doing so by other slaves, the constant wish to take risks to escape). But if he'd treated this like Roger Corman did his Edgar Allen Poe adaptations, it could have been even more effective - although I'll admit it probably wouldn't have won the Oscar. Chiwetel Ejiofor is outstanding as the free Black man who is kidnapped and sold into slavery (with Benedict Cumberbatch as the kind but cowardly master who allows evil to happen anyway and Michael Fassbender as the just plain evil master). With McQueen's help, Ejiofor does show us the terror of the man in this predicament (amid the nicely rendered pre-Civil war environs), allowing us to imagine how we would feel and what we would do. The rest of the cast are excellent in support (including Alfre Woodard in a bit part and Lupita Nyong'o in a large but thankless one, deservedly winning an Oscar).  Still, cranking it up even further with the trappings of the horror film could have pushed this to the maximum confrontational level it deserves; it remains a humanistic classic nevertheless.

(2013) 12 Years A Slave
HISTORICAL DRAMA

 Although there were many films made about the how African Americans used to be treated when slavery was condoned, I don't ever recall seeing a film that was ever based on a real life person before, since movies like "Roots", "Sounder" and "Uncle Tom's Cabin" as well as other films about 'slavery' were classified as novels with some of it based on fact and fiction.   "12 Years A Slave" is probably one of the most accurate portrayals of slavery ever put on film solely because it's from the experiences by an actual person.   While we all know that slavery actually happened, and that we've always read about it, we had barely saw it happen to an actual person before, for much of it's history is only classified as allegedly circumstantial.   Which is the reason why it's the damning crux when it's possible historical events can be altered so that people who inflict these types of crimes can never be charged or held accountable for their actions- American law has always been unjust since it often doesn't favor toward minorities.  Adapted by a book "Twelve Years A Slave" written by Solomon Northup, directed by Steve McQueen who was synonymous for directing, "Hunger", it'd make sense that he'd be the one to be directing this film- he knows what pain feels like from the receiving end.        

At the opening, and at this point, Solomon Northup, played memorable by Chiwetel Ejiofor has already been captured and sold as a slave, but as he's already in chains lying down in a cargo ship, he's already revaluating how it all came about since he was initially supposed to be a professional violinist in Washington.  And for some reason we're seeing him in chains treated less than human as all the others who're not white.  Solomon is not like other African American slaves because he has already received the education he needed as opposed to his counterparts. For if anybody didn't know by now, it was 'once' forbidden for African Americans to receive the same opportunities as their white counterparts.  Which is why how some can see the irony whenever we see many African American children 'not' exploiting the education system, and instead chose a life of crime instead.  It is the character portrayed in this film as well as many others, many are not being recognized for the sacrifice they had to endure to get to this point- the right to vote as well as an education.   As soon as Solomon realizes that it's against the law for African Americans to be "learning" he makes some attempts to free himself by doing just that.  It's quite an unbelievable journey as he's moved from one plantation to the next.   Solomon does get his revenge by writing about this which if the opportunity was available, other people would have done the exact same thing, as a viewer I'm grateful that he did just that. In order to let the dust settle, I waited awhile to see this movie. As with all movies of this nature, 12 Years A Slave walked out to universal acclaim and ridiculously high ratings everywhere. I am pretty wary of this phenomenon. Just because a movie hits at a minority abuse point doesn't make it cinema gold. Films exist on a continuum and premises don't guarantee anything. That being said, 12 Years A Slave was an excellent movie. The acting was stellar and most importantly, no punches were pulled in the depiction of slavery. The scenarios are brutal and raw, really cutting to the core of the viewer. Ejiofor is fantastic, although those of us who are Serenity fans already knew this. Fassbender also offers up a top notch performance. The fact that this story is true just adds more weight to the movie. However, there are items that severely limit the longevity of this movie in cinematic history. Although Ejiofor and Fassbender are excellent, the performance from Nyongo'o was pretty mute, a surprising point considering her runaway Supporting Actress win. Pitt is pretty much in the movie just for awards appeal as well, an all too common occurrence that I find distasteful. I think the biggest thing that keeps this movie firmly at an 80% for me is how safe it played the game. As a whole, white and black people were fairly dichotomous in nature. One group didn't have feelings, the other did. There was a bit of talk about the psychological process of whipping slaves, but it isn't really fleshed out much and we don't get to see anyone grappling with it's effects. Cumberbatch, who offered an interesting paradox early in the film, exits quickly, which is a real shame. Pitt appears mostly as an Ex Machina figure, offering minimal depth behind his single major monologue. In conclusion, 12 Years A Slave does everything right, creating a film that is powerful, moving and right on target with current events. Unfortunately, it isn't a film that transcends itself, choosing instead to be content with ruffling no feathers and taking no risks. And what a shame that is.

Steve McQueen was teetering on the brink of a cinematic breakthrough for years. Hunger was eye-opening, Shame was more than eye-opening, but it's 12 Years a Slave that finally and rightfully thrust him into the spotlight. An adaptation of Solomon Northup's memoirs, 12 Years a Slave is the shocking story of his 12 years as a slave after he is captured from his life as a respected free black man in New York. With a broad stroke of his artistic and visceral paintbrush, McQueen brings his best technical tricks to create the perfect atmosphere for John Ridley's character-based screenplay; extended facial close ups and long stagnate camera shots give 12 Years a Slave a level of artistic quality that has never been seen in a tale of American slavery. The violence is hard to stomach, but it's necessary violence that never crosses the line to exploitative, so please don't be deterred from one of the most remarkable and resounding films ever. McQueen has created something truly remarkable here; essential cinema.

12 Years A Slave is a very compelling, albeit hard to watch, movie about a free black man kidnapped and sold into Slavery in the mid 1800's.  It's a fine film, with many things to love about it.  However, it's not a perfect movie either.  The movie takes its time developing its true intention and spends a lot of time just showing us the hardships of being a slave (as if we weren't aware).  But my biggest problem with Steve McQueen's film is the overall lack of style.  For the most part it is simply filmed and simply lit, and focuses on the actors over the rest.  It's disappointing in that sense.  However, the story is captivating and the acting at times is superb, I will grant it that.

12 Years features the talents of a wide range of actors including Brad Pitt, Paul Giamatti, Benedict Cumberbatch, Paul Dano, Sarah Paulson, and the films lead Chiwetel Ejiofor.  But the films true stars are Michael Fassbender and Lupita Nyong'o.  The chemistry between the two was unmistakable however it's not the kind I'm sure you're imagining.  Fassbender plays Edwin Epps who uses Lupita's character Patsey as his personal play toy but his wife Mistress Epps (Paulson) isn't unaware of her husbands infidelity and takes out her rage quite violently on Patsey.  The resulting scenes are traumatic, especially a rather graphic whipping session that nearly kills her.  Fassbender is a scary presence in the movie and he steels many scenes from the other actors who seem to struggle to keep up with him.  Chiwetel Ejiofor seems to be the talk of the town lately for his portrayal of Solomon Northup, the man who the movie is based on.  He is fantastic, but I don't know that he ever went above and beyond as some of the others did.  Not to discredit him, he was amazing.  But it was just another aspect of the movie that left me underwhelmed.

So being underwhelmed by the acting, filming, and lighting you may wonder what I did like about it?  I will tell you that the writing is wonderful and Hans Zimmer's score is excellent.  The filmmakers achieved the telling of this story but just did it very straight forward.  I can understand it, but for me it wasn't enough.  There are very daring films made about slavery and oppression that push the creative boundaries further and further but 12 Years instead goes for comfort over taking risks and settles for a look and feel that doesn't suit what's happening in the story.  What does end up happening is the majority of the movie winds up being kinda stale and many scenes I found dragged and left my mind wandering.

I'm realizing as I'm writing this that I have more problems than good things to say about the movie, but I want to emphasize that I didn't hate it.  I simply expected more.  When movies get the kind of hype as this one did it can destroy the experience of it as we all know.  I like to think I'm not effected by that, but who knows?  The movie is good, not great.  It's well written, well enough acted, and has a beautiful score.  The editing could have trimmed a bit, and the cinematography could have made better use of the sets and locations.  But there is still a good enough movie here for me to suggest it.  The fact that things like this happened in our not so distant past is haunting and the stories deserve to be told so I'm glad 12 Years was made despite the problems I had with it.

Steve McQueen, a black Brit, does a splendid job retelling the cruelest, and perhaps the most troubling period in American history. The contentious subject alone makes it a necessary Oscar contender. A lot of slack available here. Regardless of the style, if the issue is treated with respect it will get respect. Anytime the movie lulls, the audience will inevitably meditate on history's horrible transgressions. Still, people don't go to the cinema to be shamed or reminded of past horrors. So stylizing the movie with foreign objectivity prevents it from getting weepy or sentimental. The complexion and complexness of the story is elevated by plantation owner Edwin Apps' (Michael Fassbender's) justifications. Slavery was legal. Period. Morality is not an issue. Don't blame him, blame the law. Just the way it's still apparently legal to kill Blacks in Florida with its disturbingly primitive Stand Your Ground law. The complexity in 12YAS is supplemented by Fassbender's overall bizarre, eccentric and exceptional behaviour. He even works the fields himself. His transgressions are further justified by deflecting much of the blame on his jealous wife, another marginalized figure. Subjugation is relative and hierarchal. The issue of slavery is even further complicated by abolitionist Bass (Brad Pitt) who, intentionally or not, comes off as a liberal putz. 

It's a bold and powerful film all right, due largely to the subject at hand, if not McQueen's aloof presentation. The film gives us a formal study of callous persecution. It's framed with a stoic examination of impartiality intercut with readymade emotional content. McQueen at once immerses and detaches us from the human suffering constituted by American slavery. Notice how long he manages to linger on the hanging scene by shooting it at a distance. Lupita Nyong'o is nominated for an Oscar because her character suffers deeply. Her acting was heightened by basic editing techniques. Leave out the whipping scene or simply remove the shot of the deep, bloodied tracks lashed on her back, and she probably wouldn't be in the running. Similarly, the subject of slavery is so vexing and all-consuming that Chiwetel Ejiofor can play Solomon Northup entirely with detached resignation.

While there have been many films that focused on the period immediately preceding the Civil War and the abolishment of slavery, few have specifically followed the life of a single person during this time. And, even fewer have told the story of a free black man who was then captured and enslaved. This is exactly what happened in Steve McQueen's '12 Years a Slave,' the Academy Award-winning landmark picture.

The life story of Solomon Northup is quite amazing, as seen in 'Slave.' Played by Chiwetel Ejiofor, the main star of the film shows a lot of conviction and perseverance, never letting his experiences get to him, and always trying to survive so that he can eventually get back to his family in New York. Along the 12 years he spends as a slave, Northup comes across a variety of characters, from conflicted slave owners like Ford (Benedict Cumberbatch) and greedy slave dealers like Freeman (Paul Giamatti). And then there are those who are pure evil, like plantation master Edwin Epps (Michael Fassbender) and his wife (played by Sarah Paulson). These antagonists underscore the terrible nature and attitudes of slave owners during this time, and their treatment of human beings like Northup is painfully demonstrated in 'Slave.' One of the most powerful relationships in the film is the one between Northup and fellow slave Patsey - a role that earned Lupita Nyong'o an Oscar for best supporting actress. The pain and sadness that surrounds Patsey tries to bring everyone down around her, including Northup, but he is able to overcome these challenges. And then, of course, Brad Pitt has a small yet important role in the film, as a traveling northerner who has a seriously crucial conversation with Northup late in his time as a slave.

As a film, 'Slave' runs a little too long, but that's understandable considering it needs to cover a span of 12 years. There are few scenes that feel like they are out of place, and some that are pretty difficult to watch, but make sense in context of the larger story. In this sense, McQueen does not sugarcoat anything here, which likely adds to the overall credibility and prestige of 'Slave.' In the end, '12 Years a Slave' is a story about redemption, forgiveness and committment, and it will be remembered as an unsettling yet powerful film for years to come.

A harrowingly candid look at the pre-Civil war south, 12 Years a Slave is a profoundly evocative piece that meticulously depicts the brutal evils of slavery. English director Steve McQueen eloquently does justice to the source material of Solomon Northup's 1853 memoirs and his shrewd accounts of American's most vicious chapter. 

Hoodwinked by two hustlers into leaving his New York home for a short term violinist job, middle-class Solomon Northup (Chiwetel Ejiofor) is drugged and his paper proof of his free man status are stolen. Chained in a dank cellar and pleas for proper identification denied, his captors brand him a Georgia runaway, and proceed with the demeaning indignities that title entails. 

Sold into slavery and transported to Louisiana, Solomon begins a life of basic survival. Unable to disclose the truth of his education or literacy without risking further persecution, Northup steels himself by assuming the imposed slave name of Platt and endures his hardship by forging genuine human connections.

The screenplay is skimmed down to Northup's experiences on two plantations; the first with a marginally kindly owner William Ford (Benedict Cumberbatch), who admires his innovations and recognises his musical talents, protecting him from the ire of a venal overseer (Paul Dano). 

The second (accounting for over a decade of his enslavement) under volatile wrath of a particularly vicious drunkard, Edwin Epps (Michael Fassbender). "Distinguished for his faculty of subduing the spirit of the slave" whose attention frequently and unwarrantedly wanders to an industrious young worker Patsey (Lupita Nyong'o), enraged his sadistic jealous wife (Sarah Paulson) regularly. 

While fellow slaves weep inconsolably or beg for the strength to commit suicide, Northup never gives in to hopelessness and is resolute that no matter how long it takes he will to return to his wife and children.

A story of racism lived and survived, McQueen mesmerizingly plunges viewers into disturbingly vivid subject matter of state-sanctioned degradation with some graphically bold filmmaking choices. One scene that is particularly penetrating sees Northup dangling from a noose, one foot desperately scraping the ground as fellow slaves fain indifference and continue to work around him as noon becomes nigh.

A character who is both an observer and participant in his own nightmare, Northup's complexities where masterfully expressed through Ejiofor, a dignified presence that is bound for Oscar contention while Nyong'o is a remarkable newcomer. 

There are some minor directorial miscalculations, including the somewhat jarring casting casting of Brad Pitt and Dano as well as the somewhat artifice opposing stylisation of Northup's two lives above and below the Mason-Dixon but in the scheme, these are easily overlooked.

The Verdict: Claimed by some that with its marginally British cast and crew to not to be "American" enough, something about this movies takes you into Northup's cotton-picking hell, making you recoil at each movement of the cane whilst reminding us that behind one person's tale there are millions more untold that deserve the same treatment; an artful truth American directors are oft too close to capture without overt sentimentality.
